sources.note: Influential modern interpretation of land grants as state formation, not simple charity.

sources.citation: Reported Vikramaditya I inscription from Davangere / Madapura Lake, 2025
sources.note: Recent field find illustrating continuing discoveries in Chalukya administrative epigraphy.

episodes.notes: Chalukya copper plates document land grants with seals, boundaries, donees, taxes, immunities and commands to future officials, making them a practical archive of Deccan governance. Recent scholarship interprets such grants as instruments that linked royal courts to villages, Brahmin settlements and local elites; new inscription finds continue to refine the map. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim the Chalukyas invented copper-plate grants; do NOT present these charters as equal rights for all villagers, since they privileged temples, Brahmins and officials; do NOT confuse this with the Chola village-election story.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Copper, Roads and World Trade

episodes.title: Stone Speaks at the Qutb Complex
episodes.era: Qutb Complex building phases, c. 1193-1368 CE
episodes.region: Mehrauli, Delhi
episodes.logline: Across 170 years, masons, calligraphers and sultans turn reused columns, true arches, domes and repairs into the first great archive of Sultanate stone.
episodes.moral: Monuments remember collaboration as well as conquest.

sources.citation: Qutb Complex inscriptions of Aibak, Iltutmish, Alauddin Khalji and Firuz Shah Tughlaq
sources.note: Primary site evidence for building phases and repairs.

sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Qutb Minar and its Monuments, Delhi, List No. 233
sources.note: Authoritative conservation and monument description.

sources.citation: Finbarr Barry Flood, Objects of Translation (Princeton University Press, 2009)
sources.note: Recent study of material reuse and Indo-Islamic craft translation.

episodes.notes: The Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque reused material from multiple Hindu and Jain temples; Aibak began the minar, Iltutmish completed the core tower and tomb, Alauddin added the Alai Darwaza in 1311 and began the unfinished Alai Minar, and Firuz Shah repaired the damaged top in 1368. The Alai Darwaza is central to the story of true arch and dome technology in India, though earlier corbelled forms complicate easy firsts. Recent Flood scholarship asks writers to avoid one-note vandalism or one-note harmony. Do NOT say Aibak completed the tower, or that the mosque came from a single temple.

episodes.title: Ashvaghosha Sings the Buddha's Life
episodes.era: Kushan literary culture, c. 80-150 CE
episodes.region: Saketa, Purushapura and the Silk Road manuscript world
episodes.logline: Ashvaghosha turns Buddhist teaching into polished Sanskrit poetry whose words move from Kushan monasteries toward China and Tibet.
episodes.moral: A story can carry philosophy farther than argument alone.

sources.citation: Ashvaghosha, Buddhacharita and Saundarananda, ed. E.H. Johnston (1936)
sources.note: Surviving Sanskrit works and translations attributed to the Kushan-era poet.

sources.citation: Chinese Biography of Ashvaghosha, attributed to Kumarajiva's translation, c. 402-409 CE
sources.note: Later source for legendary court and conversion stories.

sources.citation: Patrick Olivelle, Life of the Buddha by Ashvaghosha (2008); Richard Salomon, Ancient Buddhist Scrolls from Gandhara (1999)
sources.note: Modern translation and manuscript context for Kushan Buddhist literature.

episodes.notes: Ashvaghosha's Buddhacharita and Saundarananda show the Kushan age as a scholarly and literary crossroads, using sophisticated Sanskrit kavya to tell Buddhist lives and ideals. Turfan fragments of Shariputraprakarana may preserve early Sanskrit drama associated with him, and his works survived through Chinese and Tibetan transmission along Silk Road networks. RECENT FINDINGS: continuing study of Gandharan, Turfan and Schoyen manuscript fragments refines the picture of Kushan textual culture. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT treat the starving horses moved to tears, his capture by Kanishka or his Brahmin conversion story as verified; they are later hagiography. Do NOT call him definitively India's first playwright.
episodes.chapter: The Kushan Empire and the Silk Road
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Where Gods Met and Art Was Born

episodes.title: The Pallava Alphabet Goes Overseas
episodes.era: Pallava script diffusion, c. 5th-9th centuries CE
episodes.region: Kanchipuram, the Coromandel Coast, Cambodia, Java, Champa and Burma
episodes.logline: A courtly script shaped for Sanskrit and Tamil travels with priests, traders and diplomats until it becomes an ancestor of writing systems across Southeast Asia.
episodes.moral: Ideas travel farther when people give them durable signs.

sources.citation: Pallava inscriptions at Kanchipuram and Mamallapuram compared with early Khmer, Cham, Malay and Javanese inscriptions
sources.note: Epigraphic basis for tracing Pallava-derived scripts.

sources.citation: Sheldon Pollock, The Language of the Gods in the World of Men (2006)
sources.note: Framework for Sanskrit cosmopolis and script-cultural transmission.

sources.citation: Anshuman Pandey, Proposal to Encode the Pallava Script in Unicode, L2/18-084 (2018)
sources.note: Modern palaeographic and computational documentation of Pallava script forms.

episodes.notes: Pallava-Grantha writing carried Sanskrit prestige and local administrative practice into Southeast Asian courts, helping shape Old Khmer, Cham, Kawi, Old Malay, Mon and later regional scripts, while also influencing Malayalam and southern Indian script histories. RECENT EFEO epigraphic work and digital palaeography continue to map regional variants and routes. Do NOT claim one named Pallava king personally invented every Southeast Asian script; the transmission mechanism involved merchants, monks, Brahmins and courts over centuries. This is a scholarly innovation story about writing systems, not a conquest story.
episodes.chapter: The Pallavas and the Bhakti Dawn
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Stone, Script and the Sea

episodes.title: Spice Ports and Eclipse Tables
episodes.figure: Kerala Almanac Makers and Port Kerala
episodes.era: Malabar trade and practical astronomy, c. 1340-1620
episodes.region: Calicut, Ponnani, Cochin, temples and ports of the Malabar Coast
episodes.logline: Pepper ships crowd the coast while almanac makers time eclipses, festivals and seasons, showing what accurate astronomy was worth.
episodes.moral: Knowledge flourishes when society has reasons to use it.

sources.citation: Ibn Battuta, Rihla, c. 1354; Duarte Barbosa, Book of Duarte Barbosa, c. 1516
sources.note: Primary travel accounts of Calicut and the Malabar spice economy.

sources.citation: Paramesvara, Drigganita, 1431 CE
sources.note: Primary evidence for observation-based correction of astronomical computation.

sources.citation: Kim Plofker, Mathematics in India (2009), pp. 217-220; George Gheverghese Joseph, The Crest of the Peacock, 3rd ed. (2011)
sources.note: Modern discussion of practical astronomy and maritime context.

episodes.notes: Use this as an economic context episode, not a false patronage claim. The Malabar coast was tied to Indian Ocean trade; Calicut's Zamorin ruled a pepper-port world known to Ibn Battuta, Barbosa and later Portuguese visitors. Accurate panchangas mattered for ritual timing, agriculture, eclipse observances and civic-temple calendars. ACCURACY FLAGS: there is no document proving the Zamorin commissioned Madhava's series or that navigators needed infinite series. The safe claim is contextual: prosperity, temples, calendars and port society gave astronomical learning social value, while the direct mathematical work remained inside Kerala's scholar networks.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. The House and the Court

episodes.title: The Sword That Crossed the World
episodes.era: Sangam-era industry, c. 3rd century BCE-3rd century CE
episodes.region: Kodumanal on the Noyyal River, Erode district, Tamil Nadu
episodes.logline: At a trade-route industrial town, Tamil smiths and bead makers help create the high-carbon steel tradition later prized from India to the Islamic world.
episodes.moral: Innovation can begin in furnaces far from royal courts.

sources.citation: K. Rajan, Kodumanal Excavation Report (Tamil Nadu State Department of Archaeology, 2015)
sources.note: Excavation evidence for industrial production, beads, pottery and inscriptions.

sources.citation: S. Srinivasan, 'Wootz Crucible Steel,' Papers of the Institute of Archaeology Vol. 5 (1994)
sources.note: Foundational modern archaeometallurgical study of south Indian crucible steel.

sources.citation: S. Srinivasan and S. Ranganathan, India's Legendary Wootz Steel (NIAS/IISc, 2004)
sources.note: Technical history of crucible steel production and global reputation.

episodes.notes: Kodumanal, known in Sangam tradition as Kodumanam, stood on an inland route between Malabar and Coromandel trade worlds. Excavations report furnaces, crucibles, Tamil Brahmi sherds, beads of carnelian and other stones, Roman coins and industrial debris. South Indian crucible steel, later called wootz from words such as urukku and ukku, became famous as raw material for blades forged elsewhere. RECENT FINDINGS include scientific analyses of steel residues and Sri Lankan parallels. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say wootz was invented only at Kodumanal, do NOT equate wootz with finished Damascus blades, and do NOT overdate the site beyond its stratigraphic evidence.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahanas and the Sangam Age

episodes.title: Tukaram's Songs Walk to Pandharpur
episodes.figure: Sant Tukaram and the Warkari poets
episodes.era: Warkari memory and Maratha society, c. 1608-present
episodes.region: Dehu, Alandi, Paithan and Pandharpur
episodes.logline: Vernacular songs and the Pandharpur Wari give ordinary people a shared moral language beyond court and battlefield.
episodes.moral: A people's songs can carry equality farther than orders can.

sources.citation: Tukaram Gatha, manuscript tradition and 1869 printed edition
sources.note: Core abhangas attributed to Tukaram, with textual layers requiring caution.

sources.citation: Mahipati, Bhaktavijay and Bhaktalilamrut, 18th century
sources.note: Hagiographic source preserving Warkari memory and saint traditions.

sources.citation: Christian Lee Novetzke, Religion and Public Memory (Columbia UP, 2008)
sources.note: Modern study of bhakti memory, performance and public tradition.

episodes.notes: The Warkari tradition linked Dnyaneshwar, Namdev, Chokhamela, Eknath, Tukaram and later pilgrimage practice around Vitthal of Pandharpur. KEY FACTS: Tukaram's abhangas circulated in manuscripts before the 1869 printed Gatha; Narayan Maharaj is associated with formalizing the paduka procession in 1685. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP reads saint memory as public practice, not simple biography. Do NOT claim Shivaji certainly met Tukaram, do NOT state Ramdas was certainly Shivaji's guru, and do NOT narrate Tukaram's bodily ascent to Vaikuntha as history.

episodes.title: Banda Bahadur Strikes the First Sikh Coin
episodes.era: First Sikh state and land reform, c. 1708-1716 CE
episodes.region: Nanded, Sirhind, Lohgarh and the Punjab hills
episodes.logline: A former hermit rides north, defeats Sirhind, gives land to tillers, and strikes coins in the Gurus' names rather than his own.
episodes.moral: Victory is noblest when it lifts the poor.

sources.citation: Banda Singh Bahadur's Sikh rupees, Amritsar and Mukhlisgarh-Lohgarh mints, c. 1711
sources.note: Physical evidence for Sikh sovereignty and coin legends.

sources.citation: Akhbar-i-Darbar-i-Mualla and Ibratnama, early 18th-century Persian records
sources.note: Contemporary and near-contemporary evidence for campaigns and execution.

sources.citation: Purnima Dhavan, When Sparrows Became Hawks (2011); J.S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab (1998)
sources.note: Recent and standard studies of 18th-century Sikh political formation.

episodes.notes: Madho Das, renamed Banda Singh Bahadur after meeting Guru Gobind Singh at Nanded in 1708, led a fast northern campaign and captured Sirhind on 22 May 1710. His government at Lohgarh is remembered for abolishing zamindari in controlled areas and granting land rights to cultivators, a major economic and social innovation. His coins named Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh, not Banda, establishing a Sikh numismatic principle later continued by the Misls and Ranjit Singh. ACCURACY FLAGS: conversion-meeting details and miracles are hagiographic; do NOT claim his caste background from later polemics, because contemporary Mughal records do not support it; his 1716 execution is historical but should be handled without gore.
episodes.chapter: The Sikh Gurus and Ranjit Singh

episodes.title: Mahalanobis Measures a Nation
episodes.era: Statistics, surveys and planning, 1931-1972
episodes.region: Calcutta and New Delhi
episodes.logline: Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis builds the Indian Statistical Institute and teaches a new nation how to count crops, distances and plans.
episodes.moral: Good decisions need good measurements.

sources.citation: P.C. Mahalanobis, On the Generalised Distance in Statistics, Proceedings of the National Institute of Sciences of India 2, 1936
sources.note: Primary paper introducing Mahalanobis distance.

sources.citation: P.C. Mahalanobis, On Large-Scale Sample Surveys, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 231, 1944
sources.note: Primary major paper on sample survey design.

sources.citation: Arup Banerji, Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis, National Book Trust, 1997
sources.note: Standard biography of Mahalanobis and the ISI.

episodes.notes: Mahalanobis founded the Indian Statistical Institute in a room at Presidency College on 17 December 1931, developed the Mahalanobis distance, and pioneered large-scale sample surveys for crop and social data. After independence he joined the Planning Commission and shaped the statistical framework behind the Second Five Year Plan. This is an ECONOMIC, STATISTICAL and INSTITUTIONAL innovation story: measurement became statecraft. Recent economic histories, including critiques in Economic and Political Weekly, reassess the heavy-industry bias of the Mahalanobis model without denying his survey genius. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say he invented statistics; he made major contributions to multivariate distance, survey sampling and Indian statistical institutions. Do NOT present planning outcomes as unanimously successful.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Science for Land, Life and Numbers

episodes.title: The City Where Knowledge Was Currency
episodes.era: Cosmopolitan learning city, c. 600 BCE-5th century CE
episodes.region: Taxila in ancient Gandhara, now Punjab, Pakistan
episodes.logline: At a crossroads of empires, students seek teachers through a whole city instead of entering a single campus gate.
episodes.moral: Learning thrives where roads and cultures meet.

sources.citation: John Marshall, Taxila, 3 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1951)
sources.note: Excavation baseline for Bhir Mound, Sirkap, Sirsukh and the city's long occupation.

sources.citation: Pali Jataka tales of students going to Takshashila
sources.note: Literary evidence for cultural memory of a learning center.

sources.citation: Romila Thapar, Cultural Pasts: Essays in Early Indian History (2000)
sources.note: Modern caution against calling Takshashila a university in the Nalanda sense.

episodes.notes: Takshashila was a famed learning city at Gandhara's crossroads, layered by Achaemenid, Greek, Mauryan, Indo-Scythian, Kushan and other cultures. Jataka stories remember students travelling there, while archaeology proves a cosmopolitan urban world with multiple city-sites and mixed material culture. Recent scholarship rejects simple rankings like 'world's first university' and instead emphasizes a city of teachers using gurukula patterns. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim a formal campus, fixed administration or 10,500 students as fact. Student links to Chandragupta, Chanakya or Panini are traditions; Jivaka's Takshashila training is better attested in Buddhist sources.

episodes.title: Joymoti and the Silence History Remembers
episodes.era: Court crisis before Gadadhar Singha, c. 1681 CE
episodes.region: Jerenga Pathar, Sivasagar and the Naga Hills frontier
episodes.logline: Chronicles remember Gadapani's unnamed wife, while Assam's songs remember Joymoti refusing to betray the hidden prince.
episodes.moral: Memory can honor courage while still telling the truth about evidence.

sources.citation: Tungkhungia Buranji, ed. and trans. S.K. Bhuyan (1968)
sources.note: Chronicle basis for Gadapani's exile and the unnamed wife's role.

sources.citation: Padmanath Gohain Baruah, Joymati; Lakshminath Bezbaruah, Joymoti Kuwori
sources.note: Literary sources that shaped the modern heroic narrative.

sources.citation: Jayeeta Sharma, Empire's Garden: Assam and the Making of India (2011)
sources.note: Recent analysis of Joymoti as a patriotic and cultural symbol in Assamese memory.

episodes.notes: Joymoti is powerful precisely because the evidence is layered. Buranjis support the political core: Gadapani fled, his wife suffered, and he returned to become Gadadhar Singha in 1682. But the name Joymoti, the detailed torture scenes and the exact heroic silence belong largely to oral, literary and film traditions, especially modern Assamese nationalism and Jyotiprasad Agarwala's 1935 film. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP stresses this construction. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT present nails, chains or days of torture as documented chronicle fact; frame the episode as what the chronicles say versus what Assamese memory has made sacred.

episodes.title: Chola Bronze Artists Make the Divine Dance
episodes.figure: Chola bronze artisans and temple patrons
episodes.era: Imperial Chola age, 10th-12th century CE
episodes.region: Thanjavur, Kaveri delta, Tamil Nadu
episodes.logline: Chola inscriptions list gifts of metal images, lamps, jewels, and temple service, while surviving bronzes show extraordinary artistry. The episode can follow a workshop casting a graceful image for festival processions.
episodes.moral: Art is a form of devotion, teamwork, and technical mastery.

sources.citation: South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. II, Thanjavur Brihadisvara temple inscriptions of Rajaraja I, entries listing metal images and temple endowments
sources.note: Primary evidence for temple bronzes, donations, lamps, and organized temple service.

sources.citation: C. Sivaramamurti, South Indian Bronzes, Lalit Kala Akademi, 1963
sources.note: Art-historical study of bronze styles, iconography, and casting traditions.

sources.citation: Vidya Dehejia, Art of the Imperial Cholas, Columbia University Press, 1990
sources.note: Modern scholarship connecting inscriptions, ritual movement, and Chola visual culture.

episodes.notes: Rajaraja Chola I already has a batch 1 episode; this one should not retell his biography. Keep the focus on artisans, inscriptions, processional art, and the living temple ecosystem.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Craft, Trade & the Genius of the Age

episodes.title: Nalanda, the Ocean of Learning
episodes.era: Founded under Kumaragupta I, c. 427 CE
episodes.region: Nalanda, Magadha (Bihar)
episodes.logline: Emperor Kumaragupta endows a monastery in Magadha that grows into Nalanda - thousands of students, a library called the Sea of Gems, and a beacon of learning that will draw seekers from across Asia for seven hundred years.
episodes.moral: The greatest wealth a ruler can leave is a place where knowledge is free to grow.

sources.citation: Xuanzang, Records of the Western Regions (c. 646 CE), tr. Li Rongxi (1996)
sources.note: Eyewitness account of Nalanda's scale, library and curriculum.

sources.citation: Copper-plate and seal references to Nalanda's Gupta foundation under Kumaragupta I
sources.note: Basis for the 5th-century foundation.

sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage inscription, Archaeological Site of Nalanda Mahavihara, 2016 (List no. 1502)
sources.note: Recent recognition; ASI excavations.

episodes.notes: Founded under Kumaragupta I (5th c., commonly ~427 CE). Xuanzang (7th c.) describes ~10,000 students and 2,000 teachers and the library complex Dharmaganja (Ratnasagara, Ratnodadhi, Ratnaranjaka) - but flag that the 10,000 figure is a single foreign account, possibly peak/rhetorical. RECENT: only ~10% of the site is excavated; UNESCO World Heritage in 2016; newer scholarship suggests Nalanda lingered for decades after Bakhtiyar Khilji's c.1193 attack rather than ending overnight. It taught Buddhist and non-Buddhist thought, logic, medicine, mathematics. Anchor the hero on Kumaragupta I founding it; show the place and its learners. Spoken name should say 'the First'.

episodes.title: The Echoing Caves for Ajivikas
episodes.era: Barabar and Nagarjuni cave dedications, c. 259-245 BCE and after
episodes.region: Barabar and Nagarjuni Hills, Bihar
episodes.logline: Ashoka cuts mirror-bright chambers into hard granite for the Ajivikas, where every whisper blooms into an echo and stone begins India's rock-cut architecture.
episodes.moral: True tolerance builds shelters even for paths not one's own.

sources.citation: Ashoka's Barabar cave inscriptions, including Sudama Cave year 12 and Karan Chaupar year 19
sources.note: Dated primary dedications to the Ajivikas.

sources.citation: Dasharatha Maurya's Nagarjuni Hill cave inscriptions
sources.note: Post-Ashokan Mauryan dedications continuing the cave tradition.

sources.citation: Harry Falk, Asokan Sites and Artefacts (2006); James C. Harle, The Art and Architecture of the Indian Subcontinent (1994)
sources.note: Epigraphic and art-historical context for the earliest rock-cut caves.

episodes.notes: Barabar Hill contains Sudama, Lomas Rishi, Karan Chaupar and Visvakarma caves; Sudama, dedicated by Ashoka in his 12th regnal year, is the earliest dated rock-cut cave in India. The caves' polished interiors and curved rooms create the famous echoes that inspired E.M. Forster's fictional Marabar Caves. Their Ajivika dedication is vital: Ashoka was Buddhist but patronized a heterodox determinist ascetic sect, demonstrating pluralism. RECENT FLAGS: Harry Falk's re-reading clarified Karan Chaupar's Ajivika dedication; Lomas Rishi lacks an Ashokan inscription and may be unfinished or post-Ashokan. S.P. Gupta's theory that Lomas Rishi was halted around Pushyamitra's coup is intriguing but debated, not fact.

episodes.title: Rakkasa Tangadi Breaks the Capital
episodes.era: Battle of Talikota or Rakkasa-Tangadi, January 1565 CE
episodes.region: Krishna River near Rakkasa and Tangadi; Hampi and Penukonda
episodes.logline: A shifting Deccan coalition captures and beheads Aliya Rama Raya, and Hampi's six-month sack ends the city as imperial capital.
episodes.moral: Pride and brittle alliances can undo generations of power.

sources.citation: Ferishta, Tarikh-i-Ferishta, c. 1612, trans. Briggs (1829)
sources.note: Detailed Persian account of the battle and Rama Raya's death.

sources.citation: Caesar Frederick or Cesare dei Federici, 1567, in Hakluyt's Voyages
sources.note: Post-battle eyewitness testimony to the ruined city.

sources.citation: Richard M. Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan, 1300-1761 (2005)
sources.note: Modern account rejecting communalist simplifications.

episodes.notes: The battle was fought near Rakkasa and Tangadi in January 1565, commonly called Talikota after the Sultanate camp. KEY FACTS: Bijapur, Ahmednagar, Golconda and Bidar formed a rare coalition; the Gilani brothers' defection is attested though details are debated; Aliya Rama Raya was captured and beheaded; Hampi was then plundered and never again served as capital. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP decisively rejects a clean Hindu-Muslim war frame: Rama Raya had long manipulated Sultanate politics, and both sides used mixed personnel and alliances. Date is usually 23 January but sources vary to 26 January. Show the sack as devastating, but continue the story with the Aravidu dynasty at Penukonda and Chandragiri.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Songs, Wit and Shattered Walls

episodes.title: The One-Horned Bull and the Mark of the Maker
episodes.era: Mature Harappan seals and administration, c. 2600-1900 BCE
episodes.region: Harappan sites across South Asia and finds at Mesopotamian sites
episodes.logline: A tiny steatite seal with a one-horned animal, a short script and a pierced back becomes the calling card of Harappan trade and authority.
episodes.moral: A mark can bind strangers when words are lost.

sources.citation: A. Parpola et al., Corpus of Indus Seals and Inscriptions, 3 vols. (1987-2010)
sources.note: Standard corpus of seals and inscriptions.

sources.citation: I. Mahadevan, The Indus Script: Texts, Concordance and Tables (ASI, 1977)
sources.note: Major concordance and statistical catalogue.

sources.citation: J.M. Kenoyer, Ancient Cities of the Indus Valley Civilization (1998)
sources.note: Discussion of seals, sealings and administration.

episodes.notes: About 5,000 inscribed objects are known, many small steatite seals with animals and short sign strings; the so-called unicorn is the commonest motif and sealings show practical use on goods. A 2025 network study suggests the unicorn motif may mark a broad commercial network, but the sign values and motif meanings remain unknown. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT read any inscription, do NOT say the unicorn was definitely mythical, and do NOT claim the seals prove a cuneiform-like writing system beyond debate.

episodes.title: The Prince Who Read the Hidden Books
episodes.era: Dara Shukoh's translations, 1655-1657
episodes.region: Banaras, Agra and Delhi
episodes.logline: Dara Shukoh gathers Sanskrit scholars to translate the Upanishads into Persian, searching for a meeting of Sufi and Vedantic thought.
episodes.moral: Learning across traditions can outlive defeat.

sources.citation: Dara Shukoh, Sirr-i-Akbar, John Rylands Library Persian MS 340 and Fihrist manuscript record
sources.note: Primary manuscript witness for the Persian Upanishad translation tradition.

sources.citation: Dara Shukoh, Majma al-Bahrain, ed. S.A.A. Rizvi, Aligarh, 1982
sources.note: Primary comparative text on Sufi and Vedantic vocabulary.

sources.citation: Jonardon Ganeri, The Lost Age of Reason: Philosophy in Early Modern India 1450-1700, Oxford University Press, 2011
sources.note: Recent philosophy-history reading Dara as a serious intellectual actor.

episodes.notes: Dara Shukoh completed the Sirr-i-Akbar on 8 July 1657 with Sanskrit pandits, translating about fifty-two Upanishads into Persian, after writing Majma al-Bahrain in 1655 to compare Sufi and Vedantic ideas. Recent scholarship by Ganeri and Truschke treats him as part of a broader Sanskrit-Persian intellectual world rather than an isolated curiosity. His execution in 1659 followed political defeat and religious accusations, but the apostasy charge remains entangled with succession politics; do NOT portray Dara as a modern secular liberal, and do NOT claim the translations were exact by present philological standards.

episodes.title: Govinda III Rides Toward Kanauj
episodes.era: Rashtrakuta northern campaign and Tripartite Struggle, c. 800-808 CE
episodes.region: Manyakheta, Kanauj and the Gangetic plains
episodes.logline: From the Deccan, Govinda III rides into the northern contest for Kanauj, where Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas chase one throne's prestige.
episodes.moral: Prestige won far from home can be dazzling but difficult to hold.

sources.citation: Radhanpur Copper Plates of Govinda III, c. 808 CE, Epigraphia Indica Vol. VI
sources.note: Primary Rashtrakuta source for the northern campaign.

sources.citation: Badal Pillar inscription of the Palas and Gwalior Prashasti of the Pratiharas, Epigraphia Indica Vols. II and XIV
sources.note: Rival-dynasty evidence for triangulating the Tripartite Struggle.

sources.citation: A.S. Altekar, The Rashtrakutas and Their Times (1934; reprint 1967); Sheldon Pollock, Language of the Gods (2006)
sources.note: Historical synthesis and modern reading of Kanauj's symbolic prestige.

episodes.notes: The Tripartite Struggle was a long contest in which Kanauj mattered as much for symbolic sovereignty as for territory. Govinda III's plates claim submissions by northern powers, while Pala and Pratihara inscriptions tell their own proud versions; recent scholarship treats such prashastis as claims of prestige that must be cross-read rather than maps of permanent conquest. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Govinda III permanently ruled North India; do NOT merge his campaign with Dhruva's earlier expedition; do NOT accept Rashtrakuta eulogies without rival evidence.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Copper, Roads and World Trade

episodes.title: Alauddin Fixes the Price of Wheat
episodes.era: Khalji market reforms, c. 1303-1316 CE
episodes.region: Delhi, Siri and the grain routes of the Doab
episodes.logline: After siege hunger frightens Delhi, Alauddin fixes prices, licenses traders, fills granaries and posts spies so an enormous army can eat cheaply.
episodes.moral: Order can feed a city, but coercion has a cost.

sources.citation: Ziauddin Barani, Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi, account of Alauddin's market regulations
sources.note: Most detailed source for fixed prices, spies, granaries and punishments.

sources.citation: Amir Khusrau, Khazain-ul-Futuh, 1311
sources.note: Contemporary court account giving a more benevolent explanation.

sources.citation: Satish Chandra, Medieval India: From Sultanat to the Mughals, Part I (2007)
sources.note: Modern university-level synthesis of the reforms and their purposes.

episodes.notes: Alauddin's system regulated grain, cloth, animals, slaves and general commodities through mandis, Sera-i-Adl, state transporters, granaries, market officers and barid spies. Barani links low prices to cheap army maintenance after Mongol pressure; Khusrau frames it as welfare, and modern historians often see both motives. The system lasted roughly until Alauddin's death in 1316 and was quickly dismantled, implying strong merchant resentment. Do NOT call it the world's first price control; say it was among the most systematic state market interventions in recorded medieval India, and do NOT present it as purely benevolent.

episodes.title: Thirty Gods on Kushan Coins
episodes.era: Kushan multi-faith coinage, c. 1st-2nd century CE
episodes.region: Bactria, Gandhara, Kapisa and Mathura
episodes.logline: Kushan coins place Iranian, Greek, Indian, Egyptian and Buddhist figures in one imperial language, making plural patronage visible in every marketplace.
episodes.moral: Respect grows when power learns the names of many gods.

sources.citation: Jongeward, Cribb and Donovan, Kushan, Kushano-Sasanian, and Kidarite Coins (2015)
sources.note: Catalogue documenting the extraordinary deity range on Kushan coinage.

sources.citation: Rabatak inscription, Cribb and Sims-Williams (1995/96)
sources.note: Kanishka's own Bactrian statement of kingship from Nana and all the gods.

sources.citation: Nicholas Sims-Williams, Bactrian Documents from Northern Afghanistan (ongoing)
sources.note: Corpus clarifying Bactrian language and post-Kushan administrative culture.

episodes.notes: Kushan coins display more than thirty deities across traditions, including Nana, Miiro, Aurmuzd, Ardoxsho, Buddha, Oesho, Serapis and others, all named in Bactrian written with Greek letters. The Rabatak inscription says Kanishka received kingship from Nana and all the gods and ordered divine and royal images, making plural patronage part of state display. RECENT FINDINGS: the Oesho identification is debated, with some scholars seeing Vayu-Vata conflated with Shiva, and Bactrian-document studies keep refining the cultural map. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT call this modern religious tolerance; it was strategic imperial patronage. Do NOT claim Kanishka converted exclusively to Buddhism.
episodes.chapter: The Kushan Empire and the Silk Road
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Where Gods Met and Art Was Born

episodes.title: Copper Plates and Village Sabhas
episodes.era: Pallava land grants and local institutions, c. 4th-8th centuries CE
episodes.region: Kanchipuram, Tondaimandalam and brahmadeya villages
episodes.logline: Thin copper sheets record how kings, Brahmin settlements, irrigation rights and village sabhas reshaped land, learning and local power.
episodes.moral: Institutions endure when written promises meet local responsibility.

sources.citation: Mayidavolu and Hirahadagalli copper plates of Sivaskandavarman, Epigraphia Indica, Vol. XV
sources.note: Early Prakrit Pallava grants showing Satavahana-era administrative inheritance.

sources.citation: Kasakudi, Udayendiram and Tandantottam copper plates
sources.note: Bilingual Sanskrit-Tamil grants with genealogy, boundaries, taxes and local administration.

sources.citation: R. Champakalakshmi, Trade and Urban Centres in Early Historic South India (1996); R.S. Sharma, Indian Feudalism, 3rd ed. (2001)
sources.note: Contrasting interpretations of brahmadeya grants as development and power transfer.

episodes.notes: Pallava copper plates show royal grants, land boundaries, tax exemptions, irrigation rights and the growth of brahmadeya villages administered by sabhas of Brahmin landholders. Kanchipuram also appears as a ghatikasthana, a center of learning, while Xuanzang describes a plural city with Buddhist and Hindu institutions. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP debates whether these grants developed agriculture and learning or also displaced older cultivators and concentrated power. Do NOT describe the sabha as modern democracy; it was a restricted local institution, important but socially bounded. Do NOT repeat Chola Uttaramerur details as if they were already fully Pallava.
episodes.chapter: The Pallavas and the Bhakti Dawn
episodes.chapter_part: V. Villages, Voices and the Bhakti Dawn

episodes.title: Acyuta and Melpathur at the Last Flowering
episodes.figure: Acyuta Pisharati and Melpathur Narayana Bhattathiri
episodes.era: Late Kerala school and literary synthesis, c. 1550-1621 and after
episodes.region: Trikkandiyur, Guruvayur and Cochin patronage networks, Kerala
episodes.logline: Acyuta Pisharati carries the astronomical chain forward while his student Melpathur reveals how mathematics, grammar and devotion shared one learned world.
episodes.moral: A tradition survives by becoming more than one subject.

sources.citation: Acyuta Pisharati, Uparagakriyakrama, 1592 CE; Malayalam commentary on Madhava's Venvaroha
sources.note: Dated works linking Jyeshthadeva, Acyuta and the continuing Madhava tradition.

sources.citation: Melpathur Narayana Bhattathiri, Narayaneeyam and Virakeralaprasasti
sources.note: Literary works showing devotional scholarship and Cochin patronage context.

sources.citation: K.V. Sarma, A History of the Kerala School (1972), pp. 53-62; P.P. Divakaran, The Mathematics of India (2018)
sources.note: Modern treatment of the late school and Acyuta's technical role.

episodes.notes: Acyuta Pisharati, active around 1550-1621, was from the Pisharadi temple-service community and was a student of Jyeshthadeva; his 1592 Uparagakriyakrama helps anchor the chronology. Melpathur Narayana Bhattathiri, his student, is better known for Sanskrit grammar and the devotional Narayaneeyam, but he belongs to the same intellectual ecology. ACCURACY FLAGS: the famous disease-transfer story between Acyuta and Melpathur is hagiographic, not verifiable history; do NOT confuse Melpathur with Narayana Pandita of North India, who was not a Kerala school member.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. The House and the Court

episodes.title: The Ships Arrive Laden with Gold
episodes.era: Indo-Roman sea trade, c. 1st century BCE-3rd century CE
episodes.region: Muzuris on the Malabar coast, Arikamedu, Red Sea ports and Tamilakam
episodes.logline: A Greek trade handbook, Tamil poems, Roman complaints and a Vienna papyrus together reveal pepper ships sailing between India and the Red Sea.
episodes.moral: Commerce can connect worlds while leaving puzzles in its wake.

sources.citation: Lionel Casson, The Periplus Maris Erythraei (Princeton University Press, 1989)
sources.note: Standard edition and commentary on the Greek trade manual.

sources.citation: Vimala Begley and Richard De Puma, Rome and India: The Ancient Sea Trade (University of Wisconsin Press, 1991)
sources.note: Arikamedu, Roman goods and Indo-Roman exchange.

sources.citation: Matthew A. Cobb, Rome and the Indian Ocean Trade from Augustus to the Early Third Century CE (Brill, 2018)
sources.note: Recent comprehensive study of the network and its documents.

episodes.notes: The Periplus describes Muzuris as a port of large ships and gold, while Akananuru poetry evokes Yavana vessels bringing gold and taking pepper. Pliny complains that India drained Roman wealth, and the Muzuris Papyrus records a cargo loan connected to a voyage of the Hermapollon. Arikamedu yielded amphorae, Arretine ware and beads, while Pattanam excavations have renewed the Muzuris location debate. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT identify Muzuris definitively as Kodungallur or Pattanam, do NOT call Arikamedu a Roman colony, and do NOT treat Pliny's huge sesterces figure as a precise statistic.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahanas and the Sangam Age

episodes.title: Gold Thread in Paithan and Yeola
episodes.era: Textile economies under Maratha patronage, 17th-18th centuries CE
episodes.region: Paithan, Yeola, Maheshwar, Surat and Mandu
episodes.logline: Silk, zari, reversible borders and relocated looms show how craft communities turned patronage into economic innovation.
episodes.moral: Skilled hands can weave economies as well as cloth.

sources.citation: Ptolemy, Geographia Book VII, reference to Baithana
sources.note: Early external notice linking Paithan with long-distance textile geography.

sources.citation: Nevasa excavation reports, 1966, silk fragments near Paithan
sources.note: Material evidence for early Deccan textile traditions.

sources.citation: Geographical Indications Registry of India, Paithani and Maheshwari Sari and Fabrics GI documents, 2010
sources.note: Recent official documentation of craft history, technique and communities.

episodes.notes: Paithani weaving had ancient roots at Paithan and was reshaped under later Deccan and Maratha patronage as Yeola became a major weaving center; Maheshwari weaving grew at Maheshwar with traditions of invited artisans from Surat and Mandu. KEY FACTS: distinctive Paithani tapestry techniques, peacock motifs and zari work, and Maheshwari reversible borders show technical craft innovation; GI records in 2010 preserve modern community histories. Do NOT claim an exact Peshwa relocation date without evidence, and do NOT say Ahilyabai personally designed the first Maheshwari sari as proven fact.

episodes.title: The Sarbat Khalsa Votes Without a King
episodes.figure: Jassa Singh Ahluwalia and the Dal Khalsa
episodes.era: Misl confederacy and collective sovereignty, c. 1716-1799 CE
episodes.region: Amritsar, Lahore and the wider Punjab
episodes.logline: After persecution scatters the Sikhs into bands, the Sarbat Khalsa gathers at Amritsar to make binding decisions without a king.
episodes.moral: A people can survive when they learn to decide together.

sources.citation: Gobindshahi and Nanakshahi Sikh coins from Lahore and Amritsar mints
sources.note: Physical evidence for Misl-era sovereignty and limits on personal rule.

sources.citation: Ratan Singh Bhangu, Prachin Panth Prakash, c. 1809
sources.note: Key Sikh chronicle of the Misl period.

sources.citation: Purnima Dhavan, When Sparrows Became Hawks (2011); J.S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab (1998)
sources.note: Recent interpretation of the warrior tradition and confederacy.

episodes.notes: After Banda Singh Bahadur's death, Sikh jathas survived persecution and developed the Sarbat Khalsa, a collective assembly at Amritsar whose gurmatas were binding on the community. In 1748 the forces were organized into Misls under Dal Khalsa leadership, with Jassa Singh Ahluwalia prominent; Misl-era coins make sovereignty visible. This is a political innovation story: collective authority after the human Gurus, with egalitarian ideals under military pressure. ACCURACY FLAGS: casualty numbers for the Chhota and Vadda Ghallughara vary sharply, so avoid exact totals; do NOT call the system a modern democracy without qualification, because it was a confederate, religious-military assembly with uneven regional power.
episodes.chapter: The Sikh Gurus and Ranjit Singh

episodes.title: Janaki Ammal Counts Sugarcane Chromosomes
episodes.era: Cytogenetics and conservation, 1931-1984
episodes.region: Thalassery, Michigan, Coimbatore, Britain and Allahabad
episodes.logline: Janaki Ammal studies chromosomes in sugarcane and garden plants, helping Indian agriculture while opening doors for women in science.
episodes.moral: Patient work in living cells can nourish a country.

sources.citation: Janaki Ammal, Chromosome Studies in Nicandra Physaloides, PhD thesis, University of Michigan, 1931
sources.note: Primary doctoral work documenting her cytogenetic training.

sources.citation: C.D. Darlington and Janaki Ammal, Chromosome Atlas of Cultivated Plants, George Allen and Unwin, 1945
sources.note: Landmark co-authored cytogenetics reference.

sources.citation: Gita Chadha, Janaki Ammal: Science in the Service of Life, in Feminism in India, Zubaan, 2008
sources.note: Recent feminist science-studies account of her career and erasure.

episodes.notes: Janaki Ammal earned a Michigan PhD in 1931, worked at the Sugarcane Breeding Station in Coimbatore from the 1930s, and used cytogenetics and polyploidy to support hardier sugarcane breeding for Indian conditions. During World War II she worked at the John Innes Institute and co-authored Chromosome Atlas of Cultivated Plants in 1945; after independence she led the Central Botanical Laboratory and later supported Silent Valley conservation. This is a SCIENTIFIC, AGRICULTURAL and SOCIAL innovation story. Recent feminist scholarship highlights how women scientists' records were scattered or unnamed. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say she saved India's sugar industry single-handedly; she contributed to a larger breeding program. Specific Coimbatore variety attributions are sometimes poorly preserved.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Science for Land, Life and Numbers

episodes.title: The Mathematician Who Made Numbers Dance
episodes.era: Mathematics and astronomy at Ujjain, 1114-1185 CE
episodes.region: Vijjadavida, Khandesh and Ujjain
episodes.logline: Bhaskara turns arithmetic and algebra into poems of bees, swans and planets that students copy for centuries.
episodes.moral: Teaching lasts when rigor learns to sing.

sources.citation: Bhaskara II, Lilavati and Bijaganita; H.T. Colebrooke translation (1817)
sources.note: Primary arithmetic and algebra texts in English translation.

sources.citation: Changadeva inscription at Patnadevi, 1207 CE; Epigraphia Indica I (1892)
sources.note: Epigraphic confirmation of Bhaskara's lineage and a school for his works.

sources.citation: Kim Plofker, Mathematics in India (Princeton University Press, 2009)
sources.note: Modern assessment of Bhaskara's algebra, astronomy and calculus-like results.

episodes.notes: Bhaskara II composed the Siddhanta Shiromani in 1150 CE, with Lilavati for arithmetic and Bijaganita for algebra, and his grandson's 1207 Patnadevi inscription confirms his lineage and a school devoted to his works. His verse problems made mathematics memorable, while his algebra and instantaneous-motion observations show sophisticated reasoning. Recent scholarship credits specific anticipations of later calculus ideas but not a full calculus system. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT present the daughter Lilavati story as biography; it is later tradition. Do NOT say Bhaskara invented calculus. His achievement is rigorous, influential mathematical pedagogy and problem-solving.

episodes.title: The Octagonal Coin and the Mint at Rajshal
episodes.figure: Jayadhwaj Singha and the Rajshal mint guilds
episodes.era: Ahom coinage from 1648 to the 18th century
episodes.region: Rajshal mint near Rangpur and Sivasagar
episodes.logline: After centuries without coins, Assam's kings stamp octagonal silver with dates, scripts and queens' names, turning metal into statecraft.
episodes.moral: Money carries a kingdom's identity as surely as its armies do.

sources.citation: Ahom coin collections, Assam State Museum, Indian Museum Kolkata and ASI Guwahati Circle
sources.note: Physical primary evidence for shape, weight, script, metal and royal titles.

sources.citation: M.K. Singh, 'Ahom Coinage,' Journal of the Numismatic Society of India 42 (1980-81)
sources.note: Key numismatic study of Ahom coin forms and debates over the octagonal shape.

sources.citation: Jahnabi Gogoi, Agrarian System of Medieval Assam (2002)
sources.note: Economic context for monetization after long reliance on paik labor and in-kind systems.

episodes.notes: This economic innovation story begins in 1648, when Jayadhwaj Singha issued the first Ahom coins after centuries of a largely non-monetary labor economy. Later kings standardized silver and gold coinage, used Assamese, Devanagari, Persian and occasionally other scripts, and Rudra Singha introduced annual dating. Queen Phuleshwari's name on coins under Siva Singha marks unusual female royal authority. ACCURACY FLAGS: the Yogini Tantra explanation for the octagonal form is a tradition, not settled fact; M.K. Singh suggests possible Bengal Sultanate influence. Do NOT claim coins replaced the paik system overnight; monetization was gradual and partial.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Courts of Craft and Code

episodes.title: Tamil Merchant Guilds Sail the Indian Ocean
episodes.figure: Ainnurruvar/Manigramam merchant guilds and Chola-era trade
episodes.era: Chola-era Indian Ocean trade, 11th-13th century CE
episodes.region: Tamil coast, Southeast Asia, and China Sea routes
episodes.logline: Tamil merchant guilds carried cloth, spices, metalwork, and trust across seas from the Coromandel coast to Southeast Asia. Their inscriptions abroad show that Indian Ocean trade was built on ships, agreements, and shared rules.
episodes.moral: Trust and fair dealing can carry a community farther than any single ship.

sources.citation: Lobu Tua Tamil inscription, Barus, Sumatra, Saka 1010 / 1088 CE, recording the Ainnurruvar merchant guild
sources.note: Primary overseas inscription proving Tamil merchant-guild activity in Southeast Asia.

sources.citation: Zhao Rugua, Zhu Fan Zhi, 1225, trans. Hirth and Rockhill, chapter on Chu-lien/Chola trade
sources.note: Chinese trade account describing Chola-region goods and maritime contacts.

sources.citation: K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, The Colas, chapters on overseas relations and commerce
sources.note: Scholarly synthesis connecting inscriptions, merchant guilds, and Chola-era maritime networks.

episodes.notes: This is not a retelling of Rajendra Chola I's campaign from batch 1. Keep it focused on documented merchant networks and cultural exchange rather than conquest.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Craft, Trade & the Genius of the Age

episodes.title: Kalidasa and the Cloud Messenger
episodes.era: Classical Sanskrit's peak, c. late 4th-early 5th century CE
episodes.region: Ujjain and the Gupta cultural world
episodes.logline: A poet imagines a lovelorn spirit begging a passing cloud to carry his message home, and writes Shakuntala and the tale of Rama's line - Sanskrit so radiant that, centuries later, Goethe will bow to it.
episodes.moral: Long after empires fall, beauty in words keeps an age alive.

sources.citation: Kalidasa, Abhijnanashakuntalam, Meghaduta, Raghuvamsha, Kumarasambhava; tr. Barbara Stoler Miller, Theater of Memory (1984)
sources.note: The poet's major works.

sources.citation: Aihole inscription (634 CE) naming Kalidasa with Vyasa and Valmiki
sources.note: Confirms his fame as a historical figure by the 7th c.

sources.citation: Sheldon Pollock, The Language of the Gods in the World of Men (2006)
sources.note: Kalidasa within the Gupta 'cosmopolitan Sanskrit' transformation.

episodes.notes: His works: Abhijnanashakuntalam, Meghaduta (the cloud messenger), Raghuvamsha, Kumarasambhava. DATING IS FAMOUSLY UNRESOLVED (proposals span 1st c. BCE-6th c. CE); the defensible CONSENSUS places him late 4th-early 5th c. CE, around Chandragupta II - but the 'Navaratna / nine gems of Vikramaditya's court' link is LEGENDARY (later texts only), so present the court connection as tradition, not fact. The Mandasor inscription (433 CE) may quote him; the Aihole inscription (634 CE) names him. Goethe's praise of Shakuntala put him in the world canon. Age B - gentle and lyrical. Recent feminist readings (Thapar) note Shakuntala both grants and constrains female agency.

episodes.title: The Didarganj Yakshi's Polished Secret
episodes.era: Early historic sculpture, debated Mauryan or Kushan date
episodes.region: Didarganj near Patna; Bihar Museum, Patna
episodes.logline: A riverbank reveals a shining yakshi with a fly-whisk, but her mirror polish hides a mystery: is she Mauryan splendor or a later Kushan masterpiece?
episodes.moral: Honest wonder leaves room for unanswered questions.

sources.citation: Didarganj Yakshi, found at Didarganj Kadam Rasual near Patna on October 18, 1917
sources.note: Physical Chunar sandstone sculpture with famous mirror-like polish, now in Bihar Museum.

sources.citation: James C. Harle, The Art and Architecture of the Indian Subcontinent (1994)
sources.note: Art-historical basis for questioning the traditional Mauryan date.

sources.citation: Bihar Museum, Patna, updated early historic display interpretation
sources.note: Current cautious museum framing after the sculpture's move from Patna Museum.

episodes.notes: The Didarganj Yakshi is a life-sized Chunar sandstone female figure holding a chauri, discovered by villagers in 1917 and recovered by J.N. Samaddar and D.B. Spooner. It has long been celebrated as Mauryan because of its spectacular polish, but modern art historians including Harle and Rowland argue it may be Kushan, 1st-2nd century CE, based on forelock, ornament, drapery and comparison with other yakshis. CRITICAL ACCURACY: do NOT say Mauryan polish alone proves Mauryan date; the technique persisted after the Mauryas. Mention the 1985-86 Smithsonian travel damage to the nose only as a patrimony caution if needed. Best story angle: the sculpture teaches how art history weighs style, material and provenance rather than forcing certainty.

episodes.title: Purandara Dasa Sets the First Notes
episodes.era: Haridasa bhakti and Carnatic music, c. 1484-1564 CE
episodes.region: Karnataka, Hampi, the Tungabhadra and Madhva matha networks
episodes.logline: Purandara Dasa turns devotion into lessons, songs and exercises that become the first steps of Carnatic music for generations.
episodes.moral: Art becomes immortal when it teaches everyone to begin.

sources.citation: Purandara Dasa's devaranama compositions and manuscript/oral traditions
sources.note: Primary devotional songs carrying the Purandara Vittala signature.

sources.citation: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Purandaradasa
sources.note: Concise modern reference for dates and the title father of Carnatic music.

sources.citation: Premlatha Nagarajan, Purandaradasa: The Father of Carnatic Music (2010)
sources.note: Musicological study of pedagogy and attribution.

episodes.notes: Purandara Dasa, linked to the Haridasa movement and Dvaita Vedanta, is credited with systematizing Carnatic pedagogy through svaravalis, alankaras, simple gitas and the foundational Mayamalavagowla scale. KEY FACTS: he composed in Kannada for devotional accessibility and used the mudra Purandara Vittala; the traditional 475,000-composition claim is legendary, while roughly 1,000-1,500 survive in oral and manuscript traditions. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP uses stylistic and mudra analysis to sort authentic works from later interpolations, and renewed attention to Kanakadasa highlights the movement's social critique. Do NOT claim he was certainly Krishnadevaraya's personal court musician; the stronger link is through Vyasatirtha, Krishnadevaraya's guru.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Songs, Wit and Shattered Walls

episodes.title: Four Thousand Signs and Silence
episodes.era: Harappan script use, c. 2600-1900 BCE, and decipherment debates to the present
episodes.region: Harappan seal collections in India, Pakistan, Europe and beyond
episodes.logline: Thousands of short inscriptions survive, but without a bilingual key the Indus script still holds back every name, prayer and law it may once have carried.
episodes.moral: Honesty before mystery is a form of knowledge.

sources.citation: A. Parpola, Deciphering the Indus Script (1994)
sources.note: Major scholarly statement of the Dravidian hypothesis and decipherment history.

sources.citation: S. Farmer, R. Sproat and M. Witzel, 'The Collapse of the Indus-Script Thesis,' Electronic Journal of Vedic Studies 11 (2004)
sources.note: Influential non-linguistic challenge to the script thesis.

sources.citation: R.P.N. Rao et al., 'Entropic Evidence for Linguistic Structure in the Indus Script,' Science 324 (2009)
sources.note: Peer-reviewed statistical counter-argument showing structured sign sequences.

episodes.notes: The script has roughly 400 to 700 counted signs depending on compounds, average inscriptions of only 5 to 7 signs, no bilingual text and no consensus language. Dravidian, Indo-Aryan and non-linguistic theories exist; machine-learning and entropy studies show pattern but cannot provide phonetic values. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say it has been deciphered, do NOT say it is definitely Sanskrit, Dravidian or non-linguistic, and do NOT invent Harappan personal names from signs.

episodes.title: Samugarh and the Empty Elephant
episodes.era: Mughal war of succession, 29 May 1658
episodes.region: Samugarh near Agra
episodes.logline: At Samugarh, Dara Shukoh leaves his elephant and a rumor of flight opens the road for Aurangzeb's throne.
episodes.moral: In crisis, symbols can decide what soldiers believe.

sources.citation: Francois Bernier, Travels in the Mogul Empire, 1656-1668, trans. Irving Brock, Oxford University Press, 1916
sources.note: European eyewitness for Dara's downfall and the succession struggle.

sources.citation: Saqi Mustad Khan, Maasir-i-Alamgiri, trans. Jadunath Sarkar, Royal Asiatic Society of Bengal, 1947
sources.note: Primary chronicle from the Aurangzeb side.

sources.citation: Audrey Truschke, Aurangzeb: The Life and Legacy of India's Most Controversial King, Stanford University Press, 2017
sources.note: Recent balanced reassessment of Aurangzeb, Dara and succession politics.

episodes.notes: The battle of Samugarh on 29 May 1658 pitted Dara Shukoh's larger but less disciplined force against Aurangzeb and Murad's Deccan-hardened army. Dara's empty elephant howdah became a battlefield signal of disaster, after which he fled, Shah Jahan was imprisoned, and Dara was captured and executed in 1659. Bernier is vivid but pro-Dara, while official chronicles favor Aurangzeb; do NOT reduce the war to a simple liberal-versus-fundamentalist morality play, and do NOT state with certainty why Dara dismounted because sources disagree.

episodes.title: Arab Merchants Praise Manyakheta
episodes.era: Rashtrakuta global trade, c. 851-943 CE
episodes.region: Manyakheta, Konkan ports, Bharuch, Chaul and the Arabian Sea
episodes.logline: Arab writers call the Balhara one of the world's great kings and reveal a Deccan open to horses, textiles, ports and merchant communities.
episodes.moral: Prosperity grows when roads and seas connect cultures fairly.

sources.citation: Sulaiman al-Tajir, Silsilat al-Tawarikh, c. 851 CE, in Relation de la Chine et de l'Inde
sources.note: Primary Arabic testimony calling the Rashtrakuta king Balhara one of the great world rulers.

sources.citation: Al-Masudi, Muruj al-Dhahab, c. 943 CE, excerpts in Elliot and Dowson, Vol. I
sources.note: Arabic geographical source for western India and Rashtrakuta standing.

sources.citation: Ranabir Chakravarti, 'Merchants, Merchandise, and Merchantmen,' in A Comprehensive History of India Vol. IV, Pt. I (2008)
sources.note: Recent synthesis of western seaboard trade and merchant networks.

episodes.notes: Sulaiman and Al-Masudi preserve a rare outside view of the Rashtrakutas, using Balhara as a title for the king and describing the Deccan's place in Indian Ocean trade. Recent economic histories pair these accounts with Konkan port archaeology and inscriptions such as the Agashi mosque grant to show Arab merchant settlement and negotiated privileges under western Indian rulers. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Rashtrakutas were ranked above Abbasids or China; do NOT insist Al-Masudi personally visited Manyakheta; do NOT imply Arab trade began only under the Rashtrakutas.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Copper, Roads and World Trade

episodes.title: Firuz Shah Turns Water into Villages
episodes.era: Tughlaq welfare and infrastructure, 1351-1388 CE
episodes.region: Delhi, Hauz Khas, Feroz Shah Kotla, Punjab and Haryana canal zones
episodes.logline: Firuz Shah digs canals, restores tanks, founds villages, moves Ashokan pillars, and writes a memoir that lists both welfare works and hard-edged intolerance.
episodes.moral: Public works shine brightest when remembered with honesty.

sources.citation: Firuz Shah Tughlaq, Futuhat-i-Firuz Shahi, translated in Elliot and Dowson, Vol. III
sources.note: Rare first-person royal account of canals, hospitals, villages and punishments.

sources.citation: Shams-i-Siraj Afif, Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi, c. 1398
sources.note: Main narrative source for Firuz Shah's reign.

sources.citation: ASI documentation of Hauz Khas, Feroz Shah Kotla and the Ashokan pillars in Delhi
sources.note: Material evidence for his building and monument-moving projects.

episodes.notes: Firuz Shah ruled from 1351 to 1388 and emphasized restoration after Muhammad bin Tughlaq's turbulence: canals, more than 300 villages in his own claims, sarais, hospitals, madrasas, Hauz Khas works, and the transport of Ashokan pillars to Delhi. His Futuhat is invaluable because a sultan speaks in first person, but it also records religiously harsh policies, executions and a large slave establishment. Recent environmental and heritage work has renewed attention to medieval hydraulics. Do NOT portray him as purely benevolent, and do NOT claim his anti-torture statements erased all brutality.

episodes.title: Huvishka's Amitabha in Mathura
episodes.era: Huvishka's reign and Mathura devotion, c. 150-190 CE
episodes.region: Mathura, Purushapura, Kapisa and Ayrtam
episodes.logline: In Huvishka's prosperous reign, a merchant family's Mathura inscription names Amitabha, hinting at a devotion that will one day fill East Asia.
episodes.moral: Small dedications can become long rivers of memory.

sources.citation: Govindo-Nagar Amitabha inscription, Mathura Museum, Year 28 of Huvishka
sources.note: Earliest known epigraphic reference to Amitabha Buddha.

sources.citation: Ayrtam inscription and Surkh Kotal SK4, published and revised by Harmatta and Sims-Williams
sources.note: Evidence for Huvishka-era cult and Bactrian inscriptional culture.

sources.citation: Paul Harrison, Who Gets to Ride in the Great Vehicle?, JIABS 10.1 (1987); Jongeward-Cribb-Donovan (2015)
sources.note: Scholarly work on Amitabha origins and Huvishka coinage.

episodes.notes: Huvishka ruled for about four decades and issued some of the most diverse Kushan coinage, showing Greek, Iranian, Indian and even Egyptian deities such as Serapis. The Govindo-Nagar inscription from Mathura, dated Year 28 of Huvishka, dedicates a statue to Amitabha Buddha by a merchant family and is crucial for tracing early Mahayana and Pure Land devotion. RECENT FINDINGS: Schoyen and other manuscript studies connect Huvishka's era to wider Mahayana development, but do not prove his personal doctrine. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Huvishka founded Pure Land Buddhism; the inscription shows Amitabha devotion existed, not that later East Asian Pure Land systems were complete.
episodes.chapter: The Kushan Empire and the Silk Road

episodes.title: Mariners of Mamallapuram
episodes.era: Pallava port trade and diplomacy, c. 7th-8th centuries CE
episodes.region: Mamallapuram, Nagapattinam, Sri Lanka, Tang China and the Bay of Bengal
episodes.logline: Ships at Mamallapuram carry gems, elephants, envoys, monks and scripts across the Bay of Bengal, tying Pallava Kanchi to Lanka, China and Southeast Asia.
episodes.moral: Prosperity grows when shores become meeting places.

sources.citation: Thirumangai Alvar, Periya Tirumoli
sources.note: 8th-century Tamil hymn vividly describing ships and wealth at Mamallapuram.

sources.citation: Tang Annals (Tangshu) on the Pallava embassy of c. 720 CE
sources.note: Chinese record of Rajasimha's diplomatic contact with Tang Xuanzong.

sources.citation: Kanakalatha Mukund, The World of Tamil Merchants (2015); Pierre-Yves Manguin et al., Early Interactions between South and Southeast Asia (2011)
sources.note: Modern studies of Tamil merchant and Bay of Bengal networks.

episodes.notes: Mamallapuram was a Pallava port distinct from inland Kanchipuram. Literary testimony, coins, maritime diplomacy, Sri Lankan chronicle material and Tang records connect the Pallavas to Sri Lanka, China and Southeast Asia; Rajasimha's embassy to Tang China and the remembered China Pagoda at Nagapattinam show Buddhist and diplomatic dimensions. RECENT WORK by Mukund, Manguin and Ranabir Chakravarti places the port in wider Bay of Bengal economic systems. Do NOT overstate the scale of trade from isolated coin finds, and do NOT treat the Tang honorific as proof that Rajasimha commanded Chinese armies.
episodes.chapter: The Pallavas and the Bhakti Dawn
episodes.chapter_part: V. Villages, Voices and the Bhakti Dawn

episodes.title: Whish Reads the Palm Leaves
episodes.era: Rediscovery of Kerala series, 1825-1836
episodes.region: South Malabar, Madras, Cuddapah and the Royal Asiatic Society, London
episodes.logline: A young East India Company official reads palm leaves from Malabar and tells Europe that Indian texts contained infinite series it had not expected to find.
episodes.moral: A forgotten manuscript can reopen the history of ideas.

sources.citation: C.M. Whish, On the Hindu Quadrature of the Circle, Transactions of the Royal Asiatic Society 3:3 (1834), pp. 509-523
sources.note: Primary rediscovery paper on Tantrasangraha, Yuktibhasa, Karanapaddhati and Sadratnamala.

sources.citation: John Warren, Kala Sankalita (Madras, 1825)
sources.note: Earlier Western notice of Kerala series in a calendrical study.

sources.citation: Sankara Varman, Sadratnamala, 1819 CE
sources.note: Late traditional Kerala text used by Whish to show the school was still active.

episodes.notes: John Warren noticed the series in 1825, but Whish's 1834 Royal Asiatic Society paper made the famous claim that Kerala shastras contained infinite series and fluxion-like forms. He died in 1833 before the paper appeared; his brother deposited 195 manuscripts at the Royal Asiatic Society in 1836. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP FLAG: cite the paper as 1834/1835 if needed because the volume dating is confusing. Do NOT say Whish alone discovered the school, and do NOT imply his claim was immediately accepted; it was mostly ignored for about a century.

episodes.title: The Name Carved Beside the Pillar
episodes.era: Deccan donative economy, c. 1st century BCE-3rd century CE
episodes.region: Nasik, Karla, Kanheri, Sanchi and Amaravati
episodes.logline: Across caves and stupas, merchants, monks, nuns and guilds carve their gifts into stone, turning trade wealth into enduring religious institutions.
episodes.moral: Public generosity builds institutions stronger than monuments alone.

sources.citation: H. Luders, A List of Brahmi Inscriptions, Epigraphia Indica Vol. 10 Appendix (1912)
sources.note: Early Brahmi donor inscriptions from caves, pillars, railings and cells.

sources.citation: Gregory Schopen, Bones, Stones, and Buddhist Monks (University of Hawaii Press, 1997)
sources.note: Influential studies of Buddhist monastic donations and endowments.

sources.citation: Jason Neelis, Early Buddhist Transmission and Trade Networks (Brill, 2011)
sources.note: Recent treatment of trade routes, monasteries and donations.

episodes.notes: Satavahana-era inscriptions document donations of pillars, cells, cisterns, caves and villages by setthis, guilds, monks, nuns, queens and officials. Nashik, Karla and Kanheri records reveal immunities, land grants and institutional support; Satavahana lead, copper and potin coins show a pragmatic monetary economy suited to the Deccan. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP stresses these inscriptions as economic evidence rather than royal propaganda alone. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT equate shreni exactly with a medieval European guild, do NOT say kings directed all cave construction, and do NOT call lead coinage primitive merely because it was not gold or silver.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahanas and the Sangam Age

episodes.title: The Chauth That Became Sovereignty
episodes.figure: Shahu I and the Maratha revenue officers
episodes.era: Maratha fiscal state, 1674-1818 CE
episodes.region: Pune, Satara, Malwa, Gujarat, Nagpur, Baroda and Gwalior
episodes.logline: Chauth, sardeshmukhi, hundis and coins turn scattered cavalry claims into a fiscal web across India.
episodes.moral: A state is held together by accounts as much as armies.

sources.citation: Peshwa Daftar revenue accounts and campaign financial orders
sources.note: Primary Modi-script evidence for collections, assignments and military finance.

sources.citation: Maratha Shivrai and Peshwa-era rupee coinage catalogued by the Numismatic Society of India
sources.note: Material evidence for monetary sovereignty and decentralized mints.

sources.citation: Andre Wink, Land and Sovereignty in India (Cambridge UP, 1986)
sources.note: Classic argument that chauth expressed sovereignty, not merely protection money.

episodes.notes: Maratha finance rested on chauth, sardeshmukhi, revenue assignments, moneylenders, hundis and multiple mints, including Shivrai coin traditions and later Peshwa, Holkar, Scindia, Bhonsle and Gaekwad issues. KEY FACTS: the 1719 Mughal recognition mattered because it converted pressure into a legal imperial claim; collections were divided among center, officers and troops. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP by Wink, Gordon and Guha debates whether this was extraction, sovereignty, state formation or all three. Do NOT call chauth only 'protection money,' and do NOT invent precise banking-house amounts where Daftar evidence is incomplete.

episodes.title: Ranjit Singh Enters Lahore
episodes.era: Unification of the Sikh Empire, c. 1799-1809 CE
episodes.region: Gujranwala, Lahore, Amritsar and the Sutlej frontier
episodes.logline: A young misl chief enters Lahore, becomes Maharaja, and builds a plural court where coins honor the Gurus instead of himself.
episodes.moral: The strongest rule can still choose humility.

sources.citation: Sohan Lal Suri, Umdat-ut-Tawarikh, c. 1805-1849
sources.note: Court chronicle for dates, campaigns and administration.

sources.citation: W.G. Osborne, The Court and Camp of Runjeet Sing (1840); Baron Charles Hugel, Travels in Kashmir and the Panjab (1845)
sources.note: Eyewitness European descriptions of the Lahore Durbar.

sources.citation: Priya Atwal, Royals and Rebels: The Rise and Fall of the Sikh Empire (2020)
sources.note: Recent archival study of court, family and succession politics.

episodes.notes: Ranjit Singh, born in 1780 at Gujranwala, entered Lahore on 7 July 1799 and was proclaimed Maharaja in 1801. His court was multi-faith and multilingual, with Fakir Azizuddin, Dina Nath, Dogra nobles, Sikh sardars and European officers all serving the state. Multiple European visitors report that he avoided the death penalty, while his Nanakshahi coins carried the Gurus' names rather than his own. The 1809 Treaty of Amritsar fixed the Sutlej boundary with the British and bought Punjab three decades of independence. RECENT/ACCURACY FLAGS: Priya Atwal complicates simple hero tales with court, family and succession politics; do NOT treat every wisdom anecdote as documented fact.
episodes.chapter: The Sikh Gurus and Ranjit Singh

episodes.title: Bhabha Draws a Map of Atomic India
episodes.era: TIFR and atomic energy planning, 1944-1966
episodes.region: Bombay, Bangalore, Trombay and New Delhi
episodes.logline: Homi Bhabha writes to Tata and Nehru, then builds TIFR and an atomic-energy programme for a newly independent nation.
episodes.moral: A bold institution can turn talent into national capacity.

sources.citation: H.J. Bhabha's letter to the Sir Dorabji Tata Trust, 1944, TIFR Archives, Mumbai
sources.note: Primary proposal for a national institute of fundamental research.

sources.citation: H.J. Bhabha and W. Heitler, The Passage of Fast Electrons and the Theory of Cosmic Showers, Proceedings of the Royal Society A 159, 1937
sources.note: Primary scientific work on cosmic ray showers.

sources.citation: Indira Chowdhury and Ananya Dasgupta, A Masterful Spirit: Homi J. Bhabha, 1909-1966, Penguin India, 2010
sources.note: Archival biography of Bhabha and TIFR.

episodes.notes: Bhabha trained at Cambridge, produced important work on electron-positron scattering and cosmic ray showers, and in 1944 proposed a Tata-backed institute for fundamental research. TIFR opened in Bombay in 1945; the Atomic Energy Commission followed in 1948, and Trombay became the centre of India's nuclear establishment. This is an ENGINEERING, INSTITUTIONAL and economic-development innovation story, especially through the three-stage nuclear-power vision based on India's thorium resources. Recent scholarship using TIFR archives debates whether the thorium programme was visionary or over-optimistic. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT call Bhabha the father of India's nuclear bomb; his public programme emphasized peaceful atomic energy, and the 1974 test came after his death. Do NOT repeat Mont Blanc crash sabotage rumours as fact.
episodes.chapter_part: V. Laboratories of a Free Nation

episodes.title: The Mathematician at the Edge of the Infinite
episodes.era: Kerala school of astronomy and mathematics, c. 1340-1425 CE
episodes.region: Sangamagrama and the Nila river region of Kerala
episodes.logline: Madhava follows astronomy into infinite series and gives Kerala a mathematics that reaches beyond any counting end.
episodes.moral: Patient calculation can glimpse the infinite.

sources.citation: Madhava, Venvaroha; K.V. Sarma edition (1956)
sources.note: Surviving work helping anchor Madhava's active period.

sources.citation: Jyesthadeva, Yuktibhasha; K.V. Sarma et al. translation (Springer, 2008)
sources.note: Primary proof text preserving Kerala school derivations.

sources.citation: George Gheverghese Joseph, The Crest of the Peacock, 3rd ed. (2011)
sources.note: Modern account of Kerala mathematics and its priority claims.

episodes.notes: Madhava's own works mostly vanished, but later Kerala texts credit him with infinite series for pi, sine and cosine, motivated by more accurate astronomy. The Yuktibhasha, written in Malayalam by Jyesthadeva around 1530, preserves proofs and is a landmark recent scholarly edition in the history of Indian mathematics. Mainstream historians accept independent priority over comparable European discoveries for these specific results. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say India transmitted calculus to Newton or Leibniz; there is no documentary proof. Do NOT call it modern calculus as a complete system. Tell it as brilliant infinite-series mathematics within an astronomical school.
episodes.chapter_part: V. What India Gave the World

episodes.title: Rang Ghar, the Pavilion Built Without Cement
episodes.era: Royal sports architecture, c. 1696-1751 CE
episodes.region: Rupahi Pathar, Rangpur, modern Sivasagar
episodes.logline: A boat-roofed brick pavilion rises from rice, lime and craft, letting kings watch Bihu games on the fields of Rangpur.
episodes.moral: A civilization is known by what it builds for joy as well as war.

sources.citation: ASI, List of Centrally Protected Monuments in Assam, Rang Ghar entry
sources.note: Official protected monument record for the surviving brick pavilion.

sources.citation: Tungkhungia Buranji, ed. and trans. S.K. Bhuyan (1968)
sources.note: Chronicle context for royal construction under Rudra and Pramatta Singha.

sources.citation: S.L. Baruah, A Comprehensive History of Assam (1985)
sources.note: Modern synthesis of Tungkhungia architecture and cultural patronage.

episodes.notes: Rang Ghar is an engineering and cultural episode, not merely a postcard monument. The current brick structure is usually dated to Pramatta Singha's reign, 1744-1751, while Buranji tradition remembers an earlier wooden or bamboo pavilion under Rudra Singha. Its curved boat-like roof, arched openings, crocodile finials and sticky rice-lime-egg mortar show adaptive craft in a wet landscape. ACCURACY FLAGS: avoid the absolute claim 'oldest amphitheater in Asia'; safer wording is one of Asia's oldest surviving royal sports pavilions. The story should connect Bihu games, royal spectacle and material science without inventing untested chemical formulas.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Courts of Craft and Code

episodes.title: Kulottunga, the King Who Abolished Tolls
episodes.era: Later Imperial Chola, c. 1070-1122 CE
episodes.region: The Chola empire, Kaveri to the Godavari
episodes.logline: Uniting Chola and Eastern Chalukya blood, Kulottunga wins a name no war could buy, 'Sungam Tavirtta', the king who abolished tolls, easing the burden on his people.
episodes.moral: A ruler is remembered less for what he takes than for what he lifts from his people.

sources.citation: Inscriptions granting Kulottunga I the title 'Sungam Tavirtta Cholan' (abolisher of tolls)
K. A. Nilakanta Sastri, The CōĻas, ch. on Kulottunga I

episodes.title: The Gods Take Shape at Deogarh
episodes.figure: The Master Sculptor of the Gupta Age
episodes.era: The classical moment of Indian art, 5th-early 6th century CE
episodes.region: Sarnath, Udayagiri and the Dashavatara temple at Deogarh
episodes.logline: Gupta stone-carvers give the Buddha his serene, wet-robed calm at Sarnath and raise Vishnu's temple at Deogarh with its soaring spire - setting the mould for sacred art across Asia for a thousand years.
episodes.moral: A true artist carves not just stone, but the way an age will imagine the divine.

sources.citation: The Sarnath Buddha (5th c.), Archaeological Museum, Sarnath
sources.note: Paradigm of classical Gupta Buddhist sculpture (dharmachakra mudra, transparent robes).

sources.citation: The Dashavatara (Vishnu) temple, Deogarh (early 6th c.); the Udayagiri Varaha relief (c. 401 CE)
sources.note: Early Nagara-style temple with sikhara; the earth-lifting Boar.

sources.citation: Michael Willis, The Archaeology of Hindu Ritual (2009); Walter Spink, Ajanta: History and Development (2005-2014)
sources.note: Recent scholarship on Udayagiri's meaning and Ajanta's compressed chronology.

episodes.notes: The 'classical' Gupta style synthesised the Mathura and Gandhara traditions into a serene, idealised norm copied across South and Southeast Asia. Key works: the Sarnath Buddha (clinging robes, downcast eyes, Wheel-of-Dharma gesture); the Deogarh Dashavatara temple (one of the earliest stone temples with a curvilinear sikhara - foundational for the NAGARA style; its Vishnu-on-the-serpent panel); the Udayagiri Varaha (Vishnu = Chandragupta II lifting the Earth - Michael Willis). RECENT: Walter Spink's compressed chronology dates Ajanta's great late phase to a burst c. 462-480 CE under the Gupta-allied Vakatakas. Hero is an anonymous master sculptor (craft theme, like the Chola bronze artists). Keep divine images reverent and accurate.

episodes.title: The Parade That Ended the Mauryas
episodes.era: End of the Maurya Empire, c. 185 BCE
episodes.region: Pataliputra and the fractured post-Ashokan empire
episodes.logline: At a military review, the general Pushyamitra kills the last Mauryan king Brihadratha, and the empire of Chandragupta and Ashoka gives way to the Shungas.
episodes.moral: An empire that cannot renew its bonds may fall from within.

sources.citation: Bana, Harshacharita, 7th century CE
sources.note: Later literary source for Pushyamitra assassinating Brihadratha during a military parade.

sources.citation: Ayodhya Inscription of Dhana
sources.note: Epigraphic evidence for Pushyamitra and his Ashvamedha sacrifices.

sources.citation: Romila Thapar, Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas (1961; 3rd ed. 1997); Upinder Singh (2008)
sources.note: Modern analysis of decline, fragmentation and the persecution debate.

episodes.notes: After Ashoka, the king-list becomes poorly attested: Kunala/Dasharatha, Samprati, Shalishuka, Devavarman, Shatadhanvan and Brihadratha are known mostly from Puranic lists with differing details. Pushyamitra's coup around 185 BCE is the accepted end of Mauryan rule, but Bana's assassination scene is a 7th-century literary account, not an eyewitness report. ACCURACY FLAGS: do not blame the fall simplistically on Ashoka's pacifism; historians also cite over-extension, loose network control, economic strain, succession fragmentation and external Indo-Greek pressure. Buddhist texts accuse Pushyamitra of persecution, but Thapar and others stress the lack of firm archaeological proof, Roman denarii anachronisms in Ashokavadana, and Shunga-period expansion at Bharhut and Sanchi. Show a contested, multifactor decline.

episodes.title: Tenali Rama Between Poet and Folktale
episodes.era: Krishnadevaraya's court and later folklore, c. 1480-1528 CE and after
episodes.region: Tenali, Vijayanagara court and Telugu literary tradition
episodes.logline: Behind the laughing trickster of children's tales stands Tenali Ramakrishna, an attested Telugu poet whose wit later bloomed into folklore.
episodes.moral: Enjoy legends, but honor the real person beneath them.

sources.citation: Tenali Ramakrishna, Panduranga Mahatmyam, manuscripts in Tanjore Sarasvati Mahal Library tradition
sources.note: Primary literary evidence for the historical poet.

sources.citation: Rao and Shulman, Classical Telugu Poetry: An Anthology (University of California Press, 2002)
sources.note: Context for Telugu court poetry and Panduranga Mahatmyam.

sources.citation: Tanjore Sarasvati Mahal Library catalogue
sources.note: Manuscript repository evidence for pre-modern Telugu works.

episodes.notes: Tenali Ramakrishna, also called Tenali Ramalinga, was a real Telugu poet associated with Krishnadevaraya's literary world and remembered as Vikatakavi, poet of wit. KEY FACTS: Panduranga Mahatmyam gives hard literary evidence of his stature, and the Ashtadiggajas link belongs to retrospective tradition. Accuracy flag: the famous Tenali Rama tales of impossible riddles, jester tricks and outwitting priests are mostly 17th-19th century folklore, culturally meaningful but not contemporary biography. Do NOT present individual jokes as court records, and treat the snakebite death story as traditional but not independently verified.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Songs, Wit and Shattered Walls

episodes.title: A Face in Stone a Body in Bronze
episodes.era: Mohenjo-daro sculpture and Harappan iconography, c. 2500-1900 BCE
episodes.region: Mohenjo-daro, with figurines and seals from many Harappan sites
