sources.citation: R.G. Bhandarkar, Nasik Inscriptions, Epigraphia Indica Vol. 8 (1906)
sources.note: Primary publication of the Cave 3 prashasti and grant records.

sources.citation: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum Vol. IV: Satavahana inscriptions
sources.note: Official inscription corpus for the Nashik records.

sources.citation: D.C. Sircar, Select Inscriptions Vol. I (1965); Upinder Singh (2008)
sources.note: Translations and modern cautions on the eulogy's claims.

episodes.notes: In the 19th regnal year of Pulumavi, Gautami Balashri, mother of Gautamiputra Satakarni and grandmother of the reigning king, commissioned one of the most important Satavahana inscriptions. It praises Gautamiputra as destroyer of Sakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas, restorer of Satavahana glory, and donor to Buddhist monks, while also describing Balashri's own virtues. This is an epigraphic women's-voice story: powerful, public and politically purposeful, but not proof that she was a formal queen-regnant. The phrase eka-bamhana and the territorial claims remain debated; do NOT treat a royal eulogy as a literal map.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahana Empire of the Deccan

episodes.title: Son of Gautami, Son of Vasishthi
episodes.era: Matronymic titulature across the dynasty, c. 1st-3rd century CE
episodes.region: Nashik, Karla, Kanheri and the wider Deccan
episodes.logline: Names like Gautamiputra and Vasishthiputra reveal how mothers, marriages and donations shaped Satavahana politics without making it matriarchy.
episodes.moral: Names can carry alliances as well as ancestry.

sources.citation: Nashik, Karla and Kanheri donor inscriptions, especially Epigraphia Indica Vol. 8
sources.note: Epigraphic evidence for matronymic royal names and women donors.

sources.citation: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India (2008)
sources.note: Clear modern explanation that matronymics do not prove matriarchy.

sources.citation: Richard Salomon, Indian Epigraphy (1998); Andrew Ollett, Language of the Snakes (2017)
sources.note: Epigraphic and language context for women's public inscriptions.

episodes.notes: Satavahana kings repeatedly identify themselves through mothers: Gautamiputra, Vasishthiputra and other matronymics. Scholars explain this as alliance politics in a polygynous royal house, where a prince's mother connected him to a particular elite lineage. Inscriptions also show queens, mothers, nuns and merchant wives making donations of caves, cisterns and villages, so women's property and religious agency were publicly recognized. The accuracy flag is crucial: this is social innovation in naming and donation practice, not evidence of matrilineal succession or a matriarchal state. The legal basis is inferred from inscriptions because no Satavahana law code survives.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahana Empire of the Deccan

episodes.title: The Hoard That Overstruck Nahapana
episodes.era: War with the Kshaharata ruler Nahapana, c. 60-125 CE debated
episodes.region: Jogalthambi and Nashik district, western Deccan
episodes.logline: Thousands of Nahapana's silver coins hammered with Gautamiputra's legend make conquest visible in metal.
episodes.moral: Power often leaves its clearest signature on money.

sources.citation: E.J. Rapson, Catalogue of Indian Coins in the British Museum: Andhras, Western Kshatrapas, etc. (1908)
sources.note: Classic documentation of Nahapana coins and Gautamiputra overstrikes.

sources.citation: Nashik Cave 3 inscriptions in Epigraphia Indica Vol. 8 (1906)
sources.note: Prashasti claim against the Kshaharatas and grant involving Ushavadata's former field.

sources.citation: Shailendra Bhandare, Numismatic Evidence and Satavahana Chronology, South Asian Studies 22:1 (2006)
sources.note: Recent chronological analysis of the coin evidence.

episodes.notes: This episode is the specific Jogalthambi hoard story, not the broader existing coin-over-Sakas episode. The hoard, reported from Nashik district, contained thousands of Nahapana silver karshapanas overstruck by Gautamiputra Satakarni; many still show the old portrait and legends beneath the new die. It materially confirms a political reversal and fits the Nashik prashasti's claim that Gautamiputra rooted out the Kshaharatas. The exact number of coins and the conquest date vary in scholarship, with estimates from roughly 8,000 to 13,000 coins and dates from c. 78 to c. 124 CE. Do NOT claim the hoard proves Nahapana's death or fixes an absolute year.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahana Empire of the Deccan

episodes.title: Lead, Potin and the Ship Coins
episodes.era: Satavahana monetary system, c. 1st century BCE-3rd century CE
episodes.region: Western and eastern Deccan coin zones
episodes.logline: Lead, potin and ship-marked coins turn Deccan metal resources and maritime imagination into a working money economy.
episodes.moral: Innovation can be minted from local materials.

sources.citation: E.J. Rapson, Catalogue of Indian Coins in the British Museum: Andhras, etc. (1908)
sources.note: Typology of Satavahana lead, potin, copper and ship-type coins.

sources.citation: Shailendra Bhandare, Numismatic Evidence and Satavahana Chronology (2006)
sources.note: Distribution analysis and chronological use of coinage.

sources.citation: Carla Sinopoli, Imperial Integration in the Satavahana Empire, in Empires (Cambridge UP, 2001)
sources.note: Economic integration and coin distribution in imperial archaeology.

episodes.notes: The Satavahanas made lead a major currency, unusual among large early Indian dynasties, and also issued potin, copper and occasional silver. Lead suited Deccan resources and local transactions, while ship-type coins of rulers such as Vasishthiputra Pulumavi and Yajna Sri Satakarni advertised maritime connections across western and eastern coasts. This is an economic innovation story about material choice, denomination and circulation, not a claim that coins replaced barter everywhere. Do NOT make every ship coin proof of a navy; the imagery signals maritime orientation and commercial identity, interpreted alongside port texts, inscriptions and find-spots.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahana Empire of the Deccan

episodes.title: Chisels in the Vaulted Dark
episodes.era: Western Deccan chaitya-grihas, c. 200 BCE-170 CE
episodes.region: Bhaja, Bedse, Nashik and Kanheri cave complexes
episodes.logline: Basalt workers translate wooden halls into stone at Bhaja, Bedse, Nashik and Kanheri, inventing sacred architecture inside living rock.
episodes.moral: Great engineering learns from older crafts.

sources.citation: James Fergusson and James Burgess, The Cave Temples of India (1880)
sources.note: Foundational architectural survey of western Indian rock-cut caves.

sources.citation: James Burgess, Report on the Buddhist Cave Temples and Their Inscriptions (ASI Western India, 1883)
sources.note: Cave inscriptions, including Kanheri and western Deccan donor records.

sources.citation: Pia Brancaccio, The Buddhist Caves at Ajanta (2011); Akira Shimada, Early Buddhist Architecture in Context (2012)
sources.note: Recent patronage and architectural phasing context.

episodes.notes: This scientific-engineering innovation follows the mechanics of rock-cut chaitya halls. At Bhaja, early craftsmen carved an apsidal hall with a barrel vault and surviving wooden ribs; at Bedse they elaborated facade arches and columns; at Nashik and Kanheri they extended the western Deccan cave tradition into complex monastic landscapes. The engineering challenge was to select basalt strata, lay out the building from the cliff face, remove rock without collapse, imitate timber forms in stone, and manage water through cisterns and drains. Do NOT attribute every cave to royal Satavahana funding; merchants, monks, nuns, officials and rival Kshaharatas also paid for parts of this world.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahana Empire of the Deccan

episodes.title: Pratishthana and the Aharas
episodes.era: Imperial administration, c. 1st-3rd century CE
episodes.region: Pratishthana/Paithan, Govardhana ahara and the Deccan districts
episodes.logline: From Paithan on the Godavari, Satavahana orders travel through aharas, amatyas, generals and feudatory lords who hold the Deccan together loosely.
episodes.moral: Large realms survive through networks, not commands alone.

sources.citation: Nashik Cave 3 administrative inscriptions, Epigraphia Indica Vol. 8 (1906)
sources.note: Named officers, village grants and immunities in the Govardhana ahara.

sources.citation: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, sections 52-53, Casson edition (1989)
sources.note: Paethana/Pratishthana as a major inland market-town.

sources.citation: Carla Sinopoli, Imperial Integration in the Satavahana Empire (2001); Himanshu Prabha Ray, Monastery and Guild (1986)
sources.note: Modern analysis of administrative and economic integration.

episodes.notes: Pratishthana, modern Paithan, appears in the Periplus as Paethana and in Ptolemy's geography as a royal center. The empire's working units included aharas such as Govardhana, with officers like Sivakhandila receiving royal instructions. Grants could exempt villages from entry by officials or interference by police, showing written administrative formulae. The Satavahana polity also depended on maharathis, mahabhojas, mahasenapatis, kumaras and local elites who could donate, marry into the dynasty and sometimes strike coins. Do NOT describe this as a Mauryan-style centralized bureaucracy; it was an integrated but negotiated Deccan network.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahana Empire of the Deccan

episodes.title: The Sailor's Notebook of Kalyan
episodes.era: Indo-Roman trade described c. 40-70 CE
episodes.region: Sopara, Kalyan, Chaul, Paithan and Tagara
episodes.logline: A Greek-speaking merchant's Periplus maps Deccan ports, cotton roads and guarded harbors far from the pepper world of Muziris.
episodes.moral: Trade routes are also political maps.

sources.citation: Lionel Casson, The Periplus Maris Erythraei (1989), sections 51-56
sources.note: Definitive modern edition of the Greek merchant handbook.

sources.citation: Wilfred Schoff, The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (1912)
sources.note: Classic translation and notes on Dachinabades ports.

sources.citation: Himanshu Prabha Ray, The Archaeology of Seafaring in Ancient South Asia (2003); Federico De Romanis and Marco Maiuro, Across the Ocean (2015)
sources.note: Archaeological and Indo-Mediterranean trade context.

episodes.notes: This is a Deccan port story distinct from the existing Muziris pepper episode. The Periplus describes Dachinabades south of Barygaza, naming Kalliena (usually Kalyan), Suppara (Sopara), Semyla (often Chaul), Paethana (Pratishthana) and Tagara. It lists cotton textiles, ivory, agate, carnelian and other goods moving inland and overseas, and says some foreign ships near Kalyan were escorted by royal boats to Barygaza, hinting at port regulation. Sopara also has older Ashokan evidence and cave-donor links. Do NOT call the Periplus a Roman official report; it is a Greek-language merchant guide from an Egyptian trading milieu, dated only broadly to c. 40-70 CE.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahana Empire of the Deccan

episodes.title: Prakrit Becomes the Language of Power
episodes.era: Royal Maharashtri Prakrit inscriptions, c. 1st century BCE-3rd century CE
episodes.region: Naneghat, Nashik, Karla, Kanheri and the Deccan
episodes.logline: Satavahana scribes choose Maharashtri Prakrit for royal commands and praise, making a regional language carry imperial authority.
episodes.moral: A language gains prestige when power speaks through it.

sources.citation: Satavahana inscriptions at Naneghat, Nashik, Karla and Kanheri
sources.note: Primary evidence that royal and donor records used Prakrit in Brahmi script.

sources.citation: Andrew Ollett, Language of the Snakes (University of California Press, 2017)
sources.note: Recent major study of Prakrit, Sanskrit and Satavahana language politics.

sources.citation: Sheldon Pollock, The Language of the Gods in the World of Men (2006)
sources.note: Context for Sanskrit and Prakrit as languages of political culture.

episodes.notes: Every major Satavahana royal inscription is in Maharashtri Prakrit, not Sanskrit. Ollett argues that this was not a passive vernacular habit but a prestige project that let Prakrit function as a language of power before later Sanskrit political inscription became dominant. This is the scholarly innovation episode: a regional literary register carrying genealogy, grants, conquest and ritual. It may mention Hala's Gatha Saptashati only as background, because the existing chapter already uses Hala and the Sattasai. Do NOT claim the Satavahanas rejected Sanskrit entirely or that Ollett's interpretation is the dynasty's own stated program.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahana Empire of the Deccan
episodes.chapter_part: V. The Word and the Afterlife

episodes.title: Gunadhya's Lost Great Tale
episodes.era: Legendary Satavahana literary memory, probably between c. 1st century BCE and 3rd century CE
episodes.region: Pratishthana, the Vindhya forest and later Kashmir tradition
episodes.logline: Gunadhya's lost Brihatkatha, remembered in Paishachi and later Sanskrit retellings, makes the Satavahana court a home for non-Sanskrit storytelling.
episodes.moral: Lost books can still shape living literature.

sources.citation: Somadeva, Kathasaritsagara, trans. C.H. Tawney and N.M. Penzer (1924-28)
sources.note: Principal later Sanskrit adaptation preserving the Gunadhya legend.

sources.citation: Bana, Harshacharita and Kadambari, 7th century CE
sources.note: Early references showing the Brihatkatha existed before Bana's time.

sources.citation: Sheldon Pollock, The Language of the Gods in the World of Men (2006); Andrew Ollett, Language of the Snakes (2017)
sources.note: Recent critical treatment of Paishachi, Prakrit prestige and Satavahana literary memory.

episodes.notes: The Brihatkatha itself is lost. Later tradition says Gunadhya, linked to a Satavahana court at Pratishthana, composed it in Paishachi, wrote it in blood in the forest, and burned much of it before a king rescued the remainder. That dramatic blood-and-fire story is legend from later narrative tradition. What is historically safer is that later works such as Somadeva's Kathasaritsagara, Kshemendra's Brihatkathamanjari and the Brihatkathashlokasamgraha point back to a famous earlier Great Tale, known before Bana in the 7th century. Do NOT describe Paishachi as a securely known spoken language or the Brihatkatha as surviving.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahana Empire of the Deccan
episodes.chapter_part: V. The Word and the Afterlife

episodes.title: When the Deccan Empire Split
episodes.era: Fragmentation after the late Satavahanas, c. 150-230 CE and after
episodes.region: Nashik, Andhra, Karnataka, Konkan and the far southeastern Deccan
episodes.logline: After defeats by Rudradaman and the fading of Pulumavi IV, Satavahana power breaks into Abhira, Ikshvaku, Chutu and other successor worlds.
episodes.moral: Empires often end by becoming many futures.

sources.citation: Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman I, c. 150 CE, translated in D.C. Sircar, Select Inscriptions Vol. I (1965)
sources.note: Primary evidence for Rudradaman's defeats of a Satakarni and a marriage link.

sources.citation: R. Subrahmanyam, Nagarjunakonda (1954-60): The Summary, ASI (1975)
sources.note: Evidence for Ikshvaku successor patronage and Buddhist monuments.

sources.citation: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India (2008); Shailendra Bhandare, Numismatic Evidence and Satavahana Chronology (2006)
sources.note: Modern synthesis of successor states and coin continuities.

episodes.notes: The Satavahana ending was a fragmentation rather than a single last battle. Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription says he defeated a Satakarni twice but spared him because of close connection, probably marriage alliance, showing diplomacy amid weakness. By the early 3rd century CE, after rulers often named as late Pulumavis, regional successors held the pieces: Abhiras around Nashik, Ikshvakus in the Krishna-Guntur/Nagarjunakonda zone, Chutus around Banavasi, collateral western lines and possibly early Pallavas with Prakrit epigraphic inheritance. Do NOT imply all these links are equally certain; Abhira, Ikshvaku and Chutu continuities are stronger than the debated Pallava connection.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahana Empire of the Deccan
episodes.chapter_part: V. The Word and the Afterlife

episodes.title: A Scholar Draws the Sword
episodes.era: Founding of the Kadamba kingdom, c. 345-365 CE
episodes.region: Talagunda, Kanchipuram, Sriparvata forests and Banavasi
episodes.logline: A Brahmin student leaves the Pallava college at Kanchi after a quarrel and turns the hand of ritual into the sword-hand of a new Kannada-country kingdom.
episodes.moral: A wounded dignity can become discipline, not mere rage.

sources.citation: Talagunda pillar inscription of Kakusthavarma, vv. 9-21; F. Kielhorn, Epigraphia Indica 8 (1906): 24-36
sources.note: Primary Kadamba narrative for Mayurasharma, Kanchi, the Pallava horseman quarrel and recognition.

sources.citation: Gudnapur inscription; discussed in K.V. Ramesh, Inscriptions of the Early Kadambas (ASI, 1984)
sources.note: Corroborates Mayurasharma's parentage and his assumption of kshatriya duty.

sources.citation: G.S. Gai, Inscriptions of the Early Kadambas (ICHR/Pratibha Prakashan, 1996); Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Medieval India (2016)
sources.note: Modern epigraphic corpus and synthesis for chronology and source cautions.

episodes.notes: The Talagunda pillar, a court prashasti composed about a century after the founding, says Mayurasharma of the Manavya gotra went from Talagunda with his guru Veerasharma to the ghatika at Kanchi and, after a fierce quarrel with a Pallava horseman, took up the sword. The core is attested, but the inscription does not say he was slapped, barred from study, or humiliated in a named ceremony; those are later dramatic expansions. Dates around c. 345-365 CE are reconstructed from genealogy and Pallava-Gupta synchronisms, so do NOT narrate exact regnal years as certain. Flag the transformation from sharma to varman as a political claim to kshatriya kingship, not proof of a simple caste conversion ritual.

episodes.title: Banavasi Between the Rivers
episodes.era: Kadamba capital and sacred landscape, c. 345-540 CE
episodes.region: Banavasi on the Varada river, Uttara Kannada, Karnataka
episodes.logline: On a bend of the Varada, Banavasi gathers forest routes, older Satakarni sanctuaries and the new Kadamba court into the first great capital of the Kannada country.
episodes.moral: A capital is strongest when geography, memory and power meet.

sources.citation: Talagunda pillar inscription, v. 34, in Kielhorn, Epigraphia Indica 8 (1906)
sources.note: Mentions the old Bhava temple worshipped by Satakarni and other kings and Kakusthavarma's tank.

sources.citation: Madhukeshvara temple, Banavasi, protected monument and epigraphic site; Karnataka archaeology reports
sources.note: Material focus for Banavasi's Shaiva sacred landscape with later Chalukya additions.

sources.citation: Suryanath U. Kamath, A Concise History of Karnataka (2001), pp. 30-32; K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India (1961), pp. 109-111
sources.note: Standard Karnataka and South Indian historical syntheses.

episodes.notes: Banavasi, also called Vaijayanti or Vaijayantipura in some records, was not an empty royal foundation: the region had Chutu-Satakarni and earlier sacred associations before Mayurasharma made it the Kadamba capital. The Talagunda inscription's reference to a temple of Bhava served by Satakarni and other kings is important evidence for pre-Kadamba sanctity. Do NOT move Xuanzang's seventh-century report of many Buddhist monasteries back into the fifth-century Kadamba period; it is useful afterlife context, not Kadamba-era proof. The present Madhukeshvara temple preserves a Kadamba foundation but its visible fabric includes Early and Later Chalukya changes.

episodes.title: Forest Fire in Sriparvata
episodes.era: Kadamba consolidation after the Kanchi quarrel, c. 345-365 CE
episodes.region: Sriparvata forests, Banavasi, Chandravalli and the Pallava frontier
episodes.logline: From the forest edge Mayurasharma raids, levies tribute and forces the Pallavas to recognize the kingdom that had begun as a student's fury.
episodes.moral: Rebellion becomes statecraft only when it wins order.

sources.citation: Talagunda pillar inscription, vv. 13-22; Kielhorn, Epigraphia Indica 8 (1906)
sources.note: Primary account of the Sriparvata base, night attacks, taxes and Pallava recognition.

sources.citation: Chandravalli rock inscription of Mayurasharma; cited in Kamath, A Concise History of Karnataka (2001), p. 31
sources.note: Lists defeated or confronted powers in a royal proclamation.

sources.citation: Halasi copper plates of Kakusthavarma; J.F. Fleet, Indian Antiquary 6 (1877): 22-27; G.S. Gai (1996)
sources.note: Retrospective evidence for Mayurasharma's ashvamedha claims and brahmadeya gifts.

episodes.notes: The Talagunda text describes Mayurasharma taking shelter in the Sriparvata forests, levying taxes on nearby rulers and troubling Pallava camps until the Pallava lords accepted him as friend and sovereign. The Chandravalli inscription expands the conquest list with Traikutas, Abhiras, Sendrakas, Pallavas, Punnatas and others, but it is a victory boast and should be treated as political rhetoric. The Halasi plates' claim that Mayurasharma performed ashvamedha sacrifices shows the new dynasty adopting Sanskritic sovereignty symbols. Do NOT claim a conquest from Gokarna to Kanyakumari or invent battle numbers; the sources give no such scale.
episodes.chapter_part: II. Iron Warriors and Royal Alliances

episodes.title: Kakusthavarma Bridegroom of Empires
episodes.era: Kadamba zenith and inter-dynastic diplomacy, c. 425-450 CE
episodes.region: Banavasi, Halasi, the Gupta world and Vakataka Kuntala links
episodes.logline: Kakusthavarma raises Banavasi to its diplomatic height, sending daughters into Gupta and allied courts while ruling a kingdom powerful enough to be courted.
episodes.moral: Alliances can extend a kingdom farther than armies alone.

sources.citation: Talagunda pillar inscription, vv. 30-34; Kielhorn, Epigraphia Indica 8 (1906)
sources.note: Primary evidence for Kakusthavarma's daughters marrying into Gupta and other royal families.

sources.citation: Halasi copper plates of Kakusthavarma; Fleet, Indian Antiquary 6 (1877); Gai, Inscriptions of the Early Kadambas (1996)
sources.note: Evidence for his Jain invocation and royal grants.

sources.citation: A.S. Altekar in The Vakataka-Gupta Age (repr. 2007), p. 106; Nilakanta Sastri (1961), p. 111
sources.note: Scholarly identification of a likely Kadamba princess in Vakataka records.

episodes.notes: Kakusthavarma is the dynasty's high point, but the evidence is still epigraphic poetry, not a court diary. The Talagunda verse says his daughters awakened the lotus-beds of Gupta and other royal families, which securely indicates matrimonial alliances, but it does not name the Gupta princes. The Vakataka link through Ajjhitabhattarika of Kuntala is probable, not directly named as Kakusthavarma's daughter in a Kadamba inscription. Do NOT say Kakusthavarma married a Gupta princess himself; the source says he gave daughters outward. His Halasi plates opening with Jayati Bhagavan Jinendra also show Jain patronage within a Brahmanical royal framework.
episodes.chapter_part: II. Iron Warriors and Royal Alliances

episodes.title: Three Crowns and a Divided Realm
episodes.era: Santivarma and the Triparvatha split, c. 450-475 CE
episodes.region: Talagunda, Banavasi and the debated Triparvatha country
episodes.logline: Santivarma wears the fame of three crowns but divides the Kadamba realm, creating a Triparvatha branch that will both defend and fracture the house.
episodes.moral: Shared power can protect a realm and endanger it at once.

sources.citation: Talagunda pillar inscription, v. 34; Kielhorn, Epigraphia Indica 8 (1906)
sources.note: Names Santivarma, three crowns and poet Kubja's commissioned inscription.

sources.citation: Halasi copper plates of Mrigeshavarma; G.S. Gai, Inscriptions of the Early Kadambas (1996)
sources.note: Evidence for succession after Santivarma and later conflict.

sources.citation: George M. Moraes, The Kadamba Kula (1931), pp. 28-30; Noboru Karashima ed., A Concise History of South India (2014), p. 369
sources.note: Historical reconstruction of the split and chronology.

episodes.notes: Santivarma, Kakusthavarma's son, commissioned the Talagunda pillar through the poet Kubja and is remembered there as adorned with three crowns. The Kadamba realm then split between the Banavasi line and the cadet Triparvatha line, commonly tied to Krishnavarma I and Pallava pressure. The exact location of Triparvatha is debated, with Dharwad-region and other identifications proposed, and the causes of the split are reconstructed rather than fully narrated by sources. Do NOT present the division as a neat administrative reform only; dynastic politics and frontier defense may both have mattered.
episodes.chapter_part: II. Iron Warriors and Royal Alliances

episodes.title: Mrigeshavarma Breaks the Ganga Line
episodes.era: Kadamba military revival, c. 475-519 CE
episodes.region: Banavasi, Halasi, Davanagere, Talakad and the Pallava frontier
episodes.logline: Mrigeshavarma and Ravivarma answer Pallava and Ganga pressure with a late Kadamba revival recorded in copper plates and temple grants.
episodes.moral: A dynasty can flare again before it fades.

sources.citation: Halasi copper plates of Mrigeshavarma and Ravivarma; Fleet, Indian Antiquary 6 (1877); Gai (1996)
sources.note: Primary records for victories, Jain gifts and Halasi patronage.

sources.citation: Davanagere copper plates of Ravivarma, dated 519 CE; discussed by D.C. Sircar in The Classical Age (1997)
sources.note: One chronological anchor for late Kadamba power.

sources.citation: P.B. Desai, Jainism in South India and Some Jaina Epigraphs (1957), pp. 97-110; Upinder Singh (2016), pp. 526-527
sources.note: Jain epigraphy and late Kadamba synthesis.

episodes.notes: Mrigeshavarma's records call him a destroyer of the Gangas and a fire to the Pallavas, and Ravivarma's Davanagere plates, dated 519 CE, anchor the chronology of the late Banavasi branch. Ravivarma's claims to broad suzerainty, sometimes read as Narmada-to-Kaveri influence, are copper-plate royal boasts and must be treated with caution. The same records also reveal Jain patronage, including villages and temples at Palasika/Halasi. Do NOT make Pujyapada's residence at Ravivarma's court certain; the association is important but not documented as a direct appointment letter.
episodes.chapter_part: III. Wars, Recovery and the Handoff

episodes.title: The Lion Banner Passes to Badami
episodes.era: End of early Kadamba independence, c. 519-543 CE
episodes.region: Banavasi, Triparvatha and Badami in northern Karnataka
episodes.logline: As Harivarma loses the Banavasi line to Krishnavarma II, a Chalukya house at Badami rises from the Kadamba shadow and inherits the stage.
episodes.moral: Every ending becomes the ground beneath another beginning.

sources.citation: Halasi copper plates of Harivarma and related Kadamba records; Gai, Inscriptions of the Early Kadambas (1996)
sources.note: Late Banavasi-branch evidence.

sources.citation: Badami cave inscription of Mangalesha, Saka 465 / 543 CE; K.V. Ramesh readings
sources.note: Chronological marker for early Chalukya assertion after Kadamba decline.

sources.citation: Moraes, The Kadamba Kula (1931), pp. 50-55; Kamath, A Concise History of Karnataka (2001), pp. 38-40
sources.note: Reconstruction of Kadamba-Chalukya transition and shared gotra claims.

episodes.notes: Harivarma is the last known Banavasi-branch ruler; Krishnavarma II of the Triparvatha line appears to have briefly reunified Kadamba power before the Badami Chalukyas rose around 543 CE. Chalukya inscriptions share Manavya-gotra and Hariti-putra formulas with the Kadambas, but that may be political adoption as much as descent. This story must hand off to, not duplicate, the separate Chalukyas and Rashtrakutas chapter. A one-line afterlife may mention later Goa Kadambas and maritime Gopakapattana only as a much later dynasty, c. 960-1345 CE, not as early Banavasi history.
episodes.chapter_part: III. Wars, Recovery and the Handoff

episodes.title: The Stone That Speaks Kannada
episodes.era: Early Kannada epigraphy, conventionally c. 450-500 CE
episodes.region: Halmidi village, Hassan district, Karnataka
episodes.logline: A short land-grant record at Halmidi turns Kannada from speech and poetry into the language of official stone.
episodes.moral: A language enters history when power learns to write it down.

sources.citation: Halmidi inscription; M.H. Krishna, Mysore Archaeological Department Report (1936); G.S. Gai (1996), pp. 297-305
sources.note: Primary Old Kannada land-grant record, undated and debated.

sources.citation: K.V. Ramesh, Inscriptions of the Early Kadambas (ASI, 1984); D.C. Sircar's epigraphic discussions
sources.note: Contrasting views on dating and Kadamba attribution.

sources.citation: Talagunda Lion Balustrade inscription, excavated 2013 and published by ASI in 2016
sources.note: Recent Kannada-Sanskrit bilingual find that may predate Halmidi.

episodes.notes: INNOVATION STORY - SCHOLARLY/LANGUAGE. Halmidi is conventionally celebrated as the earliest substantial Kannada-language inscription and is usually dated c. 450-500 CE in the Kadamba-Ganga world of land grants. Its exact date and Kadamba royal attribution are debated: M.H. Krishna proposed about 450 CE, many scholars prefer fifth century or about 500, D.C. Sircar argued later, and G.S. Gai questioned whether its Kakustha belongs to the royal Kadambas. Since the 2013 Talagunda Lion Balustrade inscription, published in 2016 and dated by ASI to c. 370 CE, may be older, do NOT call Halmidi definitively the oldest Kannada inscription without qualifiers. Safest claim: Halmidi is the oldest widely recognized substantial Kannada inscription and a landmark in using Kannada for administration.

episodes.title: Kubja Carves a Poem in Stone
episodes.era: Talagunda literary inscription, c. 455-470 CE
episodes.region: Praneshvara temple, Talagunda, Shivamogga district
episodes.logline: The court poet Kubja turns a granite pillar into Sanskrit kavya, preserving genealogy, politics and the Kadamba script in thirty-four crafted verses.
episodes.moral: History lasts longer when memory learns an artful form.

sources.citation: B.L. Rice, Epigraphia Carnatica vol. 7, inscription 176 (1902); F. Kielhorn, Epigraphia Indica 8 (1906): 24-36
sources.note: Editions and translations of the Talagunda pillar inscription.

sources.citation: D.C. Sircar, Select Inscriptions Bearing on Indian History and Civilisation, vol. 1, 2nd ed. (1965)
sources.note: Standard epigraphic selection including the inscription.

sources.citation: G.S. Gai, Inscriptions of the Early Kadambas (1996)
sources.note: Modern critical corpus for Kadamba inscriptions and script forms.

episodes.notes: INNOVATION STORY - SCHOLARLY/ARTISTIC. The Talagunda pillar is more than a source for Mayurasharma: it is an early Deccan example of a dynastic past shaped as polished Sanskrit kavya by a named poet, Kubja. Kielhorn identified its meters and noted its literary sophistication; the inscription itself says Kubja had his poem placed on the stone at Santivarma's order. The script belongs to the Kadamba script stream, ancestral to later Kannada and related southern scripts, but do NOT say the Kadambas invented writing or that Kubja was a Kannada poet; this inscription is Sanskrit. The 2013 Talagunda balustrade find deepens the site's language history.

episodes.title: The Stepped Pyramid Spire
episodes.era: Early Kadamba temple architecture, c. 4th-6th centuries CE
episodes.region: Halasi, Talagunda, Banavasi and later Deccan temple sites
episodes.logline: Plain horizontal tiers rise above the sanctum, creating the Kadamba shikhara that later Chalukya and Hoysala builders will remember.
episodes.moral: A simple form can carry a civilization's signature.

sources.citation: Halasi temple complex and Jain basadi, ASI protected monuments; A. Sundara and K.G. Bhatsoori, Archaeology in Karnataka (1990)
sources.note: Material evidence for early Kadamba and related structures.

sources.citation: Talagunda pillar inscription and Halasi copper plates, in Gai (1996)
sources.note: Textual references to temples, tanks and Jain construction.

sources.citation: Suryanath U. Kamath, A Concise History of Karnataka (2001), pp. 36-38; Upinder Singh (2016), pp. 526-527
sources.note: Architectural synthesis and Kadamba-nagara interpretation.

episodes.notes: INNOVATION STORY - ENGINEERING/ART. The Kadamba-nagara or Kadamba shikhara is a stepped, horizontal-tiered tower over a square sanctum, often plain and capped by a finial, distinct from more elaborate northern and southern forms. This is a scholarly architectural category, not an inscriptional boast, so phrase invention as an art-historical judgment. Halasi and Talagunda provide key evidence, while Banavasi's Madhukeshvara temple preserves a Kadamba foundation but much later fabric. Do NOT call the current Madhukeshvara temple wholly Kadamba or attribute every Halasi sculpture to a named king unless an inscription says so.

episodes.title: A Roman Coin in the Deccan Forest
episodes.era: Pre-Kadamba trade routes and Kadamba economic inheritance, 1st-6th centuries CE
episodes.region: Chandravalli near Chitradurga and Banavasi trade zones
episodes.logline: Roman denarii, a Han coin and Kadamba records show that Banavasi's rulers inherited an old Deccan trade world and stamped it with local power.
episodes.moral: Wise rulers build on routes that existed before them.

sources.citation: R. Narasimhachar, Chandravalli excavation report (1909); M.H. Krishna, Mysore Archaeological Department Report (1929); Mortimer Wheeler ASI excavations (1947)
sources.note: Excavation evidence for megalithic and Satavahana-period occupation and foreign coins.

sources.citation: Chandravalli rock inscription of Mayurasharma; cited in Kamath (2001), p. 31 and Ramesh (1984)
sources.note: Kadamba royal presence near the site.

sources.citation: Kadamba copper coins with lion and Kannada legends, including Banavasi Srimanaragi report; Karnataka archaeology reports
sources.note: Evidence for local coinage and Kannada-script legends, with attribution cautions.

episodes.notes: INNOVATION STORY - ECONOMIC. Chandravalli's Roman denarii of Augustus, a Han coin and a Roman bulla prove long-distance contacts in the pre-Kadamba Satavahana-era Deccan, while Mayurasharma's rock inscription ties the early Kadambas to this strategic landscape. Do NOT claim the Kadambas traded directly with Rome; the Roman and Han finds predate them. The Kadamba contribution is better framed as inheriting trade corridors and adding local agrarian grants, coinage and Kannada-script legends to the economic world. Recent reports of a Banavasi coin reading Srimanaragi are important but should be treated cautiously until fully published in peer-reviewed numismatic form.

episodes.title: The Agrahara Village Machine
episodes.era: Kadamba land-grant economy, c. 345-540 CE
episodes.region: Talagunda, Banavasi, Halasi, Sirsi and brahmadeya villages
episodes.logline: Tax-free villages, Vedic teachers and temple endowments turn conquest into a durable settlement economy across the Kannada country.
episodes.moral: Institutions outlast victories when they root power in daily life.

sources.citation: Halasi copper plates of Kakusthavarma; Fleet, Indian Antiquary 6 (1877); Gai (1996)
sources.note: Records Mayurasharma's ashvamedha prestige and 144 brahmadeya grants.

sources.citation: Talagunda pillar inscription, vv. 4-8; Kielhorn, Epigraphia Indica 8 (1906)
sources.note: Describes the Sthanagundur agrahara ancestry and Brahmin learning.

sources.citation: R.S. Sharma, Indian Feudalism (rev. ed. 2005); B.D. Chattopadhyaya, The Making of Early Medieval India (1994); Upinder Singh (2016)
sources.note: Frameworks for land grants, Brahmanical settlement and early medieval state formation.

episodes.notes: INNOVATION STORY - SOCIAL/ECONOMIC. The Kadambas made brahmadeya and agrahara grants central to state-making: tax-free villages supported Brahmin teachers, ritual specialists, temples and record-keeping. Halasi records credit Mayurasharma with 144 such grants, while Talagunda presents the dynasty itself as emerging from an agrahara world. Do NOT claim all 144 villages have been archaeologically identified. Also treat the later Havyaka Brahmin tradition of Ahichatra origin as tradition rather than directly inscriptional fact; the grant network is attested, but community descent details require caution.

episodes.title: Between Shiva and the Jina
episodes.era: Kadamba religious patronage, c. 345-540 CE
episodes.region: Banavasi, Talagunda and Halasi
episodes.logline: Shaiva temples, Jain invocations and learned monks share the Kadamba court, revealing a kingdom built through plural patronage rather than a single sectarian banner.
episodes.moral: A durable culture can honor more than one sacred path.

sources.citation: Halasi copper plates of Kakusthavarma and Mrigeshavarma; Fleet (1877), Desai (1957), Gai (1996)
sources.note: Jain invocation Jayati Bhagavan Jinendra and Jain donations.

sources.citation: Talagunda pillar inscription; Kielhorn, Epigraphia Indica 8 (1906)
sources.note: Shaiva invocation, genealogy and temple-tank context.

sources.citation: P.B. Desai, Jainism in South India and Some Jaina Epigraphs (1957); Vilas Sangave, Jainism in Karnataka (1981); Upinder Singh (2016)
sources.note: Religious pluralism and Jain patronage debate.

episodes.notes: Kadamba public identity combined Manavya-gotra Brahmanical genealogy, dharmamaharaja titles and Shaiva temple landscapes with substantial Jain patronage. Kakusthavarma's Halasi plates open with a Jain invocation, Mrigeshavarma and later rulers supported Jain institutions at Palasika/Halasi, and the Madhukeshvara and Praneshvara temples anchor Shaiva memory. Scholars disagree over whether individual kings were personally Jain, Shaiva, Vaishnava or Brahmanical patrons with broad tolerance; no inscription provides a simple conversion story. Do NOT claim any Kadamba king converted to Jainism, and do NOT treat Xuanzang's later Buddhist Banavasi as proof of early Kadamba Buddhist patronage.

episodes.title: Yaduraya Takes the Name of Lord
episodes.era: Traditional founding of Mysore, c. 1399; hard epigraphic baseline by 1551
episodes.region: Mysore town, the Vijayanagara world, and later court memory
episodes.logline: A small Mysore chiefdom remembers Yaduraya as its founder, but the oldest secure Wodeyar evidence begins much later than the royal legend says.
episodes.moral: Origins become stronger when legends and evidence are kept apart.

sources.citation: Annals of the Mysore Royal Family, Part II (Government Branch Press, Mysore, 1922)
sources.note: Court genealogy preserving the traditional 1399 foundation story.

sources.citation: Timmaraja II copper-plate inscription, 1551
sources.note: Earliest known Wodeyar-issued inscription; a hard baseline for the dynasty's self-documentation.

sources.citation: Aya Ikegame, Princely India Re-imagined (Routledge, 2013)
sources.note: Recent analysis of Wodeyar dynastic legitimation and later Puranic ancestry claims.

episodes.notes: The traditional account makes Yaduraya, sometimes linked to the Urs clan, a Vijayanagara-backed lord of Mysore around 1399, ruling a small cluster of villages rather than a large kingdom. KEY FACTS: the Wodeyars began as local feudatories inside the Vijayanagara political order, and their later court genealogies claimed Lunar Dynasty and Dwarka descent. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Ikegame and other modern historians read those divine-origin claims as legitimation strategies of a post-Vijayanagara royal house. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim that a contemporary Vijayanagara inscription proves 1399; do NOT present descent from Krishna or Dwarka as history rather than royal mythology.

episodes.title: Raja Wodeyar Takes the Island Fort
episodes.era: Rise after Vijayanagara's decline, especially 1578-1617 and the seizure of 1610
episodes.region: Srirangapatna, Mysore, the Kaveri island fort and Melukote
episodes.logline: Raja Wodeyar I seizes Srirangapatna in 1610 and turns Vijayanagara ritual inheritance into Mysore sovereignty.
episodes.moral: A new power often speaks through the ceremonies it inherits.

sources.citation: Annals of the Mysore Royal Family, Part II (1922)
sources.note: Palace tradition for Raja Wodeyar I and the Srirangapatna transfer.

sources.citation: Cheluvarayaswami Temple traditions and records at Melukote
sources.note: Associated with Raja Wodeyar I's crown donation and Vaishnava patronage.

sources.citation: Phillip B. Wagoner, 'Sultan Among Hindu Kings,' Journal of Asian Studies 55.4 (1996)
sources.note: Context for Vijayanagara political ritual and successor-state sovereignty.

episodes.notes: In 1610 Raja Wodeyar I took Srirangapatna from the Aravidu Vijayanagara viceroy Tirumalla and made the Kaveri island fort the effective capital of Mysore. KEY FACTS: the same year is remembered as the beginning of Mysore Dasara, continuing the Vijayanagara Mahanavami grammar of kingship while marking independent Wodeyar authority. The story belongs to the dynasty's rise after Talikota, not to the Vijayanagara chapter itself. ACCURACY FLAGS: the Alamelamma curse is folklore and should not be narrated as fact; the 1610 Dasara date rests heavily on palace tradition, even though the political shift is widely accepted.

episodes.title: Kanthirava Mints a Kingdom
episodes.era: Ranadhira Kanthirava's reign, 1638-1659
episodes.region: Srirangapatna, Satyamangalam, Yelahanka and the southern Mysore frontier
episodes.logline: Kanthirava Narasaraja I defends Srirangapatna, expands Mysore and stamps sovereignty into silver Kanthiraya coins.
episodes.moral: Institutions can make a victory last longer than a battle.

sources.citation: Kanthiraya coins in South Indian and museum numismatic collections
sources.note: Physical evidence for Mysore's early royal coinage.

sources.citation: Imperial Gazetteer of India: Provincial Series, Mysore and Coorg (1908)
sources.note: British-era synthesis of the Bijapur siege and territorial expansion.

sources.citation: Sanjay Subrahmanyam, The Political Economy of Commerce: Southern India, 1500-1650 (1990)
sources.note: Discusses commerce, Jesuit records and the circulation of Mysore coinage.

episodes.notes: Kanthirava Narasaraja I, remembered as Ranadhira Kanthirava, repulsed Bijapur pressure on Srirangapatna and expanded toward Satyamangalam and other southern zones. INNOVATION: his Kanthiraya coins, later known to Europeans as Canteroy, gave Mysore a durable monetary symbol of sovereignty and circulated long after his reign. Jesuit records from Leonardo Cinnami's 1649 mission reveal a court connected to wider Deccan and European networks. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT inflate all later Wodeyar conquests into Kanthirava's reign; treat coin specimens as firmer evidence than heroic later memory.

episodes.title: Chikka Devaraja Builds Eighteen Offices
episodes.era: Expansion and reform, 1673-1704; Attara Kacheri c. 1700
episodes.region: Srirangapatna, Bangalore, Nanjanagudu and Mysore's expanding state
episodes.logline: Chikka Devaraja Wodeyar turns a growing war-state into a bureaucracy of eighteen offices, while leaving behind both reforms and hard memories.
episodes.moral: Good governance must be judged with its costs in view.

sources.citation: Imperial Gazetteer of India: Mysore and Coorg (1908)
sources.note: Attara Kacheri, Mughal alliance, Bangalore purchase and expansion details.

sources.citation: Chikka Devaraja's Gitagopalam and Chikadevaraya Binnopam manuscripts, Oriental Research Institute, Mysore
sources.note: Surviving works that show the ruler's literary patronage.

sources.citation: D. R. Nagaraj, Allama Prabhu and the Shaiva Movement in Karnataka (2003)
sources.note: Modern social-history discussion of Jangama resistance and repression.

episodes.notes: Chikka Devaraja Wodeyar expanded Mysore, purchased Bangalore in 1687 and reorganised administration into the Attara Kacheri, the celebrated eighteen departments. INNOVATION: this was a governance story, moving Mysore toward a more formal fiscal and bureaucratic state, likely influenced by Deccan and Mughal models after diplomatic exchanges with Aurangzeb's court. He was also a Kannada and Srivaishnava literary patron. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT present a complete modern organisational chart unless using palace records directly; do NOT omit the reported violent suppression of Jangama-backed tax resistance at Nanjanagudu.

episodes.title: Hyder Ali Holds the Throne in Shadow
episodes.figure: Hyder Ali and Krishnaraja Wodeyar II
episodes.era: Hyder Ali's effective rule, c. 1761-1782
episodes.region: Srirangapatna, the Carnatic, Kolar and the Mysore army
episodes.logline: Hyder Ali rises from commander to sarvadhikari, leaving the Wodeyars on the throne but taking power into his own military state.
episodes.moral: Power can shift without the crown visibly moving.

sources.citation: Report of the Committee of Secrecy into the Causes of the War in the Carnatic (1781-1782)
sources.note: East India Company parliamentary record for the Mysore wars.

sources.citation: Kate Brittlebank, Tipu Sultan's Search for Legitimacy (Oxford University Press, 1997)
sources.note: Analyses Hyder and Tipu's use of Wodeyar legitimacy.

sources.citation: Mohibbul Hasan, History of Tipu Sultan (reprint, 2005)
sources.note: Balanced account of the Mysore state before and under Tipu.

episodes.notes: By about 1761 Hyder Ali had become Mysore's effective ruler, while Krishnaraja Wodeyar II remained a ceremonial sovereign. KEY FACTS: Hyder's rise was a military-administrative takeover inside an eighteenth-century world of Maratha, Nizam, French and Company competition; his army used disciplined infantry, artillery and rocket troops. The Wodeyars were sidelined but not erased, because their dynastic legitimacy remained useful. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT frame this as a communal conquest of a Hindu kingdom; it was a political and military transfer of power in a mixed Deccan environment.

episodes.title: Tipu Sultan's Iron Rockets
episodes.era: Tipu Sultan's rule, 1782-1799
episodes.region: Srirangapatna, Pollilur, Malabar, the Carnatic and diplomatic routes to Europe and West Asia
episodes.logline: Tipu Sultan expands Mysore's iron-cased rockets and state experiments, becoming both an anti-Company innovator and a deeply contested ruler.
episodes.moral: A complex past must be told without flattening either achievement or harm.

sources.citation: William Kirkpatrick, Select Letters of Tippoo Sultan (1811)
sources.note: Translated administrative letters from Tipu's Persian correspondence.

sources.citation: Mysorean rockets captured at Srirangapatna, Royal Artillery collections
sources.note: Physical evidence for iron-cased rocket technology.

sources.citation: R. Narasimha et al., 'Rockets in Eighteenth-Century India,' Current Science 43.4 (1985)
sources.note: Technical analysis of Mysorean rocket design and performance.

episodes.notes: Tipu Sultan enlarged the military and administrative system inherited from Hyder Ali, including iron-cased rocket brigades whose captured examples influenced British Congreve rockets. INNOVATION: he experimented with coinage, calendars, departments, sericulture and diplomacy while fighting the East India Company. His record also includes attested coercion and forced conversions in regions such as Coorg and Malabar, alongside anti-colonial resistance and economic ambition. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT call Tipu the world's first user of war rockets as fact; earlier rocket traditions existed, so attribute grand claims to later admirers and stress improvement and scale.

episodes.title: The Child Maharaja Returns
episodes.era: Fall of Tipu and Wodeyar restoration, 1799; Commission period from 1831
episodes.region: Srirangapatna, Mysore city and Company India
episodes.logline: After Tipu dies at Srirangapatna in 1799, a four-year-old Wodeyar is restored under British suzerainty, saving the dynasty but not full sovereignty.
episodes.moral: Restoration can be both rescue and restraint.

sources.citation: Alexander Beatson, A View of the Origin and Conduct of the War with Tippoo Sultaun (1800)
sources.note: Contemporary British account of the 1799 siege.

sources.citation: British Library India Office Records, Wellesley's 1799 Mysore dispatches
sources.note: Company records for the restoration and subsidiary alliance.

sources.citation: Janaki Nair, Mysore Modern: Rethinking the Region Under Princely Rule (2011)
sources.note: Recent analysis of restoration, Commission rule and princely modernity.

episodes.notes: On 4 May 1799 British forces stormed Srirangapatna and Tipu Sultan died near the Water Gate. The Company restored four-year-old Krishnaraja Wodeyar III under a subsidiary alliance, shifting the capital back to Mysore while keeping decisive British influence over the state. KEY FACTS: in 1831 the British took direct administration under the Mysore Commission, and in 1881 power was restored again to the Wodeyar line. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT state the Mir Sadiq treachery story as settled fact; present it only as a repeated and contested allegation.

episodes.title: Mummadi Opens the Treasury of Knowledge
episodes.era: Restored Mysore's cultural revival, 1799-1868
episodes.region: Mysore Palace, Jagan Mohan Palace and the Oriental Research Institute
episodes.logline: Mummadi Krishnaraja Wodeyar III turns palace memory into manuscripts, paintings and a visual encyclopedia of gods, games and yoga.
episodes.moral: A court can preserve knowledge when it becomes a workshop.

sources.citation: Sritattvanidhi manuscript, Oriental Research Institute, University of Mysore
sources.note: Royal illuminated compendium attributed to Krishnaraja Wodeyar III.

sources.citation: Devachandra, Rajavali Katha
sources.note: Court chronicle produced under Wodeyar patronage and important for Mysore historical memory.

sources.citation: Norman Sjoman, The Yoga Tradition of the Mysore Palace (1996; rev. 1999)
sources.note: Modern study and translation of the Sritattvanidhi yoga material.

episodes.notes: Krishnaraja Wodeyar III, known as Mummadi, was restored as a child but became the dynasty's great scholar-patron. INNOVATION: the Sritattvanidhi, an illuminated multi-volume Kannada compendium, codified iconography, ritual imagery and a section of yoga postures, giving the Mysore painting school a palace reference work. The Jagan Mohan Palace and court ateliers preserve his artistic world, while Devachandra's Rajavali Katha shaped later Mysore historical memory. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT assign a precise composition year to the Sritattvanidhi; the manuscript is not securely dated internally.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Palace of Learning and Image

episodes.title: The Mysore Durbar Becomes a Public Stage
episodes.figure: Krishnaraja Wodeyar III and Chamaraja Wodeyar X
episodes.era: Nineteenth-century palace culture and civic transition, 1805-1894
episodes.region: Mysore Palace, Jagan Mohan Palace and the restored princely capital
episodes.logline: The palace durbar transforms Dasara into a public stage where art, authority and civic Mysore meet.
episodes.moral: Ritual survives by learning to include a wider public.

sources.citation: Mysore Palace Dasara records and Annals of the Mysore Royal Family (1922)
sources.note: Court record tradition for durbar practice and dynastic ceremony.

sources.citation: Vikram Sampath, Splendours of Royal Mysore (Rupa, 2008)
sources.note: Modern synthesis of palace culture, music and Wodeyar patronage.

sources.citation: Aya Ikegame, Princely India Re-imagined (2013)
sources.note: Analysis of royal ritual, legitimacy and post-1799 princely identity.

episodes.notes: Krishnaraja Wodeyar III is credited with elaborating the special royal Dasara durbar from 1805, turning palace ceremony into a public grammar of restored Wodeyar legitimacy. The nineteenth century also saw palace painting, music, genealogy and civic institutions become tools for a dynasty ruling under British oversight. Chamaraja Wodeyar X's 1881 rendition era prepared the ground for representative and modernising institutions without erasing royal spectacle. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT confuse Raja Wodeyar I's 1610 Dasara foundation at Srirangapatna with Mummadi's later palace durbar elaboration.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Palace of Learning and Image

episodes.title: Shivanasamudra Lights Bangalore
episodes.figure: K. Seshadri Iyer and Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV
episodes.era: Hydroelectric Mysore, 1898-1905
episodes.region: Shivanasamudra Falls, Kolar Gold Fields, Bangalore and Mysore State
episodes.logline: Mysore harnesses the Kaveri at Shivanasamudra in 1902, sending power across distance to mines and then to Bangalore's electric streets.
episodes.moral: Science serves society when power is carried beyond the waterfall.

sources.citation: Mysore Electricity Department annual reports after 1902
sources.note: Administrative record for the Shivanasamudra hydroelectric scheme.

sources.citation: Imperial Gazetteer of India: Mysore and Coorg (1908)
sources.note: Contemporary reference to Mysore's hydroelectric development.

sources.citation: M. Visvesvaraya, Memoirs of My Working Life (Government of Mysore, 1951)
sources.note: Engineer-statesman's recollections of modern Mysore works.

episodes.notes: Under Dewan K. Seshadri Iyer and the regency for young Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV, Mysore built the Shivanasamudra hydroelectric station, opened in 1902, to power the Kolar Gold Fields. INNOVATION: it was India's first large-scale hydroelectric power station and an early Asian long-distance AC transmission project, later helping electrify Bangalore in 1905. This engineering story belongs to the Model State, not to a mere royal biography. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT state unqualified that Bangalore was the first city in Asia with electric street lights; say reportedly or among the earliest in Asia.
episodes.chapter_part: V. The Model State and the Republic

episodes.title: Visvesvaraya Raises the KRS Dam
episodes.figure: M. Visvesvaraya and Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV
episodes.era: KRS project, foundation 1911; dam built 1924; completion work to 1931
episodes.region: Kannambadi, Krishna Raja Sagara, Mandya, Mysore and the Kaveri basin
episodes.logline: Visvesvaraya and Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV turn the Kaveri into a reservoir of irrigation, drinking water and automatic engineering.
episodes.moral: A dam is strongest when imagination and public need hold together.

sources.citation: M. Visvesvaraya, Memoirs of My Working Life (1951)
sources.note: Primary account for the KRS project, opposition and engineering decisions.

sources.citation: Mysore Public Works Department KRS project records, 1911-1931
sources.note: Administrative and engineering records for construction.

sources.citation: Janaki Nair, Mysore Modern (University of Minnesota Press, 2011)
sources.note: Places KRS in the political economy of princely modernisation.

episodes.notes: The KRS Dam at Kannambadi began after Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV approved the project in 1911 and Visvesvaraya drove it through technical and political opposition. INNOVATION: the dam used automatic crest gates associated with Visvesvaraya's design, surki mortar under material constraints, and a reservoir that transformed irrigation and urban water supply. The site also preserved Tipu Sultan's earlier unfulfilled dam intention in a plaque. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim Tipu built KRS; do NOT hide the date complexity, using 1924 for the dam's main construction and 1931 for fuller completion/commissioning.
episodes.chapter_part: V. The Model State and the Republic

episodes.title: Mysore Builds a University and Factories
episodes.figure: Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV and M. Visvesvaraya
episodes.era: Educational and industrial state-building, 1912-1923
episodes.region: Mysore, Bangalore, Bhadravathi and the Model State
episodes.logline: Nalvadi Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV and Visvesvaraya make a princely state think like a laboratory, a campus and a factory floor.
episodes.moral: Prosperity grows when knowledge and industry are built together.

sources.citation: Government of Mysore, University of Mysore Act, 1916
sources.note: Founding law for the first university outside British-administered Indian provinces.

sources.citation: Karnataka Soaps and Detergents records for the Government Sandalwood Oil Factory, 1916, and Mysore Sandal Soap, 1918
sources.note: Company and state records for Mysore's sandalwood value-addition.

sources.citation: M. Visvesvaraya, Reconstructing India (1920)
sources.note: Visvesvaraya's public programme for industrial and educational modernisation.

episodes.notes: Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV's Mysore became famous as a Model State through institutions rather than conquest. INNOVATION: the University of Mysore opened in 1916 as the first university outside British-administered Indian provinces, while the Sandalwood Oil Factory, Mysore Sandal Soap, State Bank of Mysore, chambers, polytechnic and Mysore Iron Works showed state-led industrial value addition. This story should foreground systems: education, industry, banking and public administration. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT reduce the university claim to merely outside presidency towns; it was outside British-administered provinces, and do not imply all institutions were one man's work alone.
episodes.chapter_part: V. The Model State and the Republic

episodes.title: Reservations, Aircraft and the Republic
episodes.figure: Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV and Jayachamarajendra Wodeyar
episodes.era: Social reform and integration, 1918-1950
episodes.region: Mysore State, Bangalore, New Delhi and the Indian Union
episodes.logline: Mysore moves from early backward-class reservations to aircraft industry and accession, as the last Wodeyar ruler carries the state into India.
episodes.moral: The best ending to old power is service to a wider public.

sources.citation: Government of Mysore, Miller Committee Report on Backward Class Representation (1918)
sources.note: Primary report behind Mysore's early reservation policy.

sources.citation: Hindustan Aircraft Limited founding records, Bangalore, 1940
sources.note: Records for Jayachamarajendra Wodeyar's role with Walchand Hirachand.

sources.citation: Instrument of Accession, Kingdom of Mysore, National Archives of India, 1947
sources.note: Primary record for Mysore's accession to the Dominion of India.

episodes.notes: In 1918 Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV appointed the Miller Committee after non-Brahmin organisations challenged caste imbalance in public service; its recommendations helped create one of India's important early reservation systems, implemented in the early 1920s. INNOVATION: Mysore's social reform sat beside industrial modernity, and Jayachamarajendra Wodeyar later co-founded Hindustan Aircraft Limited in Bangalore in 1940 before signing accession to India and serving as Rajapramukh after 1950. He was also a serious musician and international arts patron, but the chapter ending should stress political integration. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT call Mysore the first reservation state because Kolhapur's 1902 policy preceded it; do NOT overstate Jayachamarajendra's role in HAL's later aerospace expansion.
episodes.chapter_part: V. The Model State and the Republic

episodes.title: Gargi Silences the Assembly
episodes.era: Early Upanishadic debate tradition, c. 700-600 BCE
episodes.region: Videha kingdom, Mithila and the Janaka court tradition
episodes.logline: At Janaka's learned assembly, Gargi asks what holds the universe together and turns a royal contest into a test of fearless thought.
episodes.moral: Wisdom begins when someone dares to ask.

sources.citation: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.6 and 3.8, in Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upanishads (OUP, 1998)
sources.note: Primary dialogue where Gargi challenges Yajnavalkya twice at Janaka's assembly.

sources.citation: Susie Tharu and K. Lalita, eds., Women Writing in India, Vol. 1 (1991)
sources.note: Modern feminist recovery of early women intellectuals and the Gargi passage.

sources.citation: Shyam Ranganathan, Hinduism: A Contemporary Philosophical Investigation (Routledge, 2018)
sources.note: Recent caution distinguishing the Upanishadic Gargi from later Gargi traditions.

episodes.notes: Gargi Vachaknavi appears in Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.6 and 3.8 as the only woman among the named debaters who challenges Yajnavalkya twice. KEY FACTS: the text is usually placed around 700-600 BCE, though broader 900-500 BCE ranges exist; the setting is Videha/Mithila; her questions use the warp-and-woof image to ask what space and existence are woven upon. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Brereton and Ranganathan treat the dialogue as philosophically serious while warning that later deferential Gargi traditions may be separate. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim we can prove a full biography, court office, or navaratna status; those are later traditions. The dialogue is attested, but the historical individual behind it remains partly literary.

episodes.title: Maitreyi Refuses the Wealth of the World
episodes.era: Early Upanishadic philosophy, c. 700-600 BCE
episodes.region: Videha kingdom and the Yajnavalkya household tradition
episodes.logline: When offered property, Maitreyi asks whether wealth can buy immortality and forces philosophy to answer a human hunger.
episodes.moral: Some questions are worth more than gold.

sources.citation: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4 and 4.5, in Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upanishads (OUP, 1998)
sources.note: Primary Maitreyi-Yajnavalkya dialogue in two textual versions.

sources.citation: Joel Brereton, The Composition of the Maitreyi Dialogue in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, JAOS 126.3 (2006)
sources.note: Recent textual study of the two versions and compositional layers.

sources.citation: Sureshvara, Brhadaranyakopanishad Bhashyavartika, discussed in S. Hino (1991)
sources.note: Medieval evidence that the dialogue was treated as serious philosophy.

episodes.notes: Maitreyi is remembered as a brahmavadini who asks Yajnavalkya what use wealth is if it cannot make her immortal. KEY FACTS: the dialogue survives at Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4 and again at 4.5, with variants; it became central to later Advaita commentary; her question makes a woman the catalyst for one of the Upanishad's great teachings on Atman. RECENT FINDINGS: Brereton's 2006 study shows the two versions are distinct compositional layers but share a stable philosophical core. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT make her an independently documented author or assume a recoverable biography. Say these are among the oldest words attributed to a named Indian woman, with historicity debated.

episodes.title: Avvaiyar Walks the Sangam Road
episodes.era: Sangam-age Tamil poetry, c. 1st-3rd century CE
episodes.region: Tamil country, Tagadur, chieftain courts and maritime trade routes
episodes.logline: A woman poet moves between warriors, ports and courts, turning Tamil verse into counsel, diplomacy and memory.
episodes.moral: A poet's voice can travel where armies should not.

sources.citation: Purananuru, Narrinai, Kuruntokai and Akananuru poems attributed to Avvaiyar I
sources.note: Primary Sangam corpus preserving her attributed poems and chieftain context.

sources.citation: A.K. Ramanujan, Poems of Love and War from the Eight Anthologies (Columbia University Press, 1985)
sources.note: Reliable translations and literary framing for Sangam poems.

sources.citation: Eva Wilden, Manuscript, Print and Memory: Relics of the Cankam in Tamilnadu (De Gruyter, 2014)
sources.note: Recent work on compilation, transmission and the Avvaiyar attribution problem.

episodes.notes: Avvaiyar I is the earliest of several poets later remembered by the same honorific, with dozens of Sangam poems attributed to her, especially in the Purananuru. KEY FACTS: she is linked with Athiyaman Neduman Anji of Tagadur and with diplomatic counsel among Tamil chieftains; her poems witness a world of gift exchange, ports, merchants and war bands. RECENT FINDINGS: Wilden's transmission study and Keezhadi-era archaeology help contextualize Sangam urban literacy and trade, but do not prove individual biography. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT merge Avvaiyar I with the medieval didactic Avvaiyar of Aathichoodi, and do NOT use gooseberry or Murugan legends as history. Her poems are the evidence.
episodes.chapter_part: II. Queens Who Governed and Fought

episodes.title: Didda Keeps the Kashmir Throne
episodes.era: Kashmir regency and queen regnant, c. 958-1003 CE
episodes.region: Srinagar, Lohara, the Kashmir valley and Pir Panjal routes
episodes.logline: Against palace factions and landlord revolts, Didda rules Kashmir in her own name and leaves a dynasty behind.
episodes.moral: Power is tested by survival, not praise.

sources.citation: Kalhana, Rajatarangini Books V-VI, translated by Marc Aurel Stein (1900)
sources.note: Main narrative source for Didda's regencies and reign, written about 140 years later.

sources.citation: D.R. Ganguly, Kashmir coins of Ksemagupta and Didda, Epigraphia Indica 27 (1947-48)
sources.note: Coin evidence independently corroborating Didda's royal prominence.

sources.citation: Priti Khanna Kaw, History and Society in Kashmir (Vikas, 2004)
sources.note: Recent reassessment of Didda's rule and Kalhana's gendered moralizing.

episodes.notes: Didda, a Lohara princess married to Ksemagupta of Kashmir, served as regent after 958 and ruled in her own right from 980 to 1003. KEY FACTS: Kalhana depicts her suppressing Damara chiefs, surviving court intrigue, appointing ministers and naming her nephew Samgramaraja as heir, founding the Lohara succession. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Kaw and other historians read Kalhana critically, separating misogynistic moral judgment from evidence of administrative skill; coins naming Ksemagupta-Didda are important corroboration. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT present poisoning accusations, the Tunga affair, or motives as proven; Kalhana is indispensable but not an eyewitness. Do NOT say she fought Mahmud of Ghazni, whose Kashmir campaigns came after her death.
episodes.chapter_part: II. Queens Who Governed and Fought

episodes.title: Chand Bibi Holds Ahmednagar
episodes.era: Deccan Sultanate resistance to Mughal expansion, 1595-1600 CE
episodes.region: Ahmednagar Fort, Bijapur and the Deccan Sultanates
episodes.logline: As Mughal guns batter Ahmednagar, Chand Bibi turns regency into command and diplomacy into survival.
episodes.moral: Courage can defend a city, but wisdom knows when to bargain.

sources.citation: Muhammad Ferishta, Tarikh-i-Ferishta, translated by John Briggs, Vol. III (1829)
sources.note: Near-contemporary Persian narrative of Chand Bibi and the Ahmednagar siege.

sources.citation: Abul Fazl, Akbarnama, translated by H. Beveridge, Vol. III
sources.note: Mughal court account of Prince Murad's Deccan campaign.

sources.citation: Richard Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan, 1300-1761 (Cambridge University Press, 2005)
sources.note: Modern context for Deccan Sultanate politics and Mughal pressure.

episodes.notes: Chand Bibi, Nizam Shahi princess and Adil Shahi queen, acted as regent in Bijapur and later led Ahmednagar's defense against Prince Murad in 1595-1596. KEY FACTS: she negotiated the February 1596 settlement ceding Berar while saving the fort, appealed for a Deccan coalition, and was killed by her own soldiers in 1600 amid suspicion of surrender. INNOVATION ANGLE: her story is also economic administration, because Berar was a revenue-rich province and the treaty was a fiscal-diplomatic calculation. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Deccan studies frame her within connected early modern politics, not isolated romance. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT treat wall-repair scenes or later miniatures as eyewitness proof; they are tradition and later art. The siege, treaty and authority are documented.
episodes.chapter_part: II. Queens Who Governed and Fought

episodes.title: Udayamati Builds the Stepwell of Memory
episodes.era: Chaulukya Gujarat hydraulic architecture, c. 1063-1068 CE
episodes.region: Patan, ancient Anhilwara, Gujarat
episodes.logline: A queen turns grief for Bhimadeva into Rani-ki-Vav, a seven-level water temple carved deep into the earth.
episodes.moral: Public works can make private grief serve generations.

sources.citation: Rani-ki-Vav prashasti inscriptions, published in G.T. Mankodi, Rani Ki Vav (IGNCA, 1991)
sources.note: Primary epigraphic basis for Udayamati's patronage.

sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage dossier, Rani-ki-Vav at Patan, Gujarat, list 922 (2014)
sources.note: Archaeological description, dimensions and world heritage assessment.

sources.citation: G.T. Mankodi, Rani Ki Vav (Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts, 1991)
sources.note: Authoritative modern monograph based on ASI excavation and conservation.

episodes.notes: Udayamati of the Chaulukya dynasty commissioned Rani-ki-Vav at Patan as a memorial to Bhimadeva I, probably within a few years of his death in 1064. KEY FACTS: the stepwell descends about seven levels, roughly 65 m long, 20 m wide and 28 m deep, with hundreds of major sculptures and a design often described as an inverted temple. INNOVATION: it solved hydraulic, civic and architectural problems in alluvial soil while supporting a Maru-Gurjara artisan economy. RECENT FINDINGS: ASI excavation and conservation from 1986 onward and UNESCO listing in 2014 reframed it as world-class water engineering, not merely ornament. ACCURACY FLAGS: use c. 1063-1068, not a false exact date; Udayamati's patronage is secure, but her biography is sparse.

episodes.title: Akka Mahadevi Takes the Open Road
episodes.era: Lingayat and Vachana movement, c. 1130-1160 CE
episodes.region: Udutadi, Basavakalyana and Srisailam in Karnataka and the Deccan
episodes.logline: Akka Mahadevi leaves courtly safety for the road, making Kannada verse a language of freedom before Chenna Mallikarjuna.
episodes.moral: The soul is strongest when it refuses a borrowed cage.

sources.citation: Akka Mahadevi's vachanas, translated in A.K. Ramanujan, Speaking of Siva (Penguin, 1973)
sources.note: Primary poetic corpus in the Vachana tradition.

sources.citation: Sunyasampadane, translated by L.M.A. Menezes and S.M. Angadi (Karnatak University, 1993)
sources.note: Medieval source for Anubhava Mantapa debates and hagiographic memory.

sources.citation: R.C. Hiremath, ed., Akkamahadevi Vachana (Kannada Sahitya Parishat, 2006)
sources.note: Modern critical edition of the Kannada vachanas.

episodes.notes: Akka Mahadevi is one of the strongest named women voices in 12th-century Kannada literature, with roughly 430 vachanas attributed to her. KEY FACTS: her poems address Shiva as Chenna Mallikarjuna; Lingayat memory places her in the Anubhava Mantapa at Basavakalyana with Basavanna and Allama Prabhu; her verse challenged caste, gender convention and empty ritual. INNOVATION: the vachana form made philosophy a spare vernacular utterance with a signature deity, helping transform Kannada literary history and social reform. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Padigar, Amaladass-Talib and critical editions reassess hagiography against texts. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT overstate the Kaushika marriage, naked wandering, or death at Srisailam as documented fact; those come through later hagiography. Her poems are the firm base.

episodes.title: Lal Ded Gives Kashmir a Voice
episodes.era: Kashmiri mystical poetry, c. 1320-1373 CE
episodes.region: Pandrethan, Bijbehara and the Kashmir valley
episodes.logline: Ignored by court chronicles yet remembered in every valley, Lal Ded turns Kashmiri speech into a sacred literary voice.
episodes.moral: What power forgets, people may still sing.

sources.citation: Lal Ded's vakhs, in Ranjit Hoskote, I, Lalla: The Poems of Lal Ded (Penguin, 2011)
sources.note: Authoritative recent translation and critical apparatus for the poetic corpus.

sources.citation: Mulla Ali Raina, Tadhkirat-ul-Arifin (1587)
sources.note: Earliest written biographical record, later and hagiographic.

sources.citation: Susie Tharu and K. Lalita, Women Writing in India, Vol. 1 (1991)
sources.note: Modern recovery of Lal Ded among early women writers.

episodes.notes: Lal Ded, also called Lalla or Lalleshwari, is conventionally dated to the 14th-century Kashmir Sultanate period. KEY FACTS: about 150-170 vakhs are attributed to her; they translate Kashmir Shaiva and mystical insight into Kashmiri speech; Nund Rishi's later verses acknowledge her spiritual authority. INNOVATION: her vakhs are among the earliest substantial Kashmiri compositions and helped form a shared literary memory across Hindu and Muslim communities. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Hoskote's 2011 edition compares manuscript and oral traditions and warns against communal ownership claims. ACCURACY FLAGS: contemporary Kashmir chronicles are silent; do NOT call every biography detail proven, and do NOT force her into modern Hindu/Muslim categories. The poems and later acknowledgments are the evidence.

episodes.title: Savitribai Opens the Schoolroom Door
episodes.era: Girls' education and anti-caste reform, 1848-1897 CE
episodes.region: Bhidewada, Pune, Naigaon and colonial Maharashtra
episodes.logline: Carrying books through abuse, Savitribai Phule opens a girls' school and makes education an anti-caste revolution.
episodes.moral: A classroom can be a battlefield for dignity.

sources.citation: Savitribai Phule, Kavya Phule (1854), translated in Women Writing in India, Vol. 2 (1993)
sources.note: Her own published poetry, one of the earliest such works by an Indian woman.

sources.citation: Dnyanodaya newspaper and Bombay Education Department reports, c. 1848-1853
sources.note: Contemporary evidence for the Phule schools and enrollment.

sources.citation: Rosalind O'Hanlon, Caste, Conflict, and Ideology (Cambridge University Press, 2002 ed.)
sources.note: Modern scholarly account of the Phules' schools and anti-caste reform.

episodes.notes: Savitribai Phule, trained by Jyotirao Phule and missionary-linked normal schools, helped open a girls' school at Bhidewada in Pune in early 1848 and later helped run multiple schools. KEY FACTS: the curriculum included mathematics, science and social studies; she co-founded institutions for women, widows and oppressed castes, including Mahila Seva Mandal, Balhatya Pratibandhak Griha and Satyashodhak Samaj; she died nursing plague patients in 1897. INNOVATION: formal girls' education, civil-society schooling and anti-caste social institutions. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: O'Hanlon, Chakravarti and Sperandio place her at the intersection of caste and gender reform. ACCURACY FLAGS: the spare-sari story is powerful but often later commemorative; mention it cautiously. Do NOT reduce her to Jyotirao's helper; her writings and organizing are independent evidence.

episodes.title: Pandita Ramabai Builds a House of Freedom
episodes.era: Women's education and institution building, 1858-1922 CE
episodes.region: Pune, Calcutta, Bombay, Kedgaon, England and the United States
episodes.logline: A Sanskrit scholar turns testimony, books and shelters into institutions where widows and girls can rebuild their lives.
episodes.moral: Learning becomes power when it opens doors for others.

sources.citation: Pandita Ramabai, The High-Caste Hindu Woman (Philadelphia, 1887)
sources.note: Primary English-language reform text written for an international audience.

sources.citation: Report of the Indian Education Commission (Hunter Commission), Calcutta, 1883
sources.note: Published record of Ramabai's testimony on female education.

sources.citation: Uma Chakravarti, Rewriting History: The Life and Times of Pandita Ramabai (Kali for Women, 1998)
sources.note: Authoritative modern biography using archives and Ramabai's writings.

episodes.notes: Pandita Ramabai Sarasvati was honored by Calcutta University in 1878 as a woman Sanskrit scholar, testified before the Hunter Commission in 1882, and built major institutions for women. KEY FACTS: Arya Mahila Samaj began in 1882; Sharada Sadan opened in 1889; Mukti Mission at Kedgaon from 1898 housed, educated and employed large numbers of women through farms, workshops, a press and industrial training. INNOVATION: social reform, scholarship and women-run economic institution building on a rare scale. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Uma Chakravarti, Meera Kosambi and Tanika Sarkar highlight her complex position between feminism, conversion, nationalism and caste. ACCURACY FLAGS: acknowledge her Christian conversion without making it the whole story; do NOT flatten her as either missionary pawn or nationalist saint. Her own books and institutions are primary evidence.

episodes.title: Anandi Joshi Crosses the Black Water
episodes.era: Women's medical education, 1883-1887 CE
episodes.region: Kalyan, Pune, Serampore, Philadelphia and Kolhapur
episodes.logline: After losing a child for lack of care, Anandi Joshi crosses the sea to earn a medical degree for women who need women doctors.
episodes.moral: Pain can become a promise to heal.

sources.citation: Caroline Healey Dall, The Life of Dr. Anandabai Joshee (Roberts Brothers, 1888)
sources.note: Near-contemporary biography preserving letters and the Serampore speech.

sources.citation: Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania records and Anandi Joshi, Obstetrics Among the Aryas (1886)
sources.note: Graduation record and MD thesis held by Drexel University Heritage Collections.

sources.citation: Meera Kosambi, Crossing Thresholds: Feminist Essays in Social History (Permanent Black, 2007)
sources.note: Recent historical analysis of Anandi's life, marriage and education.

episodes.notes: Anandi Gopal Joshi, born Yamuna in 1865, resolved to study medicine after her infant son died for lack of medical care. KEY FACTS: her 1883 Serampore speech argued that Indian women needed women doctors; she graduated from the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania in 1886; her thesis, Obstetrics Among the Aryas, compared Indian obstetric knowledge with Western medicine; she was appointed to Kolhapur but died of tuberculosis in 1887. INNOVATION: she was the first Indian woman to receive a Western medical degree, though Kadambini Ganguly is the key parallel as the first Indian woman doctor to practice in South Asia. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Kosambi and Drexel archival work complicate older heroic narratives. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT present Gopalrao only as a benevolent husband; documented coercion must be acknowledged carefully. Do NOT call Anandi a long-practicing physician; she died before she could serve.

episodes.title: Kamala Sohonie Wins the Laboratory Bet
episodes.era: Indian women in modern biochemistry, 1933-1939 CE
episodes.region: IISc Bangalore, Newnham College Cambridge, Delhi and Coonoor
episodes.logline: Rejected by C.V. Raman because she was a woman, Kamala Sohonie earns her place and discovers a key clue in cellular respiration.
episodes.moral: A closed door is not the same as a final answer.
