Early Buddhist and Jain traditions know a town called Nalanda, but the excavated monastic university is not securely visible before the early Gupta period. KEY ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say the Buddha, Mahavira or Ashoka founded the university; those are traditions about the place or later religious memory, not archaeological proof for the institution. Recent scholarship uses Faxian together with seals, coins and excavations to place Nalanda's institutional rise after c. 400 CE.
episodes.chapter: Nalanda and the Great Monastic Universities
episodes.chapter_part: I. Finding Nalanda in the Evidence

episodes.title: The Seal That Named Shakraditya
episodes.figure: Nalanda seal makers and Kumaragupta I
episodes.era: Gupta founding phase, c. 415-550 CE
episodes.region: Nalanda near Rajgir, Magadha
episodes.logline: A clay seal, Gupta coins, and a pilgrim's memory point to Shakraditya, probably Kumaragupta I, as the royal patron behind Nalanda's first great monastery.
episodes.moral: Truth often survives in small marks of clay.

sources.citation: Clay seal of Shakraditya from the Nalanda site
sources.note: Primary archaeological evidence naming the founder remembered as Shakraditya.

sources.citation: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji, compiled 646 CE
sources.note: Records Shakraditya and later kings building up Nalanda.

sources.citation: Sukumar Dutt, Buddhist Monks and Monasteries of India (1962); Frederick Asher, Nalanda (2015)
sources.note: Modern treatment of the Shakraditya-Kumaragupta identification and its limits.

episodes.notes: This is the source-problem version of the founding, not a repeat of a Gupta glory tale. A seal identifies Shakraditya as founder, and many scholars identify him with Kumaragupta I, supported by coins found at the site and Xuanzang's later list of royal builders. KEY FACTS: successive Gupta-period patrons enlarged the complex; donors were not all Buddhist, and seals with Lakshmi, Ganesha, Shiva-linga and Durga show a plural patronage environment. ACCURACY FLAGS: the identification of Shakraditya with Kumaragupta is strong but still a scholarly reconstruction; do NOT present a single inaugural day or a modern university charter.
episodes.chapter: Nalanda and the Great Monastic Universities
episodes.chapter_part: I. Finding Nalanda in the Evidence

episodes.title: Harsha Feeds a Hundred Villages
episodes.era: Harsha's patronage, c. 606-647 CE
episodes.region: Nalanda, Kannauj, and the village endowments of Magadha
episodes.logline: Harsha's grants turn learning into an economy, as villages send rice, butter and milk to sustain monks who debate from dawn to dusk.
episodes.moral: Great learning needs daily bread.

sources.citation: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji, account of Nalanda and Harsha
sources.note: Primary report for Harsha's patronage and the hundred villages.

sources.citation: Seal of Harshavardhana found at Nalanda
sources.note: Material evidence linking Harsha to the site.

sources.citation: Sukumar Dutt, Buddhist Monks and Monasteries of India (1962); Scharfe, Education in Ancient India (2002)
sources.note: Modern analysis of village grants and monastic support systems.

episodes.notes: According to Xuanzang, Harsha assigned one hundred villages to Nalanda, with households supplying daily food. Yijing later gives a different figure of two hundred villages, which may reflect growth, different counting, or pilgrim exaggeration. This story should emphasize the social and economic innovation: education that looked free to residents depended on land revenue, agrarian surplus, stewards, kitchens and royal legitimacy. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Nalanda was free in a modern tuition-funded sense; do NOT repeat the 10,000-student figure without qualification, because Asher argues the excavated rooms cannot house such a number.
episodes.chapter: Nalanda and the Great Monastic Universities
episodes.chapter_part: I. Finding Nalanda in the Evidence

episodes.title: Silabhadra Teaches the Traveler
episodes.era: Xuanzang's Nalanda years, c. 637-643 CE
episodes.region: Nalanda, Magadha, with routes to China and Central Asia
episodes.logline: A monk from China finds the aged master Silabhadra at Nalanda and carries Yogachara learning home in hundreds of Sanskrit texts.
episodes.moral: A teacher's lesson can cross mountains.

sources.citation: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji, compiled 646 CE
sources.note: Primary account of his Nalanda study, Silabhadra, curriculum and departure.

sources.citation: Tang biographies of Xuanzang and translation catalogues
sources.note: Evidence for texts carried to China and later translation work.

sources.citation: Sally Wriggins, Xuanzang: A Buddhist Pilgrim on the Silk Road (1996); Tansen Sen, Buddhism, Diplomacy, and Trade (2003)
sources.note: Modern scholarship on the journey and knowledge transfer.

episodes.notes: Xuanzang left China in 629, reached India after Central Asian travel, visited Nalanda around 637 and 642, and studied Yogachara, logic and Sanskrit under the abbot Silabhadra. He reportedly carried 657 Sanskrit texts, relics and images back to China and translated many works. KEY ACCURACY FLAGS: Silabhadra's age of 106 is according to Xuanzang and should be voiced as such; do NOT say Xuanzang discovered Nalanda, and do NOT invent a simple China-versus-India civilizational contest. The story is a trans-Asian scholarly partnership built through pilgrimage, translation and debate.
episodes.chapter: Nalanda and the Great Monastic Universities

episodes.title: Yijing Hears the Morning Bell
episodes.era: Yijing's stay, c. 673-683 CE
episodes.region: Nalanda's monasteries, pools and lecture halls
episodes.logline: A bell rings, monks walk to the bathing pools, and Yijing records the rules that made Nalanda a disciplined residential city of learning.
episodes.moral: Discipline turns a crowd into a community.

sources.citation: Yijing, Da Tang Xiyu Qiu Fa Gaoseng Zhuan, c. 691 CE; trans. J. Takakusu (1896)
sources.note: Primary source for daily monastic practice and rules.

sources.citation: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji, physical description of Nalanda
sources.note: Primary account for buildings, teachers and curriculum.

sources.citation: Frederick Asher, Nalanda (2015); Scharfe, Education in Ancient India (2002)
sources.note: Modern assessment of institutional scale and routines.

episodes.notes: Yijing gives the richest account of ordinary Nalanda life: bathing rules, pools, monastic clothing, bells, dining rules and the authority of the Nalanda Nikaya. This is a social-innovation story about a residential institution where thousands could live under shared discipline. RECENT/CRITICAL FLAGS: descriptions of three named libraries and a nine-storey library come mainly from later Tibetan tradition, not Yijing; do NOT present them as excavated fact. Use the pools, bells and rules because they are better attested, while keeping numbers cautious.
episodes.chapter: Nalanda and the Great Monastic Universities

episodes.title: The Gate of Questions
episodes.era: Nalanda's high scholastic culture, 7th-11th century CE
episodes.region: Nalanda and the debate halls of eastern India
episodes.logline: At the gate, tradition says applicants faced scholars with questions sharp enough to decide who could enter the world's hardest classroom.
episodes.moral: A question can be a doorway.

sources.citation: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji, Nalanda curriculum and teacher rankings
sources.note: Primary evidence for high scholastic standards, though not all entrance legends.

sources.citation: Tibetan and later Sanskrit scholastic traditions on dvarapanditas
sources.note: Later evidence for gate-examiner memory; must be used cautiously.

sources.citation: Hartmut Scharfe, Education in Ancient India (2002); Frederick Asher, Nalanda (2015)
sources.note: Modern caution on admissions, numbers and institutional claims.

episodes.notes: Make this a source-critical institution story. Nalanda's curriculum included Buddhist philosophy, grammar, logic, medicine, astronomy and study of rival schools for debate. Later traditions speak of dvarapanditas, gate scholars who tested entrants, and of most applicants failing. That memory fits Nalanda's debate culture, but the exact nine-out-of-ten rejection claim is not a contemporary statistic. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT stage a modern exam hall; do NOT claim secular degree programs; do NOT say every caste or region had equal access unless a source says so. The innovation is rigorous peer selection and debate as a public method of learning.
episodes.chapter: Nalanda and the Great Monastic Universities

episodes.title: Dignaga Sets the Rules of Proof
episodes.era: Buddhist logic and epistemology, c. 480-660 CE
episodes.region: South Asia's scholastic networks, with later Nalanda lineages and Tibet
episodes.logline: Dignaga and Dharmakirti turn argument into a science of perception and inference that will train monastic thinkers for centuries.
episodes.moral: Clear thinking is a tool for compassion.

sources.citation: Dignaga, Pramana-samuccaya, c. 5th-6th century CE
sources.note: Primary philosophical text preserved largely through Tibetan tradition.

sources.citation: Dharmakirti, Pramana-varttika, c. 7th century CE
sources.note: Primary work on valid cognition, inference and Buddhist epistemology.

sources.citation: Tom Tillemans, 'Dharmakirti', Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (2011); Vincent Eltschinger, Buddhist Epistemology as Apologetics (2010)
sources.note: Modern scholarship on the pramana tradition and its social context.

episodes.notes: This is the chapter's scholarly and scientific-method innovation story. Dignaga reduced valid knowledge to perception and inference; Dharmakirti expanded the system into a rigorous theory of cognition, causality and debate. Their works shaped Tibetan curricula and South Asian philosophical controversy. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim either man is securely documented as a resident teacher at Nalanda; their association is through the broader Nalanda-linked scholastic lineage and later tradition. Avoid saying Buddhist logic replaced all other Indian logic; it debated Nyaya and other schools intensely.
episodes.chapter: Nalanda and the Great Monastic Universities

episodes.title: Shantideva Takes the Lion Seat
episodes.era: Late 7th to early 8th century CE
episodes.region: Nalanda, Magadha
episodes.logline: Mocked as idle, Shantideva steps onto a lion seat and tradition says he recites a poem that still teaches courage and compassion.
episodes.moral: Hidden work can bloom in public.

sources.citation: Shantideva, Bodhicaryavatara, c. 8th century CE
sources.note: Primary Sanskrit and Tibetan text on the bodhisattva path.

sources.citation: Vibhutichandra, Bodhicaryavatara-tatparya-panjika-visesadyotani; Bu-ston, History of Buddhism
sources.note: Later biographical traditions for the lion-seat episode.

sources.citation: Kate Crosby and Andrew Skilton, trans., The Bodhicaryavatara (Oxford, 1995); Paul Williams, Mahayana Buddhism (2009)
sources.note: Modern translation and doctrinal context.

episodes.notes: The Bodhicaryavatara and Sikshasamuccaya are real texts with enormous later influence. The famous scene of monks humiliating Shantideva and his miraculous recitation is hagiographic, preserved in later biographies, so narrate it as tradition, not courtroom fact. Use it to show Nalanda's culture of public recitation, peer judgement, literary composition and ethical philosophy. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT include miraculous disappearance as literal history; do NOT give exact birth and death years without 'c.'; do NOT reduce the poem to sentiment, because chapter 9 is a rigorous Madhyamaka argument.
episodes.chapter: Nalanda and the Great Monastic Universities

episodes.title: The Self-Governing Sangha
episodes.era: Nalanda administration, c. 5th-12th century CE
episodes.region: Nalanda Mahavihara, Magadha
episodes.logline: A self-governing sangha used stamped clay seals to authenticate documents, mark property and keep a vast university alive.
episodes.moral: Even great ideas need careful record keepers.

sources.citation: Nalanda terracotta seals and sealings, ASI excavations 1915-1937
sources.note: Primary material evidence for the mahavihara's institutional name, official marks and administrative practice.

sources.citation: Hiranand Sastri, Nalanda and Its Epigraphic Material, Memoirs of the Archaeological Survey of India No. 66 (1942)
sources.note: Catalogue and study of Nalanda's seals, sealings and inscriptions, including monastic formulae.

sources.citation: Frederick Asher, Nalanda (Oxford University Press, 2015); Hartmut Scharfe, Education in Ancient India (Brill, 2002)
sources.note: Modern assessments of Nalanda's excavated evidence, corporate monastic life and institutional limits.

episodes.notes: This material-institutional innovation story must focus on Nalanda's own administrative sealings, not on royal village-grant diplomacy. Nalanda's palm-leaf records mostly perished, but clay seals and sealings survived because they were fired or hardened in the archaeological layers. Many bear institutional formulae such as the Arya-bhikshu-sangha of the great Nalanda monastery, showing the monastery as a corporate body that authenticated documents, marked property, received gifts and represented itself through an official seal. This is administration made visible: stewards, scribes, storage, correspondence and legal memory behind the famous debates. RECENT/CRITICAL FLAGS: do NOT claim a modern registrar's office, university bureaucracy or exact staffing chart; the sealings prove administrative practice, not every procedure. Do NOT confuse this with the Shakraditya founding seal in story #2; that story dates the origin, while this one explains how a working sangha bureaucracy left durable traces.
episodes.chapter: Nalanda and the Great Monastic Universities

episodes.title: Somapura Draws the Great Mandala
episodes.era: Pala architecture, c. 781-821 CE and after
episodes.region: Somapura Mahavihara, Paharpur, Bengal, now Bangladesh
episodes.logline: At Somapura, builders shape a vast brick monastery around a central shrine whose plan echoes across Buddhist Asia.
episodes.moral: Architecture can carry ideas across borders.

sources.citation: Seals from Somapura reading Shri-Somapure-Shri-Dharmapaladeva-Mahavihara
sources.note: Primary site evidence linking the monastery to Dharmapala.

sources.citation: K.N. Dikshit, Paharpur: Memoirs of the Archaeological Survey of India No. 55 (1938)
sources.note: Foundational excavation report for Somapura.

sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage documentation for Somapura Mahavihara (1985)
sources.note: Modern conservation and architectural assessment.

episodes.notes: Somapura was one of the largest Pala mahaviharas, with a vast quadrangle, cells for monks, terracotta plaques and a central cruciform shrine. Its plan influenced or paralleled Buddhist architecture in Burma, Java and Cambodia, though exact lines of influence must be stated cautiously. RECENT/CRITICAL FLAGS: use seals and archaeology for the foundation; do NOT rely on later population numbers as exact; mention that an 11th-century fire or attack in the region is attested but avoid inventing a battle scene. This is an artistic and engineering innovation story about brick planning, sacred geometry and transregional style.
episodes.chapter: Nalanda and the Great Monastic Universities

episodes.title: The Cooled Library of Vikramashila
episodes.era: Pala university engineering, c. 8th-12th century CE
episodes.region: Vikramashila near Kahalgaon, Bihar
episodes.logline: Beside a great monastery, excavators find a library building cooled by water channels, hinting at how fragile palm-leaf knowledge was protected.
episodes.moral: Care for knowledge is also care for materials.

sources.citation: B.P. Sinha, Excavations at Vikramshila, Patna University reports, 1960-69
sources.note: Excavation evidence for the monastery plan.

sources.citation: ASI excavations at Vikramashila, 1972-82
sources.note: Reports identifying the library building and water-cooling interpretation.

sources.citation: Taranatha, History of Buddhism in India; Blue Annals
sources.note: Later Tibetan sources for Vikramashila's scholastic role, used cautiously.

episodes.notes: Do not repeat the Pala chapter's gate-scholar story. Focus on built environment: excavations uncovered a large square monastery with cells, a central stupa and a structure interpreted as a library cooled by water from an adjoining reservoir, useful for preserving palm-leaf manuscripts in a hot climate. KEY ACCURACY FLAGS: passive cooling is an archaeological interpretation, not a surviving engineering manual; do NOT claim exact shelf counts or manuscript totals. The story shows scientific and practical innovation in preservation, architecture and institutional infrastructure.
episodes.chapter: Nalanda and the Great Monastic Universities

episodes.title: Valabhi Trains the Ministers
episodes.era: Maitraka Valabhi, c. 6th-8th century CE
episodes.region: Valabhi in Saurashtra, Gujarat
episodes.logline: On the western sea, Valabhi teaches monks, merchants and future ministers a practical curriculum of law, politics and administration.
episodes.moral: Learning serves the world when it meets public duty.

sources.citation: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji, account of Valabhi
sources.note: Primary report of monasteries and thousands of monks.

sources.citation: Yijing, records comparing Valabhi's learning with Nalanda
sources.note: Primary comparative testimony from a Buddhist pilgrim.

sources.citation: Maitraka copper plate grants, 6th-8th century CE; Hartmut Scharfe, Education in Ancient India (2002)
sources.note: Epigraphic and modern evidence for patronage and curriculum.

episodes.notes: Valabhi was a western Indian university in a port-linked capital, not a copy of Nalanda. It taught Buddhist learning along with practical subjects such as niti, varta, law, administration and economics, and its graduates were reputedly recruited as ministers. Merchant wealth and Maitraka copper-plate grants supported the institution. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT call Valabhi purely Buddhist or purely secular; do NOT give a precise destruction date, because the late-8th-century end, often linked to Arab raids, is not archaeologically fixed. This is the chapter's practical governance and economic curriculum story.
episodes.chapter: Nalanda and the Great Monastic Universities

episodes.title: Dharmasvamin in the Ashes
episodes.era: Khalji raids and aftermath, c. 1193-1235 CE
episodes.region: Nalanda, Odantapuri and Bihar
episodes.logline: A Tibetan pilgrim reaches a damaged Nalanda, finds an old teacher and a few students, and shows that the end was violent, real and more complex than legend.
episodes.moral: Honest memory faces loss without inventing certainty.

sources.citation: Biography of Dharmasvamin, visit of 1234-35, trans. George Roerich (1959)
sources.note: Primary eyewitness-derived account of Nalanda's reduced survival.

sources.citation: Minhaj-i-Siraj Juzjani, Tabaqat-i-Nasiri, completed 1260 CE
sources.note: Primary Islamic source for Bakhtiyar Khalji's Bihar campaign and Odantapuri destruction.

sources.citation: Frederick Asher, Nalanda (2015); Johan Elverskog, Buddhism and Islam on the Silk Road (2010)
sources.note: Recent source-critical scholarship on destruction, survival and myth.

episodes.notes: State the violence plainly and soberly. Bakhtiyar Khalji's campaigns devastated Buddhist monastic institutions in Bihar and Bengal; monks were killed or dispersed, Odantapuri was sacked according to Minhaj, and Nalanda's upper archaeological layers show catastrophic burning. Dharmasvamin visited in 1234-35 and found Nalanda damaged, mostly deserted, but not totally dead: the elderly Rahula Sribhadra still taught a small group, with local patron Jayadeva helping. KEY ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim the library burned for three months; no contemporary source gives that figure. Do NOT attribute Minhaj's Odantapuri passage directly to Nalanda. Do NOT whitewash the destruction or deny its religious-institutional target; frame it politics-first within Ghurid expansion, monastic wealth, and the collapse of Pala protection.
episodes.chapter: Nalanda and the Great Monastic Universities

episodes.title: The Sepoy's Sacred Body
episodes.era: Bengal Army crisis and Meerut outbreak, 1856-1857
episodes.region: Meerut, Awadh, Bihar and the Bengal Army cantonments
episodes.logline: When eighty-five cavalrymen are stripped and shackled for refusing cartridges, the Bengal Army's carefully built caste institution turns into the fuse of revolt.
episodes.moral: Honor betrayed can turn discipline into rebellion.

sources.citation: Court martial proceedings of the 85 troopers, 3rd Bengal Cavalry, Meerut, 9 May 1857; India Office Records, British Library
sources.note: Primary record for the refusal, sentencing and public humiliation.

sources.citation: G.W. Forrest, ed., Selections from the Letters, Despatches and Other State Papers, 1857-58, vol. 1 (1893-1912)
sources.note: Official correspondence on Meerut and Bengal Army grievances.

sources.citation: Kim A. Wagner, The Great Fear of 1857 (2010); Rudrangshu Mukherjee, Awadh in Revolt, expanded ed. (2001)
sources.note: Recent scholarship on rumor, social panic and structural sepoy grievances.

episodes.notes: The Bengal Army recruited heavily from high-caste Purbiya networks in Awadh and Bihar, creating a social institution around caste honor, shared villages, cooking rules and allowances. The Pattern 1853 Enfield cartridge crisis mattered because soldiers believed biting greased cartridges would defile Hindus with beef fat and Muslims with pork fat, but the exact grease in all issued cartridges remains unproved. On 9 May 1857 the 85 troopers of the 3rd Bengal Cavalry were sentenced to ten years and publicly shackled at Meerut; the next evening comrades freed them and marched to Delhi. Do NOT claim the cartridges were definitely defiling or that the entire revolt was preplanned; state the documented belief, humiliation and wider Awadh/pay grievances.

episodes.title: Azimullah Khan's Printed Word
episodes.era: Global circuits and rebel print culture, 1853-1859
episodes.region: Kanpur, Bithur, London, Constantinople and Delhi
episodes.logline: A Kanpur orphan becomes Nana Sahib's envoy, studies Britain's vulnerabilities abroad, and helps turn print into a weapon of rebel imagination.
episodes.moral: Ideas travel farther when courage learns to print them.

sources.citation: Payam-e-Azadi, Urdu pamphlet, Delhi, 1857; reproduced in V.D. Savarkar, The Indian War of Independence 1857 (1909)
sources.note: Early vernacular text associated with Azimullah and Hindu-Muslim-Sikh solidarity, but authorship is not proven.

sources.citation: India Office Records, Nana Sahib pension correspondence, IOR/L/PS, 1853-54
sources.note: Primary evidence for Azimullah's London mission over the Peshwa pension.

sources.citation: Francis Jarman, 'Azimullah Khan: A Reappraisal,' South Asia XXXI.3 (2008); Michael H. Fisher, Counterflows to Colonialism (2004)
sources.note: Modern reassessment of Indian agency in Britain and Azimullah's role.

episodes.notes: Azimullah Khan, educated after the famine of 1837-38, became Nana Sahib's secretary and went to Britain in 1853 to plead for the discontinued Peshwa pension. He observed imperial politics, passed through Constantinople during the Crimean War, and returned to Bithur with knowledge of British weakness and a French printing press. The Payam-e-Azadi is important for its early language of shared freedom across Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs, but sole authorship by Azimullah rests mainly on later attribution. Do NOT claim he certainly met Dickens, Carlyle or Tennyson, and do NOT present the pamphlet as a fully modern nation-state manifesto; treat it as rebel print culture with global circuits.

episodes.title: Bakht Khan Builds an Army Court
episodes.era: Delhi rebel government during the siege, July-September 1857
episodes.region: Delhi, Bareilly and the Ridge siege lines
episodes.logline: A veteran artilleryman arrives from Bareilly and tries to turn Delhi's swelling rebel army into a state with courts, taxes and rations.
episodes.moral: Revolt needs institutions as much as bravery.

sources.citation: Two Historic Trials in Red Fort, Bahadur Shah Zafar trial proceedings, January-March 1858
sources.note: Testimony on Bakht Khan's authority and the rebel court.

sources.citation: William Dalrymple, The Last Mughal (2006)
sources.note: Uses National Archives of India Urdu and Persian Mutiny Papers to reconstruct Delhi rebel governance.

sources.citation: G.B. Malleson, History of the Indian Mutiny, vols. 4-6 (1878-1880)
sources.note: Colonial narrative based on official papers and captured correspondence; useful but biased.

episodes.notes: Bakht Khan entered Delhi on 1 July 1857 with the Bareilly Brigade and was given real command under Bahadur Shah Zafar, though court factions and Prince Mirza Mughal limited him. He attempted tax collection, discipline through an adalat, rationing and a more aggressive strategy against the British Ridge. Recent use of the Mutiny Papers has made Delhi's improvised rebel administration clearer than older colonial histories allowed. His plea that Zafar leave Delhi and continue resistance is broadly attested, but his later death is unknown. Do NOT invent a heroic last stand or a fully coherent national government; show disciplined state-building under siege and its structural failure.

episodes.title: Nana Sahib's Rebel Treasury
episodes.era: Kanpur rebel finance and sovereignty, June-July 1857
episodes.region: Bithur and Kanpur on the Ganges
episodes.logline: At Kanpur, seized Company treasure becomes rebel pay, courts, coinage and a fragile claim to restored Maratha sovereignty.
episodes.moral: Money can launch rebellion, but only trust can sustain it.

sources.citation: Mowbray Thomson, The Story of Cawnpore (1859)
sources.note: Eyewitness account of the Kanpur siege and Nana Sahib's administration, with survivor bias.

sources.citation: Nana Sahib paisa coins, British Museum Coins and Medals South Asia Collection, IOC.234/235 series
sources.note: Surviving numismatic assertion of rebel sovereignty.

sources.citation: Andrew Ward, Our Bones Are Scattered (1996); Correspondence Relative to the Affairs of Oudh, British Parliamentary Papers, 1856
sources.note: Modern Kanpur study and macro-fiscal context of annexation and pension grievances.

episodes.notes: Nana Sahib's grievance began with the Company's refusal to continue the Peshwa pension after Baji Rao II's death. In June 1857 he seized the Kanpur treasury and magazine, promised double pay to keep sepoys from leaving for Delhi, appointed Azimullah as collector, and issued paisa coins as a sovereign act. The fiscal experiment was real but short-lived because the treasury could not sustain thousands of troops without stable territorial revenue. Do NOT merge this story with the Bibighar killings, and do NOT assert Nana Sahib personally ordered those killings; use him here to explain rebel finance, pension politics, coinage and the economic anatomy of revolt.

episodes.title: Khan Bahadur Khan's Bareilly State
episodes.era: Rohilkhand rebel government, 1857-1860
episodes.region: Bareilly, Rohilkhand and the Nepal frontier
episodes.logline: In Rohilkhand, Khan Bahadur Khan runs courts, revenue and coinage for nearly a year before the last noose closes at Bareilly Kotwali.
episodes.moral: Regional memory can carry a kingdom's unfinished claim.

sources.citation: Trial records of Khan Bahadur Khan Rohilla, India Office Records, IOR/L/MIL/17/5 series
sources.note: Primary evidence for his government, capture and conviction.

sources.citation: G.B. Malleson, History of the Indian Mutiny, vol. 6 (1880); G.W. Forrest, Selections, vol. 3
sources.note: Colonial accounts of Rohilkhand operations and administration.

sources.citation: Khan Bahadur Khan coins, Bareilly mint, 1857-58, described in numismatic catalogues
sources.note: Material evidence of restored sovereignty claims.

episodes.notes: Khan Bahadur Khan, grandson of Rohilla leader Hafiz Rahmat Khan, took authority after Bareilly mutinied in May 1857 and governed from June 1857 to May 1858. He held courts, collected revenue, maintained order, struck coins, sent Bakht Khan to Delhi and later cooperated with Ahmadullah Shah. Captured after flight toward Nepal, he was hanged at Bareilly Kotwali on 24 February 1860. English scholarship remains thinner here than for Delhi or Kanpur, so cite the trial and colonial records carefully. Do NOT reduce Rohilkhand to a Delhi side note; it was a functioning regional rebel state with restorationist legitimacy.

episodes.title: The Chapati and the Telegraph
episodes.era: Information networks before and during the rising, January-May 1857
episodes.region: Awadh, Rohilkhand, Mathura, Meerut, Delhi, Ambala and Punjab
episodes.logline: As mysterious chapatis pass from village to village, electric wires carry Meerut's alarm toward Punjab and change the war's balance in hours.
episodes.moral: The speed of a message can decide the fate of armies.

sources.citation: Mark Thornhill, The Personal Adventures and Experiences of a Magistrate (1884)
sources.note: Firsthand British account of chapatis moving through Mathura district.

sources.citation: The Friend of India, 5 March 1857
sources.note: Contemporary report of the chapati phenomenon.

sources.citation: Kim A. Wagner, The Great Fear of 1857 (2010); G.W. Forrest, Selections, vol. 1
sources.note: Recent interpretation of chapatis and primary telegraph correspondence.

episodes.notes: The chapati movement is attested by British observers across districts, but its meaning is not: Wagner argues it may have been a plague-dispersal ritual misread as conspiracy, while older writers linked it to rebel planning. The telegraph is firmer: after the Meerut outbreak on 10 May 1857, warnings reached Ambala and Punjab before lines failed, helping British commanders mobilize forces that kept Punjab from joining the revolt. This is a scientific and logistical innovation story contrasting organic village networks with colonial electric infrastructure. Do NOT claim chapatis were a proven coded signal; do show the technological asymmetry that shaped military outcomes.
episodes.chapter_part: III. The Battles and Their Costs

episodes.title: The Maulvi Wins at Chinhat
episodes.era: Awadh fighting and the Lucknow Residency siege, June 1857-June 1858
episodes.region: Faizabad, Chinhat, Lucknow, Shahjahanpur and Powayan
episodes.logline: Ahmadullah Shah lures Henry Lawrence into Chinhat's trap, wins the revolt's great open-field victory, and dies for a bounty at Powayan.
episodes.moral: Courage needs strategy, not merely fury.

sources.citation: G.B. Malleson, History of the Indian Mutiny, vol. 4 (1879)
sources.note: Detailed colonial account of Ahmadullah Shah and Chinhat; read for facts and bias.

sources.citation: G.W. Forrest, Selections, vol. 4, Lucknow section; Henry Lawrence dispatches
sources.note: Primary reports for Chinhat and the Residency crisis.

sources.citation: Rudrangshu Mukherjee, Awadh in Revolt, 1857-1858 (2001)
sources.note: Modern study of Awadh resistance and rebel leadership.

episodes.notes: Ahmadullah Shah of Faizabad combined religious authority, travel, organization and military skill, fighting in a broad Awadh coalition rather than a communal frame. On 30 June 1857 at Chinhat, his forces defeated Henry Lawrence's column, forcing the British into the Lucknow Residency siege; Lawrence died on 4 July after being wounded by shellfire. After Lucknow fell, Ahmadullah fought around Shahjahanpur until the Raja of Powayan killed and beheaded him on 5 June 1858 for the British reward of 50,000 silver pieces. Do NOT state he certainly organized the chapati movement; Malleson attributed it, but modern scholars are skeptical.
episodes.chapter_part: III. The Battles and Their Costs

episodes.title: Bakht Khan's Last Argument at Delhi
episodes.figure: Bakht Khan, John Nicholson and William Hodson
episodes.era: The fall of Delhi, September 1857
episodes.region: Delhi, Kashmir Gate, the Ridge, Humayun's Tomb and Khooni Darwaza
episodes.logline: When British guns break Delhi's walls, Bakht Khan urges continued resistance as the city falls to engineering, street fighting and vengeance.
episodes.moral: A lost city can still ask whether surrender is the end.

sources.citation: William Hodson, Twelve Years of a Soldier's Life in India (1859)
sources.note: Hodson's own defense of the execution of Mughal princes.

sources.citation: Two Historic Trials in Red Fort; G.W. Forrest, Selections, vols. 1-2
sources.note: Trial testimony and official siege correspondence.

sources.citation: William Dalrymple, The Last Mughal (2006)
sources.note: Recent archival reconstruction of Delhi's fall and cultural destruction.

episodes.notes: On 14 September 1857 British and allied troops stormed Delhi after siege guns opened breaches; engineers blew the Kashmir Gate, John Nicholson was mortally wounded, and street fighting continued until 20 September. Hodson captured Bahadur Shah Zafar at Humayun's Tomb and on 21 September shot Mirza Mughal, Mirza Khizr Sultan and Mirza Abu Bakr at Khooni Darwaza without trial, an act he acknowledged. British troops looted and sacked the city, destroying homes, manuscripts and much of Delhi's Urdu-Persian cultural world. Bakht Khan's exact words to Zafar are reconstructed, but his plea to continue resistance is broadly attested. State violence plainly and attributed; do NOT romanticize the sack as clean liberation.
episodes.chapter_part: III. The Battles and Their Costs

episodes.title: The Ghat and the Garden at Kanpur
episodes.figure: Nana Sahib, Mowbray Thomson and Colonel Neill
episodes.era: Kanpur, June-July 1857
episodes.region: Kanpur, North India
episodes.logline: Kanpur's boat landing, Bibighar and British reprisals become the revolt's darkest moral battlefield, where every claim must be weighed against evidence and testimony.
episodes.moral: Truth must face every atrocity without choosing hatred.

sources.citation: Mowbray Thomson, The Story of Cawnpore (1859)
sources.note: Eyewitness account by one of the Satichaura survivors, partial and survivor-biased.

sources.citation: Tatya Tope trial testimony, India Office Records, 1859; Papers Relating to the Mutinies in the East Indies, 1857-58
sources.note: Rebel-side testimony and official parliamentary documentation.

sources.citation: Andrew Ward, Our Bones Are Scattered (1996)
sources.note: Detailed modern reconstruction of Kanpur, Satichaura, Bibighar and reprisals.

episodes.notes: At Satichaura Ghat on 27 June 1857, the boats meant to evacuate Wheeler's besieged garrison came under a sudden deadly attack as they left; who opened fire first remains disputed, with British survivor accounts and Tatya Tope's testimony disagreeing. On 15 July about 206 women and children held at Bibighar were killed by hired men after the sepoy guards reportedly refused the order, and their bodies were afterwards placed in a well. Nana Sahib's direct order is disputed and MUST NOT be asserted as fact. After retaking Kanpur, Colonel Neill imposed a deliberate religious degradation on condemned prisoners, forcing high-caste captives to defile themselves cleaning the stained Bibighar floor before they were hanged, and the British also executed rebels by hanging and by blowing from cannon. State the documented killing on BOTH sides soberly and attributed to the sources (Mowbray Thomson, Tatya Tope, Andrew Ward), with NO whitewash and no sensationalism.
episodes.chapter_part: III. The Battles and Their Costs

episodes.title: Ghalib Among the Ruins
episodes.figure: Mirza Ghalib and Bahadur Shah Zafar
episodes.era: Delhi literary testimony and Rangoon exile, 1857-1862
episodes.region: Delhi and Rangoon
episodes.logline: Ghalib's letters and Zafar's exile poems preserve the sound of a literary world surviving its own destruction.
episodes.moral: When cities fall, poems become witnesses.

sources.citation: Mirza Ghalib, Dastambu (1858), translated by Khwaja Ahmad Faruqi (1970)
sources.note: Persian survival memoir written under pressure to prove loyalty.

sources.citation: Bahadur Shah Zafar, Kulliyyat-i-Zafar, ed. Imtiaz Ali Arshi (1944 and later editions)
sources.note: Collected poetry, including Rangoon exile verse.

sources.citation: Ralph Russell and Khurshidul Islam, Ghalib: Life and Letters (1969); William Dalrymple, The Last Mughal (2006)
sources.note: Literary context and archival reconstruction of Delhi's cultural collapse.

episodes.notes: Ghalib lived through the siege and aftermath of Delhi, but he was not a rebel commander or simple nationalist voice; Dastambu is a self-protective Persian prose text addressed to British power. His more candid Urdu letters mourn burned libraries, dead friends, silenced music and the end of Mughal Delhi's elite culture. Zafar, exiled to Rangoon after trial, continued writing ghazals until his death on 7 November 1862. Recent scholarship treats these works as literary evidence, not decorative quotations. Do NOT invent Ghalib's movements during the siege or imply he joined the revolt; use him and Zafar as primary witnesses to cultural destruction.

episodes.title: The Awadh Land Settlement Undone
episodes.era: Annexation, revolt and Taluqdari Settlement, 1856-1859
episodes.region: Awadh, Lucknow and rural eastern Uttar Pradesh
episodes.logline: A land settlement meant to bypass Awadh's talukdars instead binds landlords, peasants and sepoy families into one of 1857's deepest coalitions.
episodes.moral: Policy that ignores society can set the countryside aflame.

sources.citation: Correspondence Relative to the Affairs of Oudh, British Parliamentary Papers, 1856, Cmd. 2085
sources.note: Primary documents on annexation and revenue policy.

sources.citation: Rudrangshu Mukherjee, Awadh in Revolt, 1857-1858 (2001); Eric Stokes, The Peasant Armed (1986)
sources.note: Key modern works on talukdars, peasants and sepoy social geography.

sources.citation: Thomas R. Metcalf, The Aftermath of Revolt: India 1857-1870 (1964)
sources.note: Explains the post-revolt Taluqdari Settlement and colonial policy reversal.

episodes.notes: After annexing Awadh in 1856, Company officials tried to settle revenue directly with raiyats and reduce talukdar power, disrupting chiefs, soldiers, retainers and sepoy families tied to that order. Mukherjee and Stokes show the revolt's Awadh geography maps closely onto these economic and social grievances, not cartridges alone. Rebel Lucknow policy tried to reverse the settlement, and after suppression Canning's 1859 Taluqdari Settlement restored many landlord rights to stabilize rule. This is an economic and social innovation story about revenue systems and backlash. Do NOT portray all talukdars as altruistic patriots; their motives mixed local authority, survival, family interests and anti-Company politics.

episodes.title: How 1857 Was Remembered
episodes.era: Historiography from colonial mutiny to subaltern revolt, 1864-2010
episodes.region: London, Delhi and Indian archives
episodes.logline: The same uprising is retold as mutiny, war of independence, national memory and subaltern revolt, revealing how history changes with its tellers.
episodes.moral: To know the past, examine who is speaking.

sources.citation: John William Kaye, A History of the Sepoy War in India, 1857-58 (1864-1876); G.B. Malleson, History of the Indian Mutiny (1878-1880)
sources.note: Colonial canonical narrative, valuable but systematically framed as mutiny.

sources.citation: V.D. Savarkar, The Indian War of Independence 1857 (1909); S.N. Sen, Eighteen Fifty-Seven (1957)
sources.note: Nationalist and centenary reinterpretations.

sources.citation: Ranajit Guha, 'The Prose of Counter-Insurgency,' Subaltern Studies II (1983); Gautam Bhadra, 'Four Rebels of Eighteen-Fifty-Seven,' Subaltern Studies IV (1985)
sources.note: Subaltern challenge to both colonial and elite nationalist accounts.

episodes.notes: 1857's archive has always been a battlefield: Kaye and Malleson made it a sepoy mutiny, Savarkar's banned 1909 book made it the First War of Independence, Sen's 1957 government history moderated nationalist claims, and Subaltern Studies asked how peasants, artisans and lower-status rebels disappeared from both British and nationalist narratives. Recent work by Wagner, Dalrymple and regional historians favors granular local causes and source criticism. Do NOT treat any single label as complete truth; explain that colonial records are indispensable yet biased, nationalist retellings are inspiring yet sometimes invent intent, and subaltern readings recover agency while relying on hostile trial records.

episodes.title: The Proclamation That Made a Raj
episodes.era: Transfer from Company to Crown, 1858-1870
episodes.region: Allahabad, London, Calcutta and the princely states
episodes.logline: After the uprising, an Act of Parliament and a royal proclamation end Company rule, promise religious non-interference, and create the British Raj.
episodes.moral: Promises of peace must be judged by what power actually does.

sources.citation: Government of India Act 1858, 21 & 22 Vict. c. 106, 2 August 1858
sources.note: Primary constitutional document transferring Company territories to the Crown.

sources.citation: Queen Victoria's Proclamation to the Princes, Chiefs and People of India, 1 November 1858, India Gazette and London Gazette
sources.note: Primary text promising non-interference, princely rights, public service access and limited amnesty.

sources.citation: Thomas R. Metcalf, The Aftermath of Revolt: India 1857-1870 (1964)
sources.note: Classic study of how the post-revolt state implemented and limited these promises.

episodes.notes: The Government of India Act 1858 dissolved Company rule, created the Secretary of State for India and Council of India, and made Canning the first Viceroy. Victoria's Proclamation, read at Allahabad on 1 November 1858, promised non-interference in religion, respect for princely adoption, equal access to public employment and amnesty with exceptions. These promises were real policy shifts, especially ending the Doctrine of Lapse, but equality in service was delayed for decades and key rebels such as Bahadur Shah Zafar and Begum Hazrat Mahal were excluded. Recent constitutional historians note Victoria's personal role in stronger religious language. Do NOT present the Proclamation as full equality; show the birth of the Raj as reform, conciliation and tightened imperial control together.

episodes.title: The Type That Spoke Bengali
episodes.figure: Panchanan Karmakar and the Serampore Trio
episodes.era: Serampore print revolution, c. 1800-1827
episodes.region: Serampore, Calcutta and the Bengali reading world
episodes.logline: In Danish Serampore, a Bengali type-cutter and three missionaries turn metal letters into the machinery of a new public language.
episodes.moral: Ideas travel farther when people build the tools to share them.

sources.citation: William Carey, Grammar of the Bengalee Language (Serampore, 1801)
sources.note: Primary printed evidence for Serampore's early Bengali publishing project.

sources.citation: Samachar Darpan, Vol. 1 No. 1, May 23, 1818
sources.note: The first Bengali-language newspaper issued from the Serampore Mission Press.

sources.citation: Anindita Ghosh, Power in Print (Oxford University Press, 2006)
sources.note: Recent scholarship recovering elite and popular Bengali print cultures, including Battala print.

episodes.notes: The Serampore Mission Press began in 1800 under William Carey, Joshua Marshman and William Ward, but the craft story must give full credit to Panchanan Karmakar, the Bengali goldsmith and type-cutter who made practical Bengali moveable type for the press. The press issued Carey's Bengali grammar in 1801, Samachar Darpan in 1818, and Serampore College's chartered educational vision in 1827. Recent print history stresses that the revolution did not remain elite: cheap Battala chapbooks, almanacs and popular literature reached readers excluded from the usual bhadralok story. Accuracy flags: do NOT call Serampore the first press in India, because Goa and Calcutta had earlier presses; do NOT claim Carey invented Bengali type; do NOT omit the missionary conversion motive or the Danish-jurisdiction loophole that let Serampore operate outside direct Company control.
episodes.chapter_part: I. The Press and the Question

episodes.title: The Man Who Asked Why
episodes.era: Early reform and Brahmo Sabha, c. 1803-1833
episodes.region: Radhanagar, Patna, Varanasi, Calcutta and Bristol
episodes.logline: A multilingual scholar questions inherited dogma in Persian, Sanskrit, Bengali and English, then builds a new public forum for reasoned reform.
episodes.moral: Questioning can be an act of service.

sources.citation: Rammohun Roy, Tuhfat ul Muwahhidin, c. 1803-1804
sources.note: Early Persian rationalist critique of religious superstition, later printed in 1884.

sources.citation: Brahmo Sabha Trust Deed, January 8, 1830
sources.note: Primary institutional record for the monotheistic reform association.

sources.citation: David Kopf, The Brahmo Samaj and the Shaping of the Modern Indian Mind (1979); Sumit Sarkar, Writing Social History (1997)
sources.note: Standard and revisionist readings of Rammohun's reform politics.

episodes.notes: Rammohun Roy, born in 1772, studied Bengali, Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic and English, worked for the East India Company, wrote Tuhfat ul Muwahhidin around 1803-04, founded the Atmiya Sabha around 1815 and the Brahmo Sabha in 1828, and used Sambad Kaumudi and Mirat-ul-Akhbar as vehicles for public argument. Recent scholarship treats him neither as a pure saint nor a simple colonial collaborator: he worked within colonial institutions, argued for Western scientific education in his 1823 Amherst letter, and also remained limited on caste and women's property. Accuracy flags: do NOT claim the Brahmo Samaj name belongs to 1828; do NOT state as fact the popular story that he saw a sister-in-law's sati, because it is not attested in his own writings; do NOT flatten his conservative social limits.
episodes.chapter_part: I. The Press and the Question

episodes.title: Fire on the Pyre
episodes.figure: Rammohun Roy and Lord William Bentinck
episodes.era: Sati abolition debate, 1818-1833
episodes.region: Calcutta, Bengal Presidency and London
episodes.logline: Petitions, newspapers and council minutes converge as Bengal Regulation XVII makes sati a crime, while widows' own voices remain mostly absent.
episodes.moral: A humane law is only the beginning of justice.

sources.citation: Bengal Regulation XVII of 1829, December 4, 1829
sources.note: Primary law abolishing sati in British Bengal.

sources.citation: Rammohun Roy, Conference between an Advocate for and an Opponent of the Practice of Burning Widows Alive (1818/1820)
sources.note: Primary reform polemic against sati.

sources.citation: Lata Mani, Contentious Traditions (University of California Press, 1998)
sources.note: Major recent reinterpretation of the sati debate and the absence of women's voices.

episodes.notes: Colonial records counted hundreds of sati incidents in Bengal in the 1810s, including 839 in 1818, and Rammohun used print and petitioning to argue that the practice lacked binding scriptural authority. Bentinck's Regulation XVII of December 4, 1829 criminalized sati in British Bengal and was later upheld in London, while Radhakanta Deb's Dharma Sabha organized a massive counter-petition against interference. Recent feminist scholarship warns that women were largely made objects of debate by colonial officials and elite Hindu men; the law did not end widow poverty, stigma, shaved heads, food restrictions or regional continuation beyond British Bengal. Accuracy flags: do NOT present Rammohun as single-handed abolisher; do NOT omit the larger conservative counter-mobilization; do NOT turn abolition into a simple colonial rescue story.

episodes.title: The Firebrands of Hindu College
episodes.era: Young Bengal and Hindu College, 1826-1831
episodes.region: Entally, Hindu College and Calcutta's debating societies
episodes.logline: A teenage Anglo-Indian teacher turns a classroom into a storm of free thought, scandal and debate before cholera ends his life at twenty-two.
episodes.moral: A small circle can still light difficult questions.

sources.citation: Henry Derozio, Poems (Calcutta, 1827) and The Fakeer of Jungheera (1828)
sources.note: Primary writings by Derozio.

sources.citation: Academic Association records and Calcutta press notices, 1828-1831
sources.note: Contemporary evidence for Young Bengal debating culture and controversy.

sources.citation: Rosinka Chaudhuri, Gentlemen Poets in Colonial Bengal (2002); Supriya Chaudhuri, ODNB entry on Derozio (2009)
sources.note: Recent literary and biographical scholarship.

episodes.notes: Derozio was born in Calcutta in 1809, taught at Hindu College from May 1826, inspired the Academic Association in 1828, and was dismissed in April 1831 under conservative pressure before dying of cholera on December 26, 1831. His students debated caste, press freedom, women's rights and rational religion, sometimes deliberately violating purity taboos by eating beef or drinking wine. Recent scholarship stresses the movement's reach was real but tiny: an elite Calcutta circle, not a mass awakening of Bengal. Accuracy flags: do NOT call Derozio the first modern nationalist; do NOT erase his Anglo-Indian Christian background; do NOT romanticize his death beyond the common cholera realities of colonial Calcutta.

episodes.title: Dwarkanath's Smokestacks and Ships
episodes.era: Anglo-Indian enterprise, c. 1828-1846
episodes.region: Jorasanko, Raniganj, the Hooghly, Assam and London
episodes.logline: Coal mines, banks, river steamers, tea and opium make Dwarkanath Tagore a dazzling partner in empire and a warning about colonial wealth.
episodes.moral: Enterprise without conscience leaves a troubled inheritance.

sources.citation: Carr, Tagore and Company records and Bengal Presidency commercial records
sources.note: Primary evidence for banking, coal, shipping, indigo, tea and opium businesses.

sources.citation: The London Mail obituary of Dwarkanath Tagore, August 7, 1846
sources.note: Contemporary press account of his London death and reputation.

sources.citation: Blair Kling, Partner in Empire (University of California Press, 1976)
sources.note: Standard scholarly biography emphasizing colonial commerce and opium.

episodes.notes: Dwarkanath Tagore became a Union Bank director in 1828, co-founded Carr, Tagore and Company around 1834, purchased Raniganj coal interests, ran Hooghly tug services, invested in Assam tea and profited from indigo and the Company-regulated opium trade to China. He funded reform causes and supported Calcutta Medical College, but his wealth was entangled with exploitative colonial circuits; his businesses collapsed soon after his 1846 death in London. Recent economic history treats him as both a pioneering Indian entrepreneur and a partner in empire. Accuracy flags: do NOT call him India's first industrialist without qualification; do NOT omit opium; do NOT imply his sons inherited a stable fortune.

episodes.title: The Cadaver in the Lecture Hall
episodes.era: Calcutta Medical College and anatomical teaching, 1835-1848
episodes.region: Calcutta Medical College, Bengal Presidency
episodes.logline: In a locked room at Calcutta Medical College, Madhusudan Gupta lifts a scalpel and forces modern medicine to negotiate with old ideas of purity.
episodes.moral: Knowledge advances when courage respects evidence and context.

sources.citation: The Centenary of the Medical College, Bengal, 1835-1934 (Calcutta, 1935)
sources.note: Institutional history preserving early College traditions and records.

sources.citation: Anirban Das and Samita Sen, 'A History of the Calcutta Medical College and Hospital, 1835-1936' in Science and Modern India (2011)
sources.note: Recent institutional analysis of colonial medicine.

sources.citation: David Arnold, Colonizing the Body (University of California Press, 1993)
sources.note: Major study of state medicine and bodily authority in colonial India.

episodes.notes: Calcutta Medical College was founded in 1835 to train Indian medical personnel for a colonial state, not simply to improve Indian public health. Madhusudan Gupta, a Sanskrit-educated Brahmin physician, used Ayurvedic textual precedent and elite negotiation to justify dissection before making the first celebrated cut, most often dated January 10, 1836 though some sources give October 28. By 1848, hundreds of dissections were reported annually. Recent work emphasizes the colonial army's needs, continued Indian resistance to Western medicine, and the disputed corpse-procurement story involving Dwarkanath Tagore. Accuracy flags: do NOT call it the first dissection in Asia; do NOT assert the Fort William cannon salute as fact; do NOT present Gupta as rejecting tradition rather than arguing through it.

episodes.title: Vidyasagar Opens the Widow's Door
episodes.era: Widow remarriage reform, 1855-1856 and after
episodes.region: Birsingha, Calcutta and the Bengal Legislative Council
episodes.logline: Vidyasagar turns scripture, petitions and personal risk into a law for widow remarriage, while his own caste limits complicate the halo.
episodes.moral: Reform is strongest when it also faces its own limits.

sources.citation: Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act, Act XV of 1856, July 25, 1856
sources.note: Primary legislation legalizing Hindu widow remarriage.

sources.citation: Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar, Barna Parichay (1855) and widow-remarriage petitions (1855)
sources.note: Primary evidence for his educational and reform activity.

sources.citation: Sumit Sarkar, Writing Social History (1997); Tanika Sarkar, Hindu Wife, Hindu Nation (2001)
sources.note: Critical readings of Vidyasagar, gender reform and caste limits.

episodes.notes: Vidyasagar, born in 1820, became a Sanskrit College scholar, prose reformer and girls' education advocate, then argued from Parasara Smriti and other texts for legal widow remarriage. Act XV passed on July 25, 1856 despite a Dharma Sabha counter-petition with nearly 40,000 signatures, and the first remarriage under the Act took place on December 7, 1856. Recent scholarship foregrounds a patriarchal bargain: elite men debated widows' lives, while widows' own voices remain scarce. The honest portrait must include Vidyasagar's 1859 letter opposing education for lower castes and his earlier resistance to admitting a suvarnavanik student to Sanskrit College. Accuracy flags: do NOT claim the Act ended widow suffering; do NOT use the exact 200,000 rupee expenditure figure as certain; do NOT make him a caste radical.

episodes.title: Blank Verse and the Demon-Hero
episodes.era: Bengali literary transformation, 1858-1873
episodes.region: Sagardari, Calcutta, Madras, Versailles and London
episodes.logline: A poet who once chased English fame returns to Bengali and makes the Ramayana's defeated enemy a Miltonic tragic hero.
episodes.moral: A borrowed form can become new when it speaks in one's own tongue.

sources.citation: Michael Madhusudan Dutt, Meghnad Badh Kavya (Calcutta, 1861)
sources.note: Primary Bengali epic in blank verse.

sources.citation: Michael Madhusudan Dutt's letters to Gour Das Bysack, 1848-1873
sources.note: Major primary source for his life, ambitions and debts.

sources.citation: Rosinka Chaudhuri, Gentlemen Poets in Colonial Bengal (2002); Sudipta Kaviraj, The Unhappy Consciousness (1995)
sources.note: Modern literary-historical scholarship on colonial Bengali writing.

episodes.notes: Michael Madhusudan Dutt, born in 1824 in Jessore, converted to Christianity in 1843, wrote in English in Madras, then returned to Calcutta and Bengali around 1858. Meghnad Badh Kavya (1861) introduced blank verse into Bengali epic and made Ravana's son Meghnad the tragic hero; his sonnets later adapted Petrarchan form. Recent scholarship reads his European aspiration and return to Bengali as a colonial formation, not simple patriotism. Accuracy flags: do NOT call him a straightforward Bengali nationalist; do NOT omit his Christian conversion, debts, European sojourn and poverty; do NOT credit him with inventing modern Bengali prose, which Rammohun and Vidyasagar had already shaped.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. The Word and the Image Made New

episodes.title: Vande Mataram's Troubled Birth
episodes.era: The Bengali novel and contested nationalism, 1865-1937
episodes.region: Naihati, Calcutta and the nationalist public sphere
episodes.logline: Bankim's song gives a movement words of devotion, but Anandamath also leaves a legacy that later India must argue over.
episodes.moral: A powerful song can unite and unsettle at once.

sources.citation: Bankim Chandra Chatterjee, Anandamath (Calcutta, 1882)
sources.note: Primary novel containing Vande Mataram.

sources.citation: Congress Working Committee resolution on Vande Mataram, October 1937
sources.note: Primary political compromise limiting public use to the first two stanzas.

sources.citation: Sudipta Kaviraj, The Unhappy Consciousness (Oxford University Press, 1995)
sources.note: Major analysis of Bankim's ideological contradictions.

episodes.notes: Bankim Chandra, one of the first Calcutta University graduates, served as a colonial deputy magistrate while creating the Bengali novel, including Durgeshnandini (1865) and Anandamath (1882). Vande Mataram, composed between about 1875 and 1882 and set to music by Tagore in 1896, became a Swadeshi and national song; only the first two stanzas were later endorsed for public use because later stanzas invoke goddess imagery. The notes must state plainly that Anandamath portrays Muslim rulers as oppressors in a communally fraught historical fiction, while also being used in anti-colonial mobilization. Accuracy flags: do NOT call Vande Mataram the National Anthem; do NOT make Bankim simply pro-independence, since he accepted British legitimacy; do NOT omit either the nationalist power or the Muslim critique of the song and novel.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. The Word and the Image Made New

episodes.title: Abanindranath Paints the Motherland
episodes.era: Bengal School of Art and Swadeshi, 1896-1905
episodes.region: Government School of Art, Jorasanko and Calcutta
episodes.logline: A British principal, a Tagore painter and Japanese wash techniques help imagine Bharat Mata as a new visual language for Swadeshi India.
episodes.moral: Art can awaken belonging, but symbols must be read carefully.

sources.citation: Abanindranath Tagore, Bharat Mata (1905), Rabindra Bharati Society, Calcutta
sources.note: Primary art object of Swadeshi nationalist iconography.

sources.citation: E.B. Havell, A Handbook of Indian Art (1920)
sources.note: Primary articulation of the Bengal School aesthetic program.

sources.citation: Natasha Eaton, 'Swadeshi Color,' The Art Bulletin 95:4 (2013); R. Siva Kumar, Santiniketan: The Making of a Contextual Modernism (1997)
sources.note: Recent debates on color, nationalism and the limits of the Bengal School label.

episodes.notes: E.B. Havell became principal of the Government School of Art in 1896 and pushed students toward Indian and Asian models rather than European academic realism. Abanindranath Tagore developed a wash style shaped by Mughal miniatures and Japanese nihonga contacts, then painted Bharat Mata in 1905 amid the Partition of Bengal and Swadeshi agitation. Recent art history complicates a simple nationalist story: Havell was a British institutional enabler, Japanese influence mattered, and R. Siva Kumar warns that later Santiniketan modernists should not be collapsed into a single Bengal School. Accuracy flags: do NOT describe the movement as purely anti-colonial or purely indigenous; do NOT omit feminist critiques that making the nation a mother can eclipse actual women as agents.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. The Word and the Image Made New

episodes.title: Song Offerings to the World
episodes.era: Gitanjali, the Nobel and Visva-Bharati, 1910-1921
episodes.region: Jorasanko, Santiniketan, London and Stockholm
episodes.logline: Tagore reshapes his Bengali songs into English prose poems, wins the Nobel, and turns world fame toward an experimental school under open skies.
episodes.moral: A voice rooted at home can still speak to the world.

sources.citation: Rabindranath Tagore, Gitanjali (Bengali, 1910) and Gitanjali: Song Offerings (London, 1912)
sources.note: Primary Bengali collection and English creative reworking.

sources.citation: Nobel Prize in Literature citation for Rabindranath Tagore, November 13, 1913
sources.note: Primary award record.

sources.citation: Tagore's letter returning his knighthood, May 30, 1919
sources.note: Primary protest after the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.

sources.citation: Oxford Tagore Translations project (Oxford University Press, 2010-) and scholarship on the English Gitanjali
sources.note: Recent translation work showing differences between Bengali originals and English versions.

episodes.notes: Rabindranath Tagore published the Bengali Gitanjali in 1910, made a 103-poem English prose selection in 1912 with W.B. Yeats's preface, and received the Nobel Prize on November 13, 1913, becoming the first non-European literature laureate. He used his fame and funds to strengthen Santiniketan and later Visva-Bharati, while his 1919 knighthood renunciation after Jallianwala Bagh showed his moral politics. Recent scholarship emphasizes that English Gitanjali is a creative adaptation, not a literal translation, and that European advocates helped its reception. Accuracy flags: do NOT claim Jana Gana Mana was written to welcome King George V, a claim Tagore denied; do NOT call Tagore a narrow nationalist, since he criticized aggressive nationalism in works such as Ghare Baire.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. The Word and the Image Made New

episodes.title: Ladyland: Rokeya's Feminist Vision
episodes.era: Muslim women's education and feminist writing, 1905-1932
episodes.region: Pairaband, Bhagalpur and Calcutta
episodes.logline: From strict purdah to Ladyland's solar science, Rokeya builds a school and a literature where Muslim women imagine freedom for themselves.
episodes.moral: Education lets the secluded become authors of their own future.

sources.citation: Begum Rokeya, Sultana's Dream, The Indian Ladies' Magazine (1905)
sources.note: Primary feminist utopian and science-fiction text.

sources.citation: Begum Rokeya, Matichur (1904, 1922) and Abarodhbasini (1931)
sources.note: Primary Bengali essays and critique of seclusion.

sources.citation: Bharati Ray, Early Feminists of Colonial India (Oxford University Press, 2002); Roushan Jahan, Inside Seclusion (1981)
sources.note: Recovery and analysis of Rokeya's feminist work.

episodes.notes: Rokeya was born in 1880 in Rangpur, learned Bengali and English with help from siblings despite household resistance, married Sakhawat Hossain in 1898, published Sultana's Dream in 1905, and founded Sakhawat Memorial Girls' School after her husband's death, first in Bhagalpur in 1909 and then in Calcutta in 1911. Her Anjuman-e-Khawateen-e-Islam, founded in 1916, organized Muslim women's education and employment. Recent scholarship stresses that she worked within Islamic ethical arguments, not outside or against Islam, and that her Bengali works are as important as the famous English utopia. Accuracy flags: do NOT call her anti-Islamic or merely westernized; do NOT treat Sultana's Dream as her only contribution; do NOT omit the poverty, family conflict and physical labor behind the school.

episodes.title: Bidrohi: The Rebel Poet
episodes.era: Rebel poetry and anti-communal modernism, 1917-1942
episodes.region: Churulia, Karachi, Calcutta, Alipore Jail and Dhaka
episodes.logline: A poor muezzin's son, soldier and journalist detonates Bidrohi in print, then sings Allah, Kali, Krishna and rebellion in the same breath.
episodes.moral: True rebellion refuses both tyranny and hatred.

sources.citation: Kazi Nazrul Islam, 'Bidrohi,' Bijli magazine, January 1922
sources.note: Primary publication of the rebel poem.

sources.citation: Dhumketu newspaper issues, Calcutta, 1922
sources.note: Primary source for Nazrul's seditious journalism and arrest context.

sources.citation: Kazi Nazrul Islam, Rajbondir Jabanbondi (1923)
sources.note: Primary prison statement written after arrest for sedition.

sources.citation: Fakrul Alam, The Essential Nazrul (University Press Limited, Dhaka, 2009); Rafiuddin Ahmed, The Bengal Muslims 1871-1906 (1981)
sources.note: Modern translation and context for Bengali Muslim identity.

episodes.notes: Kazi Nazrul Islam was born in Churulia in 1899, worked in mosque service and folk theatre, joined the British Indian Army in 1917, and emerged in Calcutta as a poet-journalist after the war. Bidrohi appeared in Bijli in January 1922; Dhumketu soon brought him sedition charges, imprisonment and the prison text Rajbondir Jabanbondi. His songs fused Bengali, Persian, Islamic, Hindu, kirtan, baul, ghazal and revolutionary vocabularies; his 1924 marriage to Pramila Devi and his cross-faith imagery made anti-communalism lived as well as literary. Accuracy flags: do NOT publish Bidrohi as 1921; do NOT omit his army service; do NOT confuse his pre-1947 Indian anti-colonial role with his later status as Bangladesh's national poet; do NOT reduce him to a Bengali Shelley analogy.

episodes.title: The Queen Who Came Back
episodes.era: Sivaganga resistance, c. 1772-1801
episodes.region: Sivaganga, Ramnad, Kalaiyarkoil and Virupaachi, Tamil Nadu
episodes.logline: After Company-backed forces killed her husband, Velu Nachiyar built alliances in exile and returned to recover Sivaganga from British power.
episodes.moral: Careful preparation can restore what violence takes.

sources.citation: J.H. Nelson, The Madura Country: A Manual, vol. 4 (Madras Government, 1868)
sources.note: Colonial administrative account for Sivaganga and Ramnad politics.

sources.citation: Madras Presidency and Tamil Nadu State Archives, Sivaganga Collectorate and administrative records
sources.note: Records for the Maruthu brothers, Company intervention and execution traditions.

sources.citation: Lok Sabha proceedings, 11 March 2002, on conservation of Sivaganga Palace of Rani Velu Nachiar
sources.note: Modern official recognition of the historic figure and site.

episodes.notes: Velu Nachiyar's husband Muthu Vaduganatha Thevar was killed at Kalaiyarkoil in 1772; tradition and administrative records place her exile at Virupaachi, alliance-seeking with Hyder Ali, return against Company power around 1780, and rule until about 1790. The Maruthu brothers later administered Sivaganga and were hanged by the British at Tirupputhur on 24 October 1801. RECENT FINDINGS: Tamil regional scholarship and government heritage work have recovered her from a thin English archive, but the source base remains uneven. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT call her a modern nationalist in the 19th-century sense; this was a regional anti-Company struggle. Kuyili's armoury sacrifice must be presented as Tamil oral tradition, not 18th-century archival fact, and casualty figures should not be invented.

episodes.title: The Ink That Shook an Empire
episodes.era: Print nationalism and the birth of national politics, 1876-1905
episodes.region: Calcutta, Pune and Bombay
episodes.logline: Newspapers, songs and the Indian National Congress turned scattered grievances into a national language of politics.
episodes.moral: A movement begins when people find a shared voice.

sources.citation: Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Kesari (from 1881) and Mahratta (from 1881)
sources.note: Primary vernacular and English press record of early nationalist mobilization.

sources.citation: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, Anandamath (1882)
sources.note: Primary literary source for Vande Mataram and its later movement life.

sources.citation: Indian National Congress, Proceedings of the First Session, Bombay, 28-30 December 1885
sources.note: Founding record of the all-India political institution.

episodes.notes: Between the Indian Association of 1876, Tilak's Kesari and Mahratta from 1881, Bankim's Anandamath in 1882, and the first INC session in 1885, the freedom movement gained communications machinery: vernacular print, patriotic song, and formal political assembly. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP by Sekhar Bandyopadhyay and studies of print culture emphasize this as an institutional innovation, not merely a preface to later mass politics. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say A.O. Hume founded the INC alone; Indian leaders and delegates were essential. Vande Mataram inspired many but was also debated because of its religious imagery, so present both the mobilizing power and the controversy soberly.

episodes.title: The Deaf Must Hear
episodes.era: Assembly Bomb Case and Lahore Conspiracy Case, 1929-1931
episodes.region: Delhi, Lahore and Punjab prisons
episodes.logline: Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt threw low-yield bombs, surrendered, and turned a courtroom into a platform for revolution.
episodes.moral: A clear idea can outlive the harshest sentence.

sources.citation: Statement of Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt in the Assembly Bomb Case, Sessions Court Delhi, 6 June 1929
sources.note: Primary explanation of the act and its moral argument.

sources.citation: Malwinder Jit Singh Waraich, ed., Complete Tribunal Proceedings: Lahore Conspiracy Case (2017)
sources.note: Documentary legal record of the tribunal and verdict.

sources.citation: Kama Maclean, A Revolutionary History of Interwar India (OUP, 2015)
sources.note: Recent use of CID files, images and print networks to reinterpret HSRA strategy.

episodes.notes: On 8 April 1929 Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt threw smoke bombs and leaflets in the Central Legislative Assembly, shouted Inquilab Zindabad, and surrendered. The leaflet used the idea that it takes a loud voice to make the deaf hear. The hunger strike made prison discrimination a national issue; Jatindra Nath Das died on 13 September 1929, and Singh, Rajguru and Sukhdev were sentenced on 7 October 1930 and hanged at Lahore on 23 March 1931. RECENT FINDINGS: Maclean shows this was a media-conscious political performance shaped by print, photography and surveillance. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim the bombs were intended to kill; the design, statements and injuries show symbolic action. Do not merge Rajguru and Sukhdev into the Assembly bombing; they were tied through the Lahore case.

episodes.title: Gandhi's Indigo Truth
episodes.era: Champaran Satyagraha, 1917
episodes.region: Champaran, Bihar
episodes.logline: Gandhi answered a peasant's plea by documenting indigo oppression until the state had to investigate its own injustice.
episodes.moral: Truth grows powerful when it is patiently recorded.

sources.citation: M.K. Gandhi, An Autobiography: The Story of My Experiments with Truth, Part V, Champaran chapters
sources.note: Participant account of the inquiry, arrest and settlement.

sources.citation: Government of Bihar and Orissa, Report of the Champaran Agrarian Enquiry Committee (1917)
sources.note: Official record acknowledging planter abuses and recommending reform.

sources.citation: Jacques Pouchepadass, Champaran and Gandhi: Planters, Peasants and Gandhian Politics (1999)
sources.note: Modern reconstruction using planter and district records.

episodes.notes: Raj Kumar Shukla brought Gandhi to Champaran in 1917, where tenant cultivators suffered under the tinkathia indigo system. Gandhi refused an order to leave, organized lawyers such as Rajendra Prasad and Brajkishore Prasad, collected testimony, and served on the inquiry committee that led to repayment of part of illegal exactions and abolition of the system. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP stresses Champaran as a legal-organizational innovation: investigation, disciplined refusal and negotiated reform. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT present Champaran as spontaneous revolt or instant victory; it was carefully organized and planter withdrawal took time.

episodes.title: The Women of Dharasana
episodes.era: Civil Disobedience Movement, May 1930
episodes.region: Dharasana Salt Works, Gujarat
episodes.logline: With Gandhi jailed, Sarojini Naidu led unarmed salt satyagrahis into a beating that shocked the world press.
episodes.moral: Courage can turn suffering into witness.

sources.citation: Webb Miller, United Press eyewitness dispatch from Dharasana, 21 May 1930
sources.note: Contemporary global press account of the lathi charge.

sources.citation: United States Senate Congressional Record, May 1930, reading of Miller's dispatch
sources.note: Evidence of international political reception.

sources.citation: Geraldine Forbes, Women in Modern India (Cambridge, 1996)
sources.note: Modern analysis of women's participation in Civil Disobedience.

episodes.notes: After Gandhi was arrested on 4-5 May 1930 and Abbas Tyabji was also arrested, Sarojini Naidu led volunteers at Dharasana and insisted they not resist violence. Webb Miller's dispatch described steel-tipped lathis striking unarmed satyagrahis and circulated worldwide despite censorship attempts. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP frames Dharasana as both a women's leadership story and a communications victory in global anti-colonial politics. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT erase Naidu's leadership by making the event only Gandhi's plan; casualty numbers vary, so use ranges. Do not confuse Sarojini Naidu with Annie Besant, the earlier woman INC president.

episodes.title: Amritsar 1919
episodes.era: Jallianwala Bagh massacre and Rowlatt protests, 1919
episodes.region: Amritsar, Punjab
episodes.logline: At Jallianwala Bagh, an unarmed Baisakhi crowd met imperial fire and a massacre shattered trust in British reform.
episodes.moral: Rule by terror destroys its own claim to legitimacy.

sources.citation: Report of the Disorders Inquiry Committee, the Hunter Committee Report (Government of India, 1920)
sources.note: Official inquiry including Dyer's testimony and casualty figures.

sources.citation: Rabindranath Tagore, letter to Viceroy Chelmsford returning his knighthood, 31 May 1919
sources.note: Primary Indian elite response to the massacre.

sources.citation: Kim A. Wagner, Amritsar 1919: An Empire of Fear and the Making of a Massacre (Yale, 2019)
sources.note: Recent reconstruction from military and administrative records.

episodes.notes: On 13 April 1919, after the arrests of Saifuddin Kitchlew and Satyapal amid anti-Rowlatt protests, Dyer entered Jallianwala Bagh with troops and fired without warning into a trapped crowd, many present for Baisakhi. About 1,650 rounds were fired; the official British count was 379 dead and around 1,200 injured, while Indian estimates were higher. No medical aid was sent, and later punitive measures in Punjab included the infamous crawling order. RECENT FINDINGS: Wagner shows the firing was part of a deliberate doctrine of exemplary terror, not simple panic. ACCURACY FLAGS: present casualty ranges with sources; do NOT make this communal, and attribute actions precisely rather than blurring Dyer and O'Dwyer.

episodes.title: Lakshmi Sahgal Trains the Rani Regiment
episodes.era: Rani of Jhansi Regiment and Indian National Army, 1943-1945
episodes.region: Singapore, Rangoon, Burma and the Imphal front
episodes.logline: Lakshmi Sahgal organized women from the Indian diaspora into the Rani of Jhansi Regiment, turning exile politics into disciplined military service.
episodes.moral: A freedom struggle grows wider when women claim the front line.

sources.citation: Lakshmi Sahgal, A Revolutionary Life: Memoirs of a Political Activist (1997)
sources.note: Commanding officer account of recruitment, training and the retreat.

sources.citation: National Archives of India, INA Records and Azad Hind Government papers, 1943-1945
sources.note: Primary files on INA organization and the Rani of Jhansi Regiment.

sources.citation: Vera Hildebrand, Women at War: Subhas Chandra Bose and the Rani of Jhansi Regiment (2016)
sources.note: Recent dedicated study using interviews and INA records.

episodes.notes: This episode is deliberately NOT the general Bose Chalo Delhi story. Its lens is Lakshmi Swaminathan Sahgal and the Rani of Jhansi Regiment: announced in July 1943 in Singapore, recruited largely from Indian diaspora communities in Malaya and Singapore, trained for military and medical work, and endured the Burma retreat after the failed Imphal campaign. Bose belongs in the background as founder of Azad Hind, but the narrative center is women's mobilization, command, discipline and the social shock of combat training under colonial patriarchy. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Vera Hildebrand and Sugata Bose use interviews, INA records and Southeast Asian archives to recover the regiment beyond legend. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim the regiment won battles inside India or that all members saw front-line combat; training, mobilization and retreat are the attested core. Do not turn Lakshmi Sahgal into a symbolic mascot; she was a physician, commander and later public political figure.

episodes.title: Do or Die
episodes.era: Quit India Movement, August-November 1942
episodes.region: Bombay, Bihar, Midnapore, Satara and underground India
episodes.logline: After the British arrested Congress leaders, Usha Mehta's secret radio and local parallel governments kept Quit India alive.
episodes.moral: When authority shuts every door, courage finds a signal.

sources.citation: Congress Working Committee Quit India Resolution, 8 August 1942, in Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi, vol. 83
sources.note: Primary statement of the movement and Gandhi's Do or Die call.

sources.citation: Viceroy Linlithgow telegram to Winston Churchill, 31 August 1942, India Office Records, British Library
sources.note: Colonial assessment calling it the most serious rebellion since 1857.

sources.citation: Usha Mehta oral history interviews, Nehru Memorial Museum and Library
sources.note: Primary testimony on Congress Radio and its rotating Bombay locations.

episodes.notes: Gandhi gave the Do or Die call at Gowalia Tank on 8 August 1942; by morning the top Congress leadership was arrested. Underground networks responded with Jayaprakash Narayan's escape and organizing, Nana Patil's Satara parallel government, and Usha Mehta's Congress Radio broadcasting from somewhere in India on 42.34 metres from 14 August to 12 November 1942. British repression included mass arrests, collective punishments, and documented aerial bombing in parts of Bihar and Midnapore. RECENT WORK on regional archives shows Quit India was not leaderless chaos but improvised self-rule. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT state 100,000 arrests as exact; use a 60,000-100,000 range. Congress Radio lasted 87 days, not a full three months.

episodes.title: The Ghadar Press Crosses Oceans
episodes.era: Ghadar movement and wartime conspiracy, 1913-1915
episodes.region: San Francisco, Vancouver, Punjab and Lahore
episodes.logline: Kartar Singh Sarabha and the Ghadar press carried revolutionary print from Pacific migrants back to Punjab during the First World War.
episodes.moral: Words can become dangerous when they cross borders with workers and exiles.

sources.citation: Ghadar newspaper, first issued by the Hindustan Association of the Pacific Coast, San Francisco, 1 November 1913
sources.note: Primary revolutionary newspaper printed for migrant networks.
