sources.citation: Lahore Conspiracy Case judgment and related Home Department Political files, 1915-1916, National Archives of India
sources.note: Primary colonial legal record for the Ghadar prosecutions and executions.

sources.citation: Maia Ramnath, Haj to Utopia: How the Ghadar Movement Charted Global Radicalism (2011)
sources.note: Recent transnational study of Ghadar networks and radical print culture.

episodes.notes: Kartar Singh Sarabha, a teenage Punjabi student-worker in California, joined the Hindustan Association of the Pacific Coast and helped produce the Ghadar newspaper from San Francisco in 1913. During the First World War, Ghadar organizers tried to turn migrant anger, racial exclusion and wartime opportunity into revolt in India; the plan was penetrated by informers, and Sarabha was tried in the Lahore Conspiracy Case and hanged on 16 November 1915. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP by Maia Ramnath and Seema Sohi reframes Ghadar as transnational anti-colonial organizing among workers, students and exiles, not just a failed plot. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim the 1915 uprising succeeded or that Ghadar was confined to Punjab; it was global but uneven. Do not romanticize away the severe source problem: much detail comes from colonial surveillance and trial files created by the movement's enemies.

episodes.title: Ambedkar at the Round Table
episodes.era: Round Table Conferences to Constitution, 1930-1949
episodes.region: London, Yerawada Jail and New Delhi
episodes.logline: Ambedkar carried the rights of the oppressed into imperial conferences and then into India's Constitution.
episodes.moral: Freedom is incomplete unless law protects the least powerful.

sources.citation: Round Table Conference Proceedings, HMSO, 1930-1932
sources.note: Primary record of Ambedkar's arguments on representation.

sources.citation: Poona Pact, 24 September 1932, reprinted in B.R. Ambedkar, Writings and Speeches, vol. 9
sources.note: Text of the compromise on reserved seats and joint electorates.

sources.citation: Constituent Assembly Debates, 1946-1949, Parliament of India archive
sources.note: Primary record of Ambedkar's drafting role and constitutional speeches.

episodes.notes: Ambedkar's freedom struggle ran through law: the Southborough evidence of 1919, Round Table Conferences of 1930-32, conflict with Gandhi over separate electorates, the Poona Pact of 24 September 1932, and the Constitution adopted on 26 November 1949 with Fundamental Rights and Article 17 abolishing untouchability legally. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP by Jaffrelot, Omvedt and others stresses Ambedkar's critique that political freedom without social democracy would betray millions. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT flatten Gandhi and Ambedkar into simple enemies; their conflict over representation was real and consequential, while both opposed untouchability. Do not claim the Constitution ended caste practice; it made discrimination unlawful.

episodes.title: Dadabhai Naoroji Counts the Drain
episodes.era: Economic nationalism and drain theory, 1867-1906
episodes.region: Bombay, London and Indian National Congress platforms
episodes.logline: Dadabhai Naoroji turned poverty into arithmetic, proving that empire drained Indian wealth through salaries, remittances and unequal rule.
episodes.moral: Injustice becomes harder to deny when someone counts it clearly.

sources.citation: Dadabhai Naoroji, Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901)
sources.note: Primary synthesis of the drain theory and economic critique of empire.

sources.citation: Dadabhai Naoroji, Indian National Congress presidential addresses, 1886, 1893 and 1906
sources.note: Primary political statements linking economic drain to swaraj.

sources.citation: Dinyar Patel, Naoroji: Pioneer of Indian Nationalism (Harvard University Press, 2020)
sources.note: Recent biography using Naoroji papers and British parliamentary sources.

episodes.notes: Naoroji, merchant, teacher, INC president and the first Indian elected to the British Parliament, made economic critique a weapon of the freedom struggle. From his 1867 drain calculations through Poverty and Un-British Rule in India in 1901, he argued that India was impoverished by official remittances, high European salaries, military costs, pensions and trade structures that transferred wealth to Britain without equivalent return. At the 1906 INC session he used the word swaraj as the movement's goal. RECENT FINDINGS: Dinyar Patel's 2020 biography draws on newly organized Naoroji papers to show how statistics, parliamentary lobbying and nationalist politics worked together. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT present every number as exact modern GDP accounting; Naoroji's estimates were pioneering and debated. Do not reduce him to a moderate petitioner; his economic argument radicalized the demand for self-government.

episodes.title: Pingali Venkayya Designs a Flag
episodes.era: National flag design, 1916-1947
episodes.region: Bhatlapenumarru, Vijayawada and New Delhi
episodes.logline: Pingali Venkayya's flag experiments helped give the freedom movement a symbol that independent India could carry.
episodes.moral: A simple symbol can gather a nation's hope.

sources.citation: Pingali Venkayya, Bharata Desabhimani (Telugu pamphlet, 1916)
sources.note: Primary advocacy for an Indian national flag.

sources.citation: Indian National Congress Flag Committee Report, 1931, AICC papers
sources.note: Formal Congress discussion of the tricolour with charkha.

sources.citation: Constituent Assembly Debates, Vol. IV, 22 July 1947
sources.note: Primary record of adoption of the national flag and the Ashoka Chakra.

episodes.notes: Venkayya, a farmer, geologist and nationalist from Andhra, presented Gandhi a flag design at Vijayawada in 1921; Gandhi suggested a white stripe and spinning wheel, and Congress used variants before the 1931 flag decision. On 22 July 1947 the Constituent Assembly adopted the tricolour with the Ashoka Chakra replacing the charkha. RECENT Telugu and vexillological scholarship stresses that the final flag was collaborative, while Venkayya supplied a foundational design tradition and died with little recognition in 1963. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT call the pre-1947 Congress flag the legal national flag. Do not say Venkayya personally designed the Ashoka Chakra version; the 1947 committee made that substitution. His birth year is reported as 1876 or 1878.

episodes.title: The Red Fort Trials
episodes.era: INA trials and naval unrest, 1945-1946
episodes.region: Red Fort, Delhi; Bombay, Karachi and Calcutta naval establishments
episodes.logline: The INA trials and the Royal Indian Navy uprising revealed that the empire's own armed forces no longer obeyed unquestioningly.
episodes.moral: An empire weakens when its soldiers doubt its justice.

sources.citation: Two Historic Trials in Red Fort, Publications Division, Government of India
sources.note: Published account of INA court-martial proceedings and defence arguments.

sources.citation: National Archives of India, INA Trial Records, Home/Political Department, 1945-1946
sources.note: Primary files on charges, evidence and commutation.

sources.citation: Mithi Mukherjee, India in the Shadows of Empire (OUP, 2010)
sources.note: Recent interpretation of the trials as anti-colonial legal argument.

episodes.notes: From November 1945 the British tried Shah Nawaz Khan, Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon and Prem Sahgal at the Red Fort. Bhulabhai Desai, with Nehru and others on the defence team, argued that Azad Hind created a sovereign allegiance question; the men were convicted but sentences were commuted after huge public pressure. On 18-23 February 1946, Royal Indian Navy ratings struck across 78 ships and 20 shore establishments, raising nationalist slogans before surrender after political appeals. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP treats these events as part of the final crisis of colonial legitimacy, though not the single cause of independence. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim Desai won an acquittal; the legal result and political result differed. Do not say the RIN uprising was universally endorsed; Gandhi opposed it and Patel helped negotiate surrender.

episodes.title: The Seven Conditions Recited at Rajgir
episodes.figure: Vassakara, Ananda and the Vajji Confederation
episodes.era: Vajji-Magadha rivalry, c. 5th century BCE; text fixed by c. 350-320 BCE
episodes.region: Rajagriha and Vaishali, Bihar
episodes.logline: A Magadhan minister asks how to defeat Vajji, and a Buddhist sermon preserves seven practices that kept a republic from decline.
episodes.moral: Institutions endure when their habits endure.

sources.citation: Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta, section on Vassakara's visit
sources.note: Primary Pali account of the seven conditions for Vajji welfare.

sources.citation: Anguttara Nikaya 7.21-22, Vajji Sutta; Chinese Dirghagama parallel
sources.note: Independent textual parallels for the same political teaching.

sources.citation: Oskar von Hinuber, A Handbook of Pali Literature (1996); Romila Thapar, Early India (2002); J.P. Sharma, Republics in Ancient India (1968)
sources.note: Modern dating and interpretation of republican institutions.

episodes.notes: The Mahaparinibbana Sutta frames the scene at Rajagriha: Ajatashatru's minister Vassakara asks whether Magadha can attack Vajji, and the Buddha tells Ananda seven conditions that keep the Vajjis from decline, including frequent assemblies, concord, respect for elders, protection of women, and care for shrines and ascetics. The text is religious hagiography with political memory, not a stenographic court record. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT call Vajji the world's first democracy; the polity was an aristocratic gana-sangha with restricted membership. Do NOT call the seven conditions a written constitution. The later claim of a 16-year war belongs to much later tradition and should be marked as such.
episodes.chapter: The Ancient Republics and the Mahajanapadas
episodes.chapter_part: I. The Republic and Its Hall

episodes.title: The Assembly Hall at Vaishali
episodes.era: Licchavi and Vajji republican institutions, c. 6th-5th centuries BCE
episodes.region: Vaishali, Bihar
episodes.logline: In Vaishali, chiefs gather in a hall where seats, quorums and wooden ballots reveal an ancient experiment in collective rule.
episodes.moral: Procedure can be as powerful as a throne.

sources.citation: Pali Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga, translated by I.B. Horner
sources.note: Monastic rules preserving salaka voting, quorum and seat procedures modelled on wider assembly practice.

sources.citation: Mahavastu and Jataka traditions on the Licchavi assembly and 7,707 rajas
sources.note: Later Buddhist evidence for the scale and memory of Licchavi institutions.

sources.citation: A.S. Altekar and V.K. Thakur, Report on Vaishali Excavations (1958); Dilip K. Chakrabarti, India: An Archaeological History (1999)
sources.note: Archaeological context for Vaishali, the Abhiseka-Pushkarini tank and major earthworks.

episodes.notes: The Licchavi santhagara is reconstructed from Pali and Sanskrit Buddhist texts, the Vinaya's formal procedures, and Vaishali's archaeology. The story should show the offices named in scholarship: seat-regulator, quorum officer and ballot-collector, with salaka wooden tallies and votes that could be secret, whispered or open. The Abhiseka-Pushkarini tank is archaeologically visible, while the assembly hall itself has not been conclusively identified; Raja Vishal ka Garh is associated with the tradition but debated. ACCURACY FLAGS: the 7,707 rajas number is later textual tradition, not a census. Do NOT compare the santhagara casually to a modern parliament; it was an oligarchic warrior assembly, not universal franchise.
episodes.chapter: The Ancient Republics and the Mahajanapadas
episodes.chapter_part: I. The Republic and Its Hall

episodes.title: Mahavira in the House of the Naya Chiefs
episodes.era: Early Jainism in republican north Bihar, traditional c. 6th century BCE; modern shorter chronologies debated
episodes.region: Kundagrama and Vaishali, Bihar
episodes.logline: Jain memory places Mahavira among Naya chiefs tied to the Licchavi world, where clan politics helped teachings travel between courts.
episodes.moral: Ideas often move along kinship, roads and argument.

sources.citation: Kalpa Sutra, translated by Hermann Jacobi, Sacred Books of the East vol. 22 (1884)
sources.note: Jain biographical tradition for Mahavira's birth and clan setting.

sources.citation: Acaranga Sutra and Bhagavati Sutra
sources.note: Early Jain canonical material on Mahavira and the Licchavi-Naya political world.

sources.citation: Paul Dundas, The Jains, 2nd ed. (2002); Padmanabh S. Jaini, The Jaina Path of Purification (1979); J.P. Sharma (1968)
sources.note: Source-critical studies of Jain tradition and republican clans.

episodes.notes: Mahavira's life is preserved through layered Jain traditions. The Kalpa Sutra places him in a kshatriya Naya or Jnatrika setting near Vaishali, with mother Trisala tied to the Licchavi chief Chetaka; Jain accounts describe Chetaka's marriage alliances across Vatsa, Anga, Avanti and other states as channels for Jain influence. This story is about republican clan networks, not a full retelling of Jain doctrine. ACCURACY FLAGS: Mahavira's dates are debated between Jain long chronology and shorter modern chronologies; Kundagrama's exact location is uncertain. The embryo-transfer story is Svetambara hagiography and not accepted by all Jain traditions. Do NOT present later sacred biography as contemporary political record.
episodes.chapter: The Ancient Republics and the Mahajanapadas
episodes.chapter_part: I. The Republic and Its Hall

episodes.title: The River the Two Republics Shared
episodes.era: Small gana-sanghas of the Nepal Terai, c. 5th century BCE
episodes.region: Rohini River, Kapilavastu and Ramagama
episodes.logline: Two neighboring republics quarrel over the Rohini's water, leaving behind a rare memory of irrigation, kinship and fragile diplomacy.
episodes.moral: Shared resources test the strength of shared rules.

sources.citation: Pali Vinaya Pitaka, Cullavagga; Buddhaghosa, Dhammapadatthakatha, translated by E.W. Burlingame (1921)
sources.note: Early reference and later fuller tradition for the Shakya-Koliya water dispute.

sources.citation: UNESCO and Nepal Department of Archaeology, Ramgram Conservation and Excavation Report (2014)
sources.note: Recent non-invasive survey of the Koliya-associated Ramgram stupa.

sources.citation: J.P. Sharma, Republics in Ancient India (1968); Romila Thapar, Early India (2002)
sources.note: Modern reconstructions of Shakya and Koliya political scale.

episodes.notes: The Shakya and Koliya polities were small gana-sanghas, linked by marriage and divided by water needs on the Rohini River. Early canonical material preserves hostility, while Buddhaghosa's fifth-century commentary gives the vivid mediation story; present the later dialogue as tradition. Ramgram surveys from 2011-2014 support an important Koliya Buddhist site, and Tilaurakot and Piprahwa remain part of the contested Kapilavastu archaeology. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT call Suddhodana a monarch in the later royal sense; do NOT assert a certain Kapilavastu identification; do NOT turn the Rohini story into a proven transcript of a negotiation.
episodes.chapter: The Ancient Republics and the Mahajanapadas
episodes.chapter_part: II. The Cluster of Small Republics

episodes.title: The Blacksmith's Offering at Pava
episodes.figure: Cunda and the Malla Republic of Pava
episodes.era: Malla republican institutions, c. 5th century BCE
episodes.region: Pava, modern Fazilnagar region, Uttar Pradesh
episodes.logline: A metalworker's meal and a new Malla assembly hall preserve the texture of a small republic at the edge of a great religious memory.
episodes.moral: Ordinary hands can stand at historic crossroads.

sources.citation: Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta, chapters 4-5
sources.note: Primary Pali account of Cunda, Pava and the Ubbhataka assembly hall.

sources.citation: Oskar von Hinuber, A Handbook of Pali Literature (1996); Johannes Bronkhorst, Buddhism in the Shadow of Brahmanism (2011)
sources.note: Textual and cultural context for the Malla setting.

sources.citation: J.P. Sharma, Republics in Ancient India (1968); B.C. Law, Some Kshatriya Tribes of Ancient India (1923)
sources.note: Institutional history of the Malla branches at Pava and Kusinara.

episodes.notes: The Mahaparinibbana Sutta says the Buddha stayed in Cunda the kammara's mango grove at Pava, where the Mallas had recently completed the Ubbhataka santhagara. The named assembly hall is a small but valuable institutional detail: a republic appears in the background of a religious death narrative. The difficult term sukaramaddava has been read as pork, mushrooms, truffles, bamboo shoots or a medicinal plant. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT assert what sukaramaddava was; do NOT say Cunda caused the Buddha's death, because the text explicitly protects him from blame. Pava's identification with Fazilnagar is accepted but not deeply excavated for the period.
episodes.chapter: The Ancient Republics and the Mahajanapadas
episodes.chapter_part: II. The Cluster of Small Republics

episodes.title: Dona Divides the Relics
episodes.figure: Dona and the Eight Claimant States
episodes.era: Inter-state diplomacy after the parinibbana, c. 5th century BCE tradition
episodes.region: Kusinara, Vaishali, Ramagama and the middle Ganga plain
episodes.logline: After the Teacher's death, envoys from republics and monarchies demand a share, and Dona turns rivalry into a negotiated relic settlement.
episodes.moral: Even sacred memory can become diplomacy.

sources.citation: Digha Nikaya 16, final relic-division coda
sources.note: Primary Pali list of the eight claimants and Dona's mediation.

sources.citation: UNESCO / Nepal Department of Archaeology, Ramgram survey report (2014); Vaishali relic stupa excavations, 1950s
sources.note: Material evidence tied to two claimant traditions.

sources.citation: Gregory Schopen, Bones, Stones, and Buddhist Monks (1997); J.P. Sharma (1968)
sources.note: Modern analysis of relic communities and republican sovereignty claims.

episodes.notes: The relic-division coda lists Mallas of Kusinara, Mallas of Pava, Licchavis of Vesali, Shakyas of Kapilavastu, Koliyas of Ramagama, the Brahmin of Vethadipa, Moriyas of Pipphalivana and Ajatashatru of Magadha. Dona divides the relics, while the urn and embers receive their own commemorations. This is useful as a political map: republics and monarchies stand side by side and make claims through representatives. ACCURACY FLAGS: the coda may be a later layer of the Mahaparinibbana Sutta; do NOT assert all original stupas survive or have been identified. The Moriya-Pipphalivana link to the later Mauryas is tradition, not secure fact.
episodes.chapter: The Ancient Republics and the Mahajanapadas
episodes.chapter_part: II. The Cluster of Small Republics

episodes.title: The Silver Piece with Five Punches
episodes.era: Monetization in the Mahajanapada age, c. 6th-4th centuries BCE
episodes.region: Vaishali, Rajgir, Kausambi, Ujjain and north Indian hoards
episodes.logline: Small silver pieces stamped with symbols turn markets, taxes and wages into a new language of value across early cities.
episodes.moral: A coin is a promise many strangers agree to trust.

sources.citation: Panini, Ashtadhyayi 5.1.34 and 5.2.120; Pali Canon references to kahapana
sources.note: Early textual attestations of karshapana and marked money.

sources.citation: P.L. Gupta and T.R. Hardaker, Punchmarked Coins of the Indian Subcontinent (1985); Osmund Bopearachchi, Coin Production and Monetary Circulation in Northwestern India (2007)
sources.note: Standard typology and circulation studies.

sources.citation: K.K. Maheshwari and B.R. Mani, Vaishali Coin Hoards (2012); A.K. Singh, The Numismatics of the Magadha Punch-Marked Coins (2019)
sources.note: Recent Indian numismatic work on hoards and regional series.

episodes.notes: Punch-marked karshapanas were cut silver pieces bearing multiple symbols such as sun wheels, hills, animals and geometric marks. Pali texts call them kahapanas and place them in wages, fines, gifts and trade; Panini's grammatical references are valuable but incidental, not a Panini story. Hoards and regional types suggest expanding monetized exchange across many mahajanapadas, with Avanti fish-types and Magadhan series among the examples. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim India invented coinage before all other regions; the chronology is roughly sixth century BCE and part of a wider Eurasian monetization age. Individual symbols are not securely decoded, so avoid confident dynastic meanings.
episodes.chapter: The Ancient Republics and the Mahajanapadas

episodes.title: The Shining Black Bowl
episodes.era: Second urbanization craft culture, c. 700-200 BCE, peak c. 500-300 BCE
episodes.region: Gangetic plain, Malwa and north Indian city sites
episodes.logline: A mirror-dark bowl becomes the archaeological signature of new cities, specialized kilns and elite trade in the mahajanapada world.
episodes.moral: Sometimes a civilization's change survives as a surface sheen.

sources.citation: B.B. Lal, Excavations at Hastinapur, Ancient India 10-11 (1954-55)
sources.note: Foundational definition of Northern Black Polished Ware.

sources.citation: Paul Erdosy, Urbanisation in Early Historic India (1988); Dilip K. Chakrabarti, The Archaeology of Ancient Indian Cities (1995)
sources.note: Second-urbanization framework and city-by-city material context.

sources.citation: Johannes Krabbenhoft, NBPW and the Second Urbanization in North India (2019)
sources.note: Recent social-stratification analysis of the ware.

episodes.notes: Northern Black Polished Ware is a modern archaeological label for thin, high-fired, lustrous ceramics found at sites including Rajgir, Vaishali, Kausambi, Ujjain, Ahichhatra, Hastinapur and Mathura. It marks specialized craft production and elite consumption during the second urbanization after the long post-Harappan urban gap. Recent work has refined its chronology and social meaning, while some proto-NBPW finds suggest earlier experimentation. ACCURACY FLAGS: no ancient text names NBPW; do NOT attribute it to a single ruler or state. The precise firing technique remains debated, so describe the finish as a craft achievement without claiming a solved recipe. NBPW distribution does not map perfectly onto the sixteen mahajanapadas.
episodes.chapter: The Ancient Republics and the Mahajanapadas

episodes.title: The Forty Kilometre Wall Without Mortar
episodes.era: Pre-Mauryan fortification and city defense, c. 6th century BCE with later phases
episodes.region: Rajgir, Nalanda district, Bihar
episodes.logline: Around the hills of Rajgir, builders stack huge stones without mortar, turning a mountain basin into an early fortified capital.
episodes.moral: A wall records both fear and organization.

sources.citation: Dilip K. Chakrabarti, India: An Archaeological History (1999); Bihar State Archaeology documents on the Cyclopean Wall
sources.note: Archaeological basis for the wall as a pre-Mauryan fortification.

sources.citation: Digha Nikaya 16 and Vinaya references to Rajagriha as a guarded hill city
sources.note: Textual context for Rajagriha/Girivraja as a mountain enclosure.

sources.citation: Paul Erdosy, Urbanisation in Early Historic India (1988); ASI/National Monument records
sources.note: Fortification in the second-urbanization framework.

episodes.notes: Rajgir's Cyclopean Wall runs in surviving stretches around the hills of ancient Rajagriha and is often estimated at about 40 km in circuit, built from large undressed stones without mortar. NBPW associations make its early phase pre-Mauryan, though later repairs or phases exist. Buddhist texts call the city Giribbaja or hill-enclosure and remember Magadhan fortification in the Vajji conflict context. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT assign the wall confidently to Bimbisara or Ajatashatru; early Haryanka Magadha is safer. The 40 km figure is approximate and portions are damaged. Cyclopean is a modern comparative term and does not imply Greek influence.
episodes.chapter: The Ancient Republics and the Mahajanapadas

episodes.title: Kausambi on the Yamuna Road
episodes.era: Vatsa capital and early historic city, c. 7th century BCE-4th century CE
episodes.region: Kosam, Kaushambi district, Uttar Pradesh
episodes.logline: At Kausambi, ramparts, merchant parks and an Ashokan edict show how a mahajanapada capital became a lasting urban node.
episodes.moral: A city survives by tying roads, rulers and communities together.

sources.citation: G.R. Sharma, The Excavations at Kausambi, 1957-59 (1960) and Kausambi Excavations 1949-50 (1969)
sources.note: Foundational excavation reports for ramparts and stratigraphy.

sources.citation: Ashokan Minor Pillar Edict 2, Kausambi Schism Edict, in D.C. Sircar, Inscriptions of Asoka (1967)
sources.note: Primary inscription proving Mauryan official use of the city.

sources.citation: Pali suttas set at Kosambi; Jain texts on Udayana of Vatsa
sources.note: Literary evidence for parks, merchants and the Vatsa court.

episodes.notes: Kausambi, capital of Vatsa, stood on the Yamuna and major trade routes. Excavations by G.R. Sharma revealed massive fortifications, NBPW levels and long urban occupation; Pali texts remember Ghosita's park and other merchant-supported sites, while Jain texts associate King Udayana with Vatsa. The in situ Ashokan Schism Edict addressed to Kausambi officials proves later imperial importance. ACCURACY FLAGS: no Vatsa royal inscription has been found naming the early capital; some palace attributions are stratigraphic inference. Do NOT claim the Buddhist parks have been archaeologically identified with certainty. Sharma's reports remain fundamental but predate modern AMS and digital methods.
episodes.chapter: The Ancient Republics and the Mahajanapadas

episodes.title: The Crossroads City of Avanti
episodes.era: Avanti Mahajanapada and Malwa trade, c. 6th-4th centuries BCE
episodes.region: Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh
episodes.logline: At Ujjain, Avanti sits where north and south roads meet, remembered in texts, coins and buried black-polished layers.
episodes.moral: A crossroads can make a kingdom before it makes a legend.

sources.citation: Pali Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga, Cammakkhandhaka; Digha Nikaya 19; Jain Bhagavati Sutra
sources.note: Primary references to Avanti, Pradyota, Sona Kutikanna and Jain memories.

sources.citation: P.L. Gupta and T.R. Hardaker, Punchmarked Coins of the Indian Subcontinent (1985)
sources.note: Catalogues Avanti fish-type karshapanas.

sources.citation: K.C. Jain, Malwa Through the Ages (1972); ASI reports on Ujjain excavations, 1970s; Puratattva studies (1998)
sources.note: Historical and archaeological treatment of Ujjain and Malwa.

episodes.notes: Avanti was one of the major mahajanapadas, with Ujjain at a junction of the Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha networks. Pali Vinaya material remembers Sona Kutikanna's journey from Avanti and rule adaptations for rough Avanti conditions; Jain texts place Mahavira's wanderings and Palaka traditions in the region. Distinctive fish-type punch-marked coins and NBPW layers support early urban and commercial importance. ACCURACY FLAGS: Pradyota's exact dates are uncertain and king lists conflict. Do NOT claim Ujjain's later astronomical meridian role for this period. Much early Ujjain archaeology is obscured by continuous occupation under the modern city.
episodes.chapter: The Ancient Republics and the Mahajanapadas

episodes.title: Nine Layers Deep at Ahichhatra
episodes.era: Northern Panchala capital and later sacred site, c. 6th century BCE onward
episodes.region: Ramnagar near Bareilly, Uttar Pradesh
episodes.logline: Nine layers under Ahichhatra reveal a Panchala capital whose epic fame, Jain memory and archaeology do not always say the same thing.
episodes.moral: A site is clearest when every layer keeps its date.

sources.citation: K.K. Sinha, Excavations at Ahichchhatra (U.P.), 1940-44, Ancient India 1 (1946)
sources.note: Main excavation report documenting nine occupation strata.

sources.citation: Alexander Cunningham, ASI Reports vol. 11 (1880); Luders List of Brahmi inscriptions (1912)
sources.note: Foundational identification and inscription catalogue.

sources.citation: Srinivasan Quintanilla, History of Early Stone Sculpture at Mathura (2007); Dilip K. Chakrabarti, The Archaeology of Ancient Indian Cities (1995)
sources.note: Modern analysis of Ahichhatra's sculpture and archaeological setting.

episodes.notes: Ahichhatra is identified with the Northern Panchala capital through textual geography and the scale of remains. K.K. Sinha's 1940-44 excavations revealed nine strata from pre-Mauryan levels into the medieval period, while later Jain ayagapatas and inscriptions prove the site's continued religious importance. The Mahabharata's Drona-Drupada story gives Ahichhatra epic fame, but that is not direct evidence for sixth-century BCE political history. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT treat the Nandighosha ayagapata, from the early centuries CE, as mahajanapada evidence. The lowest layers are less well published than later sculpture levels, and no early inscription securely names the Panchala capital.
episodes.chapter: The Ancient Republics and the Mahajanapadas

episodes.title: How the Monarchies Swallowed the Republics
episodes.era: End of many republics, c. 5th-4th centuries BCE; modern historiography 1903-2011 CE
episodes.region: Vajji, Shakya-Koliya territories, Magadha and Kosala
episodes.logline: Buddhist, Jain and political texts show monarchies pressing on the republics, while modern historians debate what kind of freedom those republics had.
episodes.moral: History is strongest when it admits what its sources can and cannot prove.

sources.citation: Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book 11, translated by R.P. Kangle (1960-65)
sources.note: Ancient political analysis of how monarchs could subvert sanghas and ganas.

sources.citation: Digha Nikaya 16; Mahavamsa; Pali traditions on Vidudabha and the Shakyas
sources.note: Layered sources for Vajji and small-republic absorption traditions.

sources.citation: T.W. Rhys Davids, Buddhist India (1903); Romila Thapar, Early India (2002); Johannes Bronkhorst, Buddhism in the Shadow of Brahmanism (2011)
sources.note: Historiographical debate from early republican enthusiasm to oligarchy and Greater Magadha models.

episodes.notes: The capstone should compare the sources instead of pretending certainty. The Mahaparinibbana Sutta gives the political warning about Vajji; later traditions elaborate Vassakara's infiltration and a long Magadha-Vajji war. The Arthashastra's Book 11, though composition and layers are debated, explicitly discusses winning over oligarchic sangha leaders, sowing discord and using spies. Pali traditions also remember Kosala's pressure on the Shakyas and Koliyas. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT call these modern democracies; Thapar's corrective is that they were oligarchic kshatriya assemblies. Do NOT claim to know the exact fall of Vajji. Read Rhys Davids as foundational but shaped by early twentieth-century democratic idealism; read religious texts as preserving political memory through sectarian purposes.
episodes.chapter: The Ancient Republics and the Mahajanapadas
episodes.chapter_part: V. The Sources and the Great Absorption

episodes.title: From Venad to a Kingdom Waiting to Be Built
episodes.era: Venad before Marthanda Varma, before 1729 CE
episodes.region: Southern Kerala, Thiruvananthapuram, Kanyakumari and the Malabar pepper coast
episodes.logline: Before Travancore rose, Venad was a fragile coastal chiefdom squeezed by noble houses, temple councils, pepper traders and European companies.
episodes.moral: A strong state is built by solving a real crisis.

sources.citation: V. Nagam Aiya, Travancore State Manual, 1906
sources.note: Official compilation on Venad, the Ettara Yogam, temple administration and political structure.

sources.citation: P. Shungoonny Menon, A History of Travancore from the Earliest Times, 1878
sources.note: Early Travancore history drawn from court records and palm-leaf traditions, with royalist bias.

sources.citation: K.N. Ganesh, The Process of State Formation in Travancore, Studies in History 6(2), 1990
sources.note: Modern reinterpretation of Travancore as agrarian-commercial state formation, not only heroic biography.

episodes.notes: Set the scene before 1729: Venad was ruled in name by a matrilineal royal house but constrained by Nair aristocratic houses, madampimar, and the Ettara Yogam linked to Padmanabhaswamy Temple. Pepper wealth moved through old merchant networks and European companies, especially the Dutch VOC from Kochi and the English at Anchuthengu. KEY ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT portray early Venad as a unified modern state; it was a fragmented polity with weak revenue control. The Ettuveetil Pillamar story is real as a political memory, but modern scholarship warns that exact lists, motives and dramatic incidents are partly shaped by later court narration.
episodes.chapter: The Travancore Kingdom and Marthanda Varma
episodes.chapter_part: I. A Small Coast Becomes a State

episodes.title: The Prince Who Would Not Die
episodes.era: Succession crisis and early survival, c. 1706-1729 CE
episodes.region: Attingal, Budhanoor, Nagercoil, Kalkulam and Venad
episodes.logline: A hunted heir survives cousins, nobles and assassins before using Venad's matrilineal law to claim a dangerous throne.
episodes.moral: Survival becomes strength only when it finds purpose.

sources.citation: P. Shungoonny Menon, A History of Travancore, 1878
sources.note: Main narrative for the Thampi challenge, hiding episodes and early coup.

sources.citation: V. Nagam Aiya, Travancore State Manual, 1906
sources.note: Administrative and genealogical account of the succession crisis.

sources.citation: Supreme Court of India, Civil Appeal No. 2732 of 2014, Padmanabhaswamy Temple judgment, 2020
sources.note: Modern legal judgment summarising early 18th-century temple and royal disputes from records.

episodes.notes: Marthanda Varma was born in 1706 to Queen Karthika Thirunal Umadevi of Attingal and Raghava Varma of Kilimanoor, and inherited through marumakkathayam, the matrilineal succession system. His cousins Valiya Thampi and Kunju Thampi claimed through patrilineal descent and allied with anti-royal nobles. Tell the Budhanoor survival stories as remembered court tradition, not proven eyewitness fact. KEY FLAGS: assassination attempts and the succession dispute are historically grounded, but many dramatic escapes come from Shungoonny Menon's 1878 retelling, more than a century later. Mention the Hiranyagarbha-style legitimation rituals only as attested royal-sacral politics, not as proof of ancient lineage claims.
episodes.chapter: The Travancore Kingdom and Marthanda Varma
episodes.chapter_part: I. A Small Coast Becomes a State

episodes.title: Breaking the Eight Houses
episodes.figure: Marthanda Varma and the Ettuveetil Pillamar
episodes.era: Internal consolidation of Venad, c. 1729-1733 CE
episodes.region: Thiruvananthapuram, Nagercoil and the southern Travancore heartland
episodes.logline: Marthanda Varma crushes the noble houses that had strangled royal power and replaces feudal authority with a harsher centralized state.
episodes.moral: Order won by force still carries the weight of suffering.

sources.citation: V. Nagam Aiya, Travancore State Manual, 1906
sources.note: Records executions, exiles, confiscations and the destruction of noble power.

sources.citation: P. Shungoonny Menon, A History of Travancore, 1878
sources.note: Narrates the overthrow of the Thampis, Yogakkar and Pillamar.

sources.citation: Robin Jeffrey, The Decline of Nair Dominance, 1976; K.N. Ganesh, 1990
sources.note: Modern social and agrarian readings of the fall of Nair aristocratic power.

episodes.notes: Between 1729 and 1733 the king dismantled the power of the Ettuveetil Pillamar, Yogakkar and allied madampimar. Nagam Aiya records executions, exiles, demolition of houses, seizure of lands and armies, and the sale of some women and children of defeated families to Mukkuvar fishermen; state this plainly and soberly because the record is not bloodless. The new hierarchy of Dalava, Valia Sarvadhi Kariakkars, Kariakkars, Manikars and Adhikaris reduced old Nair aristocratic control and made revenue and military command answer to the crown. ACCURACY FLAG: do NOT repeat every popular betrayal legend as fact; temple documents complicate the exact eight-house list and the identities in the 1730 execution records.
episodes.chapter: The Travancore Kingdom and Marthanda Varma
episodes.chapter_part: I. A Small Coast Becomes a State

episodes.title: Colachel 1741 India Defeats the VOC
episodes.figure: Marthanda Varma and Eustachius De Lannoy
episodes.era: Dutch-Travancore War and Battle of Colachel, 1739-1741 CE
episodes.region: Colachel, Kalkulam, Kottar and the southern Malabar coast
episodes.logline: On the monsoon coast at Colachel, Travancore breaks a Dutch expedition and captures the officer who will rebuild its army.
episodes.moral: A battlefield can turn an enemy into a teacher.

sources.citation: VOC Records, Nationaal Archief, The Hague, Malabar and Ceylon correspondence, 1739-1753
sources.note: Independent Dutch records for the war, van Imhoff's ultimatum and the later treaty.

sources.citation: M.O. Koshy, The Dutch Power in Kerala 1729-1758, 1989
sources.note: Detailed reconstruction from Dutch archival material.

sources.citation: P. Shungoonny Menon, A History of Travancore, 1878
sources.note: Travancore-side narrative of the battle and De Lannoy's capture.

episodes.notes: The Battle of Colachel on 10 August 1741 followed Dutch attempts to protect pepper contracts and allied chiefdoms against Travancore expansion. The VOC had early successes, but reinforcements were hampered by wider Batavia troubles; Travancore mobilised rapidly, and local coastal communities, including Mukkuvar fishermen and Marakkar sea merchants, appear in the record and tradition. Twenty-four Dutch officers were captured, including Eustachius De Lannoy, later Valiya Kappittan of Travancore. KEY FLAGS: Colachel was a commercial-military struggle, not a religious war. Local tales of fake cannon and night attacks should be labelled tradition unless tied to De Lannoy or VOC evidence.
episodes.chapter: The Travancore Kingdom and Marthanda Varma
episodes.chapter_part: II. Pepper, Guns and the Dutch War

episodes.title: The Treaty of Mavelikkara Ends Dutch Power
episodes.era: Treaty of Mavelikkara, 15 August 1753 CE
episodes.region: Mavelikkara, Kochi, Anjengo and the Malabar trade coast
episodes.logline: After years of war and bargaining, a treaty makes the VOC supply guns to the very kingdom it failed to subdue.
episodes.moral: Diplomacy can make victory last longer than battle.

sources.citation: Treaty of Mavelikkara, 15 August 1753, preserved in VOC and Travancore records
sources.note: Primary diplomatic text ending Dutch political intervention and regulating pepper supply.

sources.citation: M.O. Koshy, The Dutch Power in Kerala 1729-1758, 1989
sources.note: Gives treaty clauses and VOC context.

sources.citation: Susan Bayly, Saints, Goddesses and Kings, 1989
sources.note: Context on Syrian Christian merchant networks in Travancore's political economy.

episodes.notes: The 1753 treaty required Dutch non-interference, forbade support to Travancore's enemies, fixed pepper supply obligations, protected existing English factories at Anjengo, Edava and Vizhinjam, and required the Dutch to supply war material. It marked the formal collapse of Dutch political leverage in south Kerala while preserving trade on Travancore's terms. Include the state use of Syrian Christian merchants as licensed intermediaries; this was pragmatic commercial policy, not communal favoritism. KEY FLAGS: do NOT claim the Dutch vanished from trade overnight, and do NOT romanticize Marthanda Varma's famous reply about invading Europe as verbatim certainty; Koshy reports it through VOC material but exact phrasing may be paraphrase.
episodes.chapter: The Travancore Kingdom and Marthanda Varma
episodes.chapter_part: II. Pepper, Guns and the Dutch War

episodes.title: The Pepper Monopoly Controls the Coast
episodes.era: Kuttakam pepper monopoly, from 1743 CE
episodes.region: Travancore pepper lands from Quilon to Kayamkulam and the backwaters
episodes.logline: Travancore turns black pepper from a merchant prize into a royal monopoly that funds conquest, roads, soldiers and diplomacy.
episodes.moral: Control of resources can decide the fate of kingdoms.

sources.citation: VOC records cited in K.N. Ganesh, 1990
sources.note: Dutch evidence for the 1743 monopoly and punishment of illegal spice trade.

sources.citation: Treaty of Mavelikkara, 1753
sources.note: Records the 3,000-candi pepper quota and regulated commerce after war.

sources.citation: K.N. Ganesh, The Process of State Formation in Travancore, 1990
sources.note: Core analysis of pepper, agrarian control and state formation.

episodes.notes: In 1743 the crown declared pepper a Kuttakam, or royal monopoly good. European companies could no longer bypass the state and buy freely from local suppliers; licensed merchants, including Syrian Christian traders, became key intermediaries. VOC records cited by Ganesh warn that illegal spice traders could face execution, so the economic reform had coercive edges. The monopoly explains why annexations of Kayamkulam, Thekkumkur, Vadakkumkur and other pepper areas mattered. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT present this as free-market modernization; it was a revenue-maximizing state monopoly. Quantities and income figures vary across later sources, so use treaty quotas cautiously.
episodes.chapter: The Travancore Kingdom and Marthanda Varma
episodes.chapter_part: II. Pepper, Guns and the Dutch War

episodes.title: Ramayyan Dalawa Builds the King's Machine
episodes.era: Ramayyan Dalawa's ministry, c. 1737-1756 CE
episodes.region: Padmanabhapuram, Travancore's annexed territories and the backwater routes
episodes.logline: A brilliant minister turns royal ambition into campaigns, surveys, offices, roads, revenue and a working centralized administration.
episodes.moral: Great rulers need builders who turn vision into systems.

sources.citation: P. Shungoonny Menon, A History of Travancore, 1878
sources.note: Detailed account of Ramayyan Dalawa's rise, campaigns and partnership with the king.

sources.citation: V. Nagam Aiya, Travancore State Manual, 1906
sources.note: Administrative lists and history of the Dalava office.

sources.citation: K.N. Ganesh, The Process of State Formation in Travancore, 1990
sources.note: Explains the Dalava-led machinery as the instrument of state formation.

episodes.notes: Ramayyan Dalawa, a Tamil Brahmin from Yerwadi tradition, became Dalava in 1737 and served until 1756. He helped direct campaigns, revenue reorganization, diplomacy and the replacement of dispersed noble power by a bureaucratic chain under the crown. The Dalava office combined military, fiscal and commercial functions and could exist only in the new centralized state. KEY FLAGS: the emotional stories comparing king and minister to Chandragupta and Chanakya come from later court memory; use them sparingly. Do not hide that administrative consolidation disrupted defeated elites and local society, including migrations recorded by early surveyors.
episodes.chapter: The Travancore Kingdom and Marthanda Varma

episodes.title: Sri Padmanabha Dasa and the Temple State
episodes.era: Thrippadidanam, c. 1749-1750 CE
episodes.region: Sri Padmanabhaswamy Temple, Thiruvananthapuram
episodes.logline: Marthanda Varma donates his kingdom to Padmanabha and recasts kingship as service to a deity who never dies.
episodes.moral: Symbols can stabilize power when institutions are fragile.

sources.citation: Padmanabhaswamy Temple records cited in royal histories and the 2020 Supreme Court judgment
sources.note: Primary institutional basis for Thrippadidanam and temple-state continuity.

sources.citation: K.N. Ganesh, The Process of State Formation in Travancore, 1990
sources.note: Political reading of the dedication as a state-building device.

sources.citation: Supreme Court of India, Civil Appeal No. 2732 of 2014, judgment 2020
sources.note: Modern legal summary of Padmanabhadasa history and temple management.

episodes.notes: Around January 1749-1750 Marthanda Varma performed Thrippadidanam, dedicating Travancore, himself and his treasury to Sri Padmanabhaswamy and ruling thereafter as Sri Padmanabha Dasa. This created a temple-state ideology: sovereignty rested in the deity, while the king served as vice-regent and administrator. It also helped legitimate the post-feudal order and the accumulation of sacred wealth. Mention temple rebuilding, Murajapam, Bhadra Deepam, the gopura works and the later 2011 vault inventory only with caution. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT reduce the act to simple piety or to cynical politics alone; scholarship treats religious devotion and institutional strategy as intertwined. The exact date and details remain debated in partly unpublished temple records.
episodes.chapter: The Travancore Kingdom and Marthanda Varma

episodes.title: Land Water and the Kulikkanam System
episodes.era: Land survey and agrarian reorganization, c. 1739-1750s CE
episodes.region: Travancore's paddy fields, pepper lands, canals and backwaters
episodes.logline: Surveyors, canals and tax concessions turn newly planted land into cash revenue for the expanding Travancore state.
episodes.moral: Quiet measurements can change history as much as battles.

sources.citation: V. Nagam Aiya, Travancore State Manual, 1906
sources.note: Detailed descriptions of Kulikkanam, land survey, irrigation and road works.

sources.citation: Travancore land survey and revenue records of 1739-1740, as synthesized by Nagam Aiya
sources.note: Primary administrative basis for the new tax settlement.

sources.citation: K.N. Ganesh, The Process of State Formation in Travancore, 1990
sources.note: Places agrarian reorganization at the center of state formation.

episodes.notes: The 1739-1740 survey registered land, fixed temple expenses and enabled new revenue categories. Kulikkanam encouraged newly sown lands and newly planted trees through tax reductions such as Naduvukkur and Vettalivu, while cash dues tied cultivators to a monetized economy. Roads, canals and backwater communications moved soldiers, pepper, rice and messages through a difficult landscape. KEY FLAGS: specific irrigation works are less archaeologically studied than the manuals suggest, so avoid over-precise engineering claims. This was an innovation in fiscal agriculture, but it was also a system of extraction that strengthened royal control over cultivators and former jenmi rights.
episodes.chapter: The Travancore Kingdom and Marthanda Varma

episodes.title: Fifty Thousand Soldiers and a Dutch General
episodes.era: Military modernization after Colachel, c. 1741-1777 CE
episodes.region: Udayagiri Fort, Padmanabhapuram, the coast and the Travancore Lines
episodes.logline: A captured VOC officer trains Travancore's standing army in guns, drill, forts and the engineering of survival.
episodes.moral: Wisdom learns even from defeat and captivity.

sources.citation: V. Nagam Aiya, Travancore State Manual, 1906
sources.note: Army organization, Irayili service, artillery and the Nedumkotta description.

sources.citation: P. Shungoonny Menon, A History of Travancore, 1878
sources.note: Narrative of De Lannoy's service and military reforms.

sources.citation: Philip MacDougall, Naval Resistance to Britain's Growing Power in India, 1660-1800, 2014
sources.note: Recent context for coastal and naval resistance in the Indian Ocean world.

episodes.notes: After Colachel, Eustachius De Lannoy entered Travancore service, rose as Valiya Kappittan, trained infantry, improved artillery and strengthened forts such as Udayagiri. The standing army, often estimated around 50,000, included Nair infantry, cavalry recruits and European-drilled artillery; exact numbers vary. Under Dharma Raja, De Lannoy supervised the Nedumkotta, a defensive line with ditch, rampart, bamboo hedge, bastions and gun positions that later mattered against Mysore. KEY FLAGS: do NOT make De Lannoy the sole creator of Travancore power; he worked inside Marthanda Varma's fiscal state. The Great Wall comparison is hyperbole; present Nedumkotta as a major regional engineering work.
episodes.chapter: The Travancore Kingdom and Marthanda Varma
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Forts, Wood and Living Arts

episodes.title: Padmanabhapuram Wood Murals and Monsoon Design
episodes.era: Palace and mural patronage, especially c. 1745-1750s CE
episodes.region: Padmanabhapuram Palace and Krishnapuram Palace
episodes.logline: Kerala carpenters, muralists and planners shape a wooden capital of sloped roofs, herbal ceilings, courtyards and glowing wall paintings.
episodes.moral: Art endures when craft understands climate and place.

sources.citation: Padmanabhapuram Palace and Krishnapuram Palace, protected monuments
sources.note: Physical evidence for Travancore wood architecture, murals and palace planning.

sources.citation: Silparatna, Kerala architectural and mural tradition
sources.note: Textual context for Kerala craft rules and panchavarnam mural practice.

sources.citation: Kerala State Archaeology Department conservation reports; S. Raja Raja Varma, Murals of Kerala
sources.note: Modern documentation and conservation of the palace and mural traditions.

episodes.notes: Padmanabhapuram Palace, especially the Uppirikka Malika built in 1745, shows Kerala timber architecture shaped for monsoon climate: deep verandas, sloping roofs, courtyards, ventilation and refined joinery. Krishnapuram Palace, built after the Kayamkulam conquest, preserves the large Gajendra Moksham mural in the panchavarnam color system. Include details such as the Mantrashala, medicinal-herb ceiling tradition, Padmanabha's room and the 64-wood royal bed as court tradition where appropriate. ACCURACY FLAGS: the claim that Padmanabhapuram is Asia's largest wooden palace is widely repeated but should be phrased carefully; the Dutch-gift bed story is court tradition, not independently documented diplomatic proof.
episodes.chapter: The Travancore Kingdom and Marthanda Varma
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Forts, Wood and Living Arts

episodes.title: Kunchan Nambiar Invents People's Theatre
episodes.era: Travancore court arts, c. 1748-1770 CE
episodes.region: Travancore court, Ambalapuzha and Malayalam-speaking Kerala
episodes.logline: A poet in courtly Kerala turns satire, dance and clear Malayalam into Thullal, a theatre ordinary people can understand.
episodes.moral: Art becomes powerful when everyone can hear it.

sources.citation: Kunchan Nambiar's Thullal compositions, Kerala Sahitya Akademi editions
sources.note: Primary literary corpus of more than sixty Thullal stories.

sources.citation: V. Nagam Aiya, Travancore State Manual, 1906
sources.note: Notes Nambiar and Ramapurathu Warrier among Travancore court poets.

sources.citation: Farley Richmond, Darius Swann and Phillip Zarrilli, Indian Theatre: Traditions of Performance, 1990
sources.note: Performance-studies context for Thullal and Kerala theatre.

episodes.notes: Kunchan Nambiar, traditionally born c. 1705 and active at the Travancore court from about 1748, created or popularized Ottan Thullal: solo performance, rhythmic movement, music and direct Malayalam verse. It opened a space beyond Sanskritized and temple-restricted performance and used Puranic stories to satirize greedy rulers, caste abuses, priests and social hypocrisy. KEY FLAGS: the famous story that he invented Thullal after being mocked for sleeping during Chakyar Koothu is a traditional origin tale, not securely attested. Do not call it anti-religious; it worked inside sacred story worlds while making social criticism intelligible to broader audiences.
episodes.chapter: The Travancore Kingdom and Marthanda Varma
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Forts, Wood and Living Arts

episodes.title: Dharma Raja and the Model State Inheritance
episodes.figure: Dharma Raja Karthika Thirunal Rama Varma
episodes.era: Travancore after Marthanda Varma, 1758-1798 CE and later legacy
episodes.region: Travancore, Cochin, the Nedumkotta and Thiruvananthapuram
episodes.logline: Marthanda Varma dies, but his nephew inherits institutions strong enough to face Mysore, build defenses and shape Travancore's long reforming afterlife.
episodes.moral: A ruler's deepest legacy is the institution that survives him.

sources.citation: P. Shungoonny Menon, A History of Travancore, 1878
sources.note: Main narrative for Dharma Raja's succession and later Travancore.

sources.citation: V. Nagam Aiya, Travancore State Manual, 1906
sources.note: Records later institutions, Nedumkotta, education, courts, observatory and public works.

sources.citation: Robin Jeffrey, The Decline of Nair Dominance, 1976; Dick Kooiman, Conversion and Social Equality in India, 1989
sources.note: Modern analysis of social consequences and later reform dynamics.

episodes.notes: Marthanda Varma died on 7 July 1758 and was succeeded by his nephew Dharma Raja, showing that the new state was not merely personal charisma. Dharma Raja continued the Padmanabha Dasa formula, preserved Kochi as a strategic buffer, completed the Nedumkotta with De Lannoy, and later resisted Mysore pressure. In the 19th century, Travancore developed schools, courts, medical and engineering institutions, a printing press, observatory and manuscript library, producing the colonial label 'Model Native State.' KEY FLAGS: do NOT claim a straight unbroken road from Marthanda Varma to the Kerala model; institutional continuity is debated. Also state plainly that Marthanda Varma did not abolish Kerala's severe caste hierarchy; later social reform, missions, Sree Narayana Guru's movement and the 1936 Temple Entry Proclamation addressed injustices his reign left intact.
episodes.chapter: The Travancore Kingdom and Marthanda Varma

episodes.title: Bappa Rawal and the Founder Nobody Can Name
episodes.era: Guhila origins, tradition c. 728 CE; inscriptions c. 6th-10th century CE
episodes.region: Chittor, Ahar and Medapata in Rajasthan
episodes.logline: Mewar remembers Bappa Rawal as its first hero, but the earliest inscriptions reveal a real Guhila dynasty whose famous founder remains hidden behind honorific, legend and court memory.
episodes.moral: Real glory does not need invented certainty.

sources.citation: Atpur inscription, 977 CE; Ekling and Udaipur prashasti inscriptions
sources.note: Earliest hard Guhila genealogies, with the key problem that Atpur does not name Bappa.

sources.citation: Kumbhalgarh Prashasti, 1460 CE, attributed to Atri and Mahesh
sources.note: Court genealogy compiled under Rana Kumbha, valuable but retrospective.

sources.citation: R.V. Somani, History of Mewar (1976); Cynthia Talbot, Rajput Identity and the Construction of the Past (2001)
sources.note: Modern critical handling of Guhila origins and dynastic self-fashioning.

episodes.notes: The Guhila dynasty is historically secure from early inscriptions around Ahar and Medapata, but Bappa Rawal is a sources problem, not a settled biography. The 977 Atpur inscription gives a Guhila genealogy yet does not name Bappa; later Ekling, Udaipur and Kumbhalgarh records preserve Bappa as a founding figure, while scholars have variously identified him with Kalabhoja, Shiladitya or Khumana. Tradition dates his seizure of Chittor to c. 728 or 734 CE, but firm Guhila control of Chittor is epigraphically clearer only later, around the mid-10th century. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim exact Bappa birth, death or regnal years; do NOT state that he repelled Arab invasions or received Chittor by divine gift as fact; present sage Harit Rashi and Eklingji blessing stories as later bardic tradition.

episodes.title: Hammir Singh Wins Back Chittor
episodes.era: Sisodia restoration, c. 1326-1337 CE; reign c. 1326-1364 CE
episodes.region: Chittor and the hill country of Mewar
episodes.logline: After Alauddin Khalji's conquest broke Chittor, Hammir Singh of the Sisodia line fought his way back and restored Mewar's mountain throne.
episodes.moral: Recovery is built by patience as much as bravery.

sources.citation: Nayachandra Suri, Hammir Mahakavya, c. 1400 CE
sources.note: Earliest extended literary account of Hammir; a Sanskrit kavya to read critically.

sources.citation: Kumbhalgarh Prashasti, 1460 CE; Jain temple inscription of 1438 CE
sources.note: Retrospective but important epigraphic evidence for Hammir and a victory over a Sultanate force.

sources.citation: Dasharatha Sharma, Rajasthan Through the Ages (1966); R.V. Somani, History of Mewar (1976)
sources.note: Standard reconstructions of Hammir's restoration and the Singoli tradition.

episodes.notes: Hammir Singh was the Sisodia ruler who restored Chittor after the 1303 Khalji conquest and made the Sisodia branch the continuing line of Mewar. The recapture is usually placed in a c. 1326-1337 range, with the Battle of Singoli connected to defeat of a Tughlaq force. Later Nainsi ri Khyat gives a dramatic story that Hammir captured Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq and released him for ransom, but this is not corroborated by Tughlaq-era Persian chronicles and must not be stated as fact. RECENT-SCHOLARSHIP FRAME: use Rajput identity-formation studies to show how Hammir became a restoration hero, while keeping the secure core: Hammir was real, Chittor was recovered, and the Sisodia line began its long Mewar role.

episodes.title: Kumbhalgarh and the Mountain Wall
episodes.era: Rana Kumbha's fortification program, c. 1443-1458 CE
episodes.region: Kumbhalgarh, Rajsamand district, Aravalli Range
episodes.logline: High in the Aravallis, Rana Kumbha raised Kumbhalgarh's long walls as a refuge-fort where Mewar could survive even when the plains burned.
episodes.moral: Wise rulers build shelter before disaster arrives.

sources.citation: Kumbhalgarh Prashasti, 1460 CE
sources.note: Primary court inscription crediting Kumbha's building and fortification achievements.

sources.citation: UNESCO/ICOMOS Hill Forts of Rajasthan nomination dossier, 2013
sources.note: Technical documentation of Kumbhalgarh as part of the World Heritage hill-fort series.

sources.citation: Dasharatha Sharma, Rajasthan Through the Ages (1966); INTACH conservation assessments
sources.note: Political and conservation context for Kumbha's fort policy.

episodes.notes: Kumbhalgarh, about 1,100 metres above sea level, is credited to Rana Kumbha and guarded by walls commonly measured at about 36-38 km with major gates, tanks and temples. This is an engineering and statecraft story: the fort worked as a fallback mountain capital, later sheltering the Sisodias and serving Maharana Pratap after Haldighati. UNESCO's 2013 Hill Forts of Rajasthan listing and recent conservation surveys emphasize layered construction and water systems. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT call it the 'Great Wall of India' as if that were a historical name; do NOT claim it is the world's longest wall; no named architect is preserved for Kumbhalgarh, unlike Vijay Stambha.

episodes.title: Vijay Stambha Names the Sculptors
episodes.era: Vijay Stambha, foundation c. 1448 CE; completion c. 1458-1468 CE
episodes.region: Chittor Fort, Chittorgarh
episodes.logline: Kumbha's nine-storey victory tower celebrates power in stone, but its rare gift is that it also remembers architect Jaita and his sons by name.
episodes.moral: A monument is nobler when it honors its makers.

sources.citation: Vijay Stambha inscriptions, Chittor Fort
sources.note: Primary evidence naming Sutradhar Jaita, his sons Napa, Puja and Poma, and the tower's sacred program.

sources.citation: Kumbhalgarh Prashasti, 1460 CE
sources.note: Corroborates Kumbha's victories and monument-building context.

sources.citation: UNESCO/ICOMOS Hill Forts of Rajasthan dossier (2013); G.H. Ojha's epigraphic studies
sources.note: Modern architectural and epigraphic cataloguing of Chittor's monuments.

episodes.notes: The Vijay Stambha is a 37-metre, nine-storey tower inside Chittor Fort, generally linked to Kumbha's victory over Malwa and Gujarat forces after Sarangpur. Its inscriptions and iconographic program make it an art-history innovation story: Vishnu dedication, sculptural encyclopaedia, Jain imagery and unusually explicit naming of architect Sutradhar Jaita and his sons. Some inscriptional verses use the polemical term 'Mleccha' and speak of cow-rescue and destruction of an enemy centre; carry this as the monument's own political-religious language, not as narrator endorsement. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT present 1448 as the exact completion date when foundation and completion are debated; avoid value-judgments like 'greater than Qutb Minar.'

episodes.title: Kumbha Sets the Notes in Sangitaraja
episodes.era: Kumbha's scholarly reign, 1433-1468 CE
episodes.region: Chittor, Kumbhalgarh and Sanskrit musicological circles
episodes.logline: The same ruler who built forts and fought sultans also compiled Sangitaraja, a courtly map of music, dance, instruments and rasa.
episodes.moral: A defended kingdom must also cultivate beauty.

sources.citation: Rana Kumbha, Sangitaraja, 15th century; ed. Prem Lata Sharma
sources.note: Primary musicological text in five sections, preserved through manuscripts.

sources.citation: Kumbhalgarh Prashasti, 1460 CE
sources.note: Calls Kumbha by literary epithets and supports his scholar-king reputation.

sources.citation: Emmie te Nijenhuis, Indian Music: History and Structure (1974); Kapila Vatsyayan's studies of Indian arts
sources.note: Modern context for medieval music and dance theory.

episodes.notes: Sangitaraja is attributed to Rana Kumbha and covers textual song, melody, instruments, dance and aesthetic rasa. This story should show a soldier-scholar without turning court authorship into a modern single-author claim: royal Sanskrit works were often produced with scholarly assistance under a patron-author's name. Kumbha is also associated with commentaries such as Gitagovinda-Sudha-Nidhi. RECENT FLAGS: manuscript study by Rajasthan Oriental Research Institute and music historians places the text in a regional medieval tradition whose raga and tala categories differ from later standardized systems. Do NOT claim Kumbha invented specific ragas unless sourced; balance scholarship with warfare and patronage.

episodes.title: Ranakpur's Thousand Pillars
episodes.era: Ranakpur Jain Temple, 1436-1458 CE with later additions
episodes.region: Ranakpur, Pali district, Aravalli foothills
episodes.logline: A Jain merchant, an architect and Rana Kumbha turned marble, credit and royal land-grant into Ranakpur's forest of carved pillars.
episodes.moral: Civilization rises when faith, craft and governance cooperate.

sources.citation: Ranakpur copper-plate record, 1436 CE; pillar inscription, 1439 CE
sources.note: Primary documents naming patron Dharna Shah, architect Deepaka or Dwepa, and Kumbha's patronage.

sources.citation: Soma-Saubhagya Kavya
sources.note: Jain Sanskrit account of consecration traditions under Acharya Somsundar Suri.

sources.citation: Julia A.B. Hegewald, Jain Temple Architecture in India (2000); Paul Dundas, The Jains (2002)
sources.note: Art-historical and religious context for the Shvetambara Jain shrine.

episodes.notes: Ranakpur's Adinath temple is an innovation story of Jain merchant capital, Maru-Gurjara craft and royal tolerance. The 1436 copper plate and 1439 pillar inscription securely name Dharna Shah and architect Deepaka/Dwepa, while Kumbha's grant allowed the temple and settlement to flourish. The famous 1,444 marble pillars and complex halls should be described as architectural observation, not mystical numerology. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Hegewald and conservation studies place Ranakpur in wider Jain temple networks and stone-preservation debates. ACCURACY FLAGS: Dharna Shah's dream of a celestial vimana is devotional tradition; do NOT claim exact worker counts or a precise 50-year construction span as inscriptional fact.

episodes.title: The Second Saka and Rani Karnavati's Chittor
episodes.era: Second siege and saka of Chittor, 1535 CE
episodes.region: Chittor Fort and the Gujarat Sultanate frontier
episodes.logline: Regent for a child Rana, Rani Karnavati faced Bahadur Shah of Gujarat's siege-guns at Chittor, and when the walls failed the second jauhar entered Mewar's memory.
episodes.moral: Honest memory must weigh the legend against the ledger.

sources.citation: Sikandar ibn Muhammad 'Manjhu', Mirat-i-Sikandari, c. 1611 CE
sources.note: Gujarat-Sultanate account of Bahadur Shah's 1535 Chittor campaign and the siege-artillery directed by the Ottoman gunner Rumi Khan.

sources.citation: Muhnot Nainsi, Nainsi ri Khyat, 17th century; Abu'l Fazl, Akbarnama (retrospective notices)
sources.note: Rajput and Mughal-era memory of the second saka and Karnavati's regency for the young sons of Rana Sanga.

sources.citation: G.N. Sharma, Mewar and the Mughal Emperors (1954); Rima Hooja, A History of Rajasthan (2006)
sources.note: Modern reconstruction of the 1535 siege and critical assessment of the Karnavati-Humayun rakhi story.

episodes.notes: The second sack of Chittor took place in 1535, when Bahadur Shah of Gujarat besieged the fort with heavy siege-artillery directed by the Ottoman gunner Rumi Khan. Rani Karnavati (Karmavati), widow of Rana Sanga, held Chittor as regent during Mewar's weakness after Khanwa. Contemporary Gujarat chronicles record the fort's fall and a jauhar; describe the jauhar soberly and attributed, never romanticized. ACCURACY FLAGS: the famous story that Karnavati sent a rakhi to the Mughal emperor Humayun, who then marched to her aid, is NOT found in contemporary sources and appears in much later tradition (notably James Tod, 1829) - present it explicitly as later legend, not attested fact. Humayun did move against Bahadur Shah in 1535, but for imperial-strategic reasons; do not assert the rakhi as its cause. Defender and casualty numbers in the manuscripts are uncertain - flag them. Frame Bahadur Shah's campaign as Gujarat-Mewar power politics, not as a religious war.

episodes.title: Amar Singh I Makes Peace with Jahangir
episodes.era: Mewar-Mughal treaty, 1615 CE
episodes.region: Mewar and the Mughal camp in the Aravallis
episodes.logline: After decades of hill war begun by his father Pratap, Amar Singh I weighed an exhausted people against unbroken pride, and signed the peace that forty years of fighting had not forced.
episodes.moral: Some victories are counted in what a people are spared.

sources.citation: Jahangir, Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri (Memoirs), 1615 entries
sources.note: The Mughal emperor's own record of the terms granted to Amar Singh and the reception of Prince Karan Singh at court.

sources.citation: Mu'tamad Khan, Iqbalnama-i-Jahangiri; Mewar court traditions (Amar Kavya Vamshavali)
sources.note: Mughal-side and Mewar-side accounts of the negotiation led by Prince Khurram, the future Shah Jahan.

sources.citation: G.N. Sharma, Mewar and the Mughal Emperors (1954); Rima Hooja, A History of Rajasthan (2006)
sources.note: Analysis of the 1615 terms and why they uniquely preserved Mewar's distinct honor.

episodes.notes: By 1615 the long Mewar-Mughal war, begun under Pratap, had exhausted both Mewar's people and Mughal patience. Prince Khurram (the future Shah Jahan) pressed the campaign, and Amar Singh I accepted terms recorded in Jahangir's own memoirs: Mewar acknowledged Mughal suzerainty and sent Prince Karan Singh to court, but was uniquely NOT required to give a daughter in marriage to the Mughal house, and Chittor was to be held but never repaired or refortified. Present this as a negotiated peace with honor, neither a simple surrender nor a triumph. ACCURACY FLAGS: later Rajput sentiment frames Amar Singh's peace sometimes as shameful, sometimes as wise - present the debate, do not resolve it moralistically. The tradition that Amar Singh withdrew from public life in sorrow afterward should be attributed, not asserted. Keep the framing political (dynastic suzerainty and terms), not communal.

episodes.title: Panna Dai's Impossible Choice
episodes.era: After the second sack of Chittor, c. 1535-1536 CE
episodes.region: Chittor and Kumbhalgarh
episodes.logline: In Mewar's darkest palace night, tradition says Panna Dai saved young Udai Singh by sacrificing her own child to the usurper's sword.
episodes.moral: Some courage leaves no throne for itself.

sources.citation: Muhnot Nainsi, Nainsi ri Khyat, c. 1660 CE
sources.note: Earliest detailed narrative of Panna Dai's sacrifice, recorded about 125 years later.

sources.citation: G.H. Ojha, Udaypur Rajya ka Itihas (1928); R.V. Somani, History of Mewar (1976)
sources.note: Rajasthani historical syntheses that preserve and assess the tradition.

sources.citation: Rima Hooja, A History of Rajasthan (2006)
sources.note: Recent careful synthesis of Mewar's 16th-century crisis.

episodes.notes: The structural history is secure: Banvir was a real usurper, Udai Singh survived, and Mewar's line continued through him to the founding of Udaipur. The famous details - Panna replacing the prince with her son Chandan, smuggling Udai in a basket, and watching her child die - come from later bardic tradition, especially Nainsi ri Khyat, not contemporary inscriptions or Persian chronicles. This story may be told because it is central to Mewar memory, but it must be flagged as well-established tradition rather than documented fact. The surrounding context includes Bahadur Shah of Gujarat's 1535 sack of Chittor and Rani Karnavati's jauhar; present both soberly without romanticizing death.

episodes.title: Rana Punja and the Bhil Archers
episodes.era: Bhil-Mewar alliance in Pratap's hill war, 1576-1582 CE
episodes.region: Panarwa, Gogunda and the Aravalli hill forests
episodes.logline: At Haldighati and across the long hill war that recovered Mewar, Bhil archers under Rana Punja made the forest alliance a living institution.
episodes.moral: Enduring power grows from alliances of respect.

sources.citation: Abd al-Qadir Badauni, Muntakhab ut-Tawarikh, Vol. II, c. 1596 CE
sources.note: Eyewitness source naming Rana Punja and about 400 Bhil archers at Haldighati.

sources.citation: James Tod, Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan (1829), used cautiously
sources.note: Preserves traditions about the Bhil coronation tilak and Mewar alliance.

sources.citation: Unnithan-Kumar, Identity, Gender, and Poverty (1997); Satish Chandra, Medieval India (2004)
sources.note: Anthropological and historical context for Bhil-Rajput relations and Haldighati.

episodes.notes: This is a social-institution innovation story. Badauni's eyewitness account names Rana Punja of Panarwa and about 400 Bhil archers in Pratap's force at Haldighati. The broader Bhil-Mewar alliance supplied scouts, archers, forest intelligence and guerrilla support, and later tradition gives Bhil chiefs a coronation tilak role for the Maharana. Recent anthropological work treats the alliance as a durable political relationship, not picturesque folklore. ACCURACY FLAGS: no formal treaty document is known; do NOT exoticize the Bhils as mere auxiliaries; Badauni's label for Rana Punja should not be converted into a fixed caste claim without explanation.

episodes.title: Dewair and the Reconquest of the Hills
episodes.era: Battle of Dewair and Mewar's recovery, c. 1582 CE
episodes.region: Dewair, Kumbhalgarh and the Aravalli passes
episodes.logline: Six years after Haldighati, Maharana Pratap came down from the hills at Dewair and took back most of Mewar outpost by outpost - the victory the chronicles rarely headline.
episodes.moral: A long war is decided by endurance, not by one famous battle.

sources.citation: Abu'l Fazl, Akbarnama, and later Mewar chronicles
sources.note: Notices of Pratap's resurgence in the 1580s and the loss of Mughal thanas (outposts) across Mewar.

sources.citation: James Tod, Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan (1829), used cautiously
sources.note: Preserves the Mewari memory of Dewair - Tod's 'Marathon of Mewar' - and the outpost war.

sources.citation: G.N. Sharma, Mewar and the Mughal Emperors (1954); Rima Hooja, A History of Rajasthan (2006)
sources.note: Modern assessment of Pratap's reconquest, its chronology, and its limit - Chittor was never regained.

episodes.notes: After Haldighati (1576) and years of guerrilla war from Chavand, Maharana Pratap counter-attacked around 1582 at Dewair, overrunning Mughal thanas and recovering much of Mewar except Chittor and Mandalgarh. Because Akbar's attention had shifted to the northwest and the Deccan, and Mughal chronicles do not dwell on the reverse, this decisive recovery is far less famous than the drawn battle of Haldighati; restore it without inflating it. ACCURACY FLAGS: the vivid single-combat and 'Marathon of Mewar' framing come largely from Tod's 19th-century Annals and bardic tradition - attribute them and separate them from the securely-attested outcome (outposts fell, Mewar's core was recovered, Chittor was not). Do NOT claim Pratap ever retook Chittor; he did not. Do not give exact army numbers as certain.

episodes.title: Bhama Shah Opens the Treasury
episodes.era: Pratap's post-Haldighati recovery, c. 1578-1580 CE
episodes.region: Mewar and the Oswal-Jain trade networks of Rajasthan and Gujarat
episodes.logline: When Pratap's war needed money more than speeches, Jain financier Bhama Shah turned merchant credit into the fuel of sovereignty.
episodes.moral: Freedom also depends on ledgers, trust and sacrifice.

sources.citation: James Tod, Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan, Vol. I
sources.note: Collector of the bardic tradition about Bhama Shah's donation; use cautiously.

sources.citation: G.H. Ojha, Udaypur Rajya ka Itihas (1928); R.V. Somani, History of Mewar (1976)
sources.note: Biographical and institutional details of Bhama Shah and his family's service.

sources.citation: Thomas A. Timberg, The Marwaris (1978); Jain community and bhandar records discussed in regional studies
sources.note: Context for Rajasthan merchant banking, credit and Oswal-Jain networks.

episodes.notes: Bhama Shah was a real Oswal Jain minister and financier whose support helped sustain Maharana Pratap after Haldighati. His family continued in high Mewar service, making this more than a gift story: it shows how merchant capital, credit networks, tax administration and coinage supported Rajput sovereignty. Bardic accounts give huge sums such as millions of gold and silver coins; treat these as praise-poetry conventions rather than audited figures. RECENT FRAME: economic histories of Rajasthan merchant communities and Jain patronage show that bankers were political actors. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT reduce Bhama Shah to a one-time donor; do NOT claim exact donation amounts; include the broader Oswal-Jain institutional economy.

episodes.title: Sahibdin Paints the Colors of Mewar
episodes.era: Mewar painting school, 1605 CE and c. 1628-1655 CE
episodes.region: Chawand and Udaipur court ateliers
episodes.logline: From the dated Chawand Ragamala to Sahibdin's great manuscripts, Mewar's painters made color a second language of survival.
episodes.moral: A civilization proves itself by what it keeps creating.

sources.citation: Chawand Ragamala manuscript, 1605 CE; Sahibdin's Ramayana, c. 1649-1652 CE
sources.note: Dated colophons and named atelier work form primary evidence for the Mewar school.

sources.citation: Andrew Topsfield, The City Palace Museum, Udaipur: Paintings of Mewar Court Life (1990)
sources.note: Standard catalogue and art-historical reference for Mewar painting.

sources.citation: J.P. Losty, The Art of the Book in India (1982); J.P. Losty and Malini Roy, Mughal India (2012)
sources.note: Comparative manuscript and Rajput-Mughal art context.

episodes.notes: The Mewar school is securely documented by the 1605 Chawand Ragamala, whose colophon dates it to Pratap's hill capital, and by later 17th-century manuscripts associated with named painter Sahibdin. Sahibdin's Ramayana and Bhagavata Purana work for the Udaipur court shows a collaborative atelier adapting older Western Indian/Jain manuscript conventions while absorbing selected Mughal influences. Recent digitization by museums and libraries has improved access to dispersed folios and attribution work. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT name the 1605 Ragamala painters unless the colophon does; do NOT call Mewar the oldest Rajput school without qualification; do NOT present Sahibdin as sole maker of large manuscripts that were workshop productions.

episodes.title: Nannuka Plants the Moon Standard
episodes.era: Founding of the Chandela line, c. 831-845 CE
episodes.region: Khajuraho and Jejakabhukti, Bundelkhand
episodes.logline: A local chief named Nannuka steps out from Pratihara shadow, while later poets wrap his house in moon-born legend.
episodes.moral: Foundations endure when memory is separated from myth.

sources.citation: Khajuraho Inscriptions I and IV, ed. L.F. Kielhorn, Epigraphia Indica I (1892), pp. 122-153
sources.note: Primary prashasti evidence naming Nannuka as founder.

sources.citation: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji, c. 646 CE, notice of Chih-chi-to/Jijhoti
sources.note: Pre-Chandela glimpse of the region's religious landscape.

sources.citation: R.K. Dikshit, The Chandellas of Jejakabhukti (1976), pp. 25-26; Sisirkumar Mitra, The Early Rulers of Khajuraho (1977), pp. 25-30
sources.note: Standard cautious reconstruction of the early line.

episodes.notes: Nannuka is secure because two Khajuraho inscriptions remember him as the dynastic founder, but they are royal praise texts written later, not contemporary annals. He was likely a minor Pratihara feudatory in the Vindhya uplands, ruling a modest center that later became Jejakabhukti; do NOT present the Hemavati and Chandravarman moon-birth story as fact, because it is a later legitimation legend absent from the inscriptions. Recent scholarship treats the early Chandela rise as local state formation and Rajputization in an already sacred landscape, not as a sudden empire born from myth.

episodes.title: Yashovarman Seizes the Rock of Kalinjar
episodes.era: Chandela rise and Kalinjar conquest, c. 925-953 CE
episodes.region: Kalinjar Fort, Khajuraho and the Vindhya plateau
episodes.logline: Yashovarman takes the sacred fortress of Kalinjar and turns a hill kingdom into a power with a stone crown.
episodes.moral: A single strategic place can define a dynasty.

sources.citation: Khajuraho Inscription I, VS 1011/953-54 CE, ed. Kielhorn, Epigraphia Indica I
sources.note: Eulogistic but central source for Yashovarman and Kalinjar.

sources.citation: Karhad copper plate of Rashtrakuta Krishna III
sources.note: Context for the contested politics around Kalanjara and Gurjara.

sources.citation: Dikshit, The Chandellas (1976), pp. 36-51; Mitra, Early Rulers (1977), pp. 36-55
sources.note: Surveys the debate over whom Yashovarman defeated.

episodes.notes: Yashovarman's conquest of Kalanjara, later Kalinjar, is the dynasty's defining secure achievement: later rulers proudly used the title Kalanjaradhipati, Lord of Kalanjara. The Khajuraho prashasti claims victories over distant Gaudas, Khasas, Chedis, Kosalas, Mithilas, Malavas, Kurus and Kashmiris, but these are conventional exaggerations and must not be mapped as literal campaigns.
